questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a VM instance running in a VPC with single-stack subnets. You need to ensure that the VM instance has a fixed IP address so that other services hosted in the same VPC can communicate with the VM. You want to follow Google-recommended practices while minimizing cost. What should you do?

options.text: Promote the existing IP address of the VM to become a static external IP address.
Promote the existing IP address of the VM to become a static internal IP address.
Reserve a new static external IPv6 address and assign the new IP address to the VM.
Reserve a new static external IP address and assign the new IP address to the VM.

questions.explanation: For communication within the same VPC, a static internal IP address is sufficient and cost-effective. External IP addresses incur charges and are unnecessary for internal VPC communication. Promoting the existing internal IP to static maintains the fixed address requirement while following cost-minimization best practices.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are managing a fleet of Compute Engine Linux instances in a Google Cloud project. Your company's engineering team requires SSH access to all instances to perform routine maintenance tasks. You need to manage the SSH access for the engineering team, and you want to minimize operational overhead when engineers join or leave the team. What should you do?

options.text: Create a single SSH key pair to be shared by all engineering team members. Add the public SSH key to project metadata.
Create an SSH key pair for each engineer on the team, and add the public SSH key to the metadata of the relevant instances.
Create a Google Group for all engineering team members, and grant them the Compute Viewer IAM role. Manage group membership when engineers join or leave the team.
Create a Google Group for all engineering team members, and set up OS Login for this group on the project. Manage group membership when engineers join or leave the team.

questions.explanation: Configuring OS Login for a Google Group tied to the engineering team centralizes SSH access management in Cloud Identity/IAM: adding or removing a member from the group instantly grants or revokes their SSH access across every instance, with no per-instance key management. Sharing one key pair or distributing individual keys via instance metadata both require manual updates as staff change, and the Compute Viewer role does not grant SSH/login permissions at all. **Learn more:** [Manage OS Login users](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/oslogin)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to deploy an application on Cloud Run that processes messages from a Cloud Pub/Sub topic. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a Cloud Function that uses a Cloud Pub/Sub trigger on that topic. 2. Call your application on Cloud Run from the Cloud Function for every message.
1. Grant the Pub/Sub Subscriber role to the service account used by Cloud Run. 2. Create a Cloud Pub/Sub subscription for that topic. 3. Make your application pull messages from that subscription.

1. Create a service account. 2. Give the Cloud Run Invoker role to that service account for your Cloud Run application. 3. Create a Cloud Pub/Sub subscription that uses that service account and uses your Cloud Run application as the push endpoint.

1. Deploy your application on Cloud Run on GKE with the connectivity set to Internal. 2. Create a Cloud Pub/Sub subscription for that topic. 3. In the same Google Kubernetes Engine cluster as your application, deploy a container that takes the messages and sends them to your application.

questions.explanation:
For Cloud Run, Google recommends using an authenticated Pub/Sub push subscription rather than a pull subscription, because Cloud Run is a request-driven, scale-to-zero service that receives HTTP requests rather than continuously polling for messages. The recommended configuration is to create a dedicated service account, grant it the Cloud Run Invoker (roles/run.invoker) role on the target Cloud Run service, and then create a Pub/Sub push subscription that uses that service account for authentication (OIDC token) with the Cloud Run service URL configured as the push endpoint. This allows Pub/Sub to securely invoke the Cloud Run service for each message while ensuring only authorized callers can reach the service.

**Learn more:** [Use Pub/Sub with Cloud Run tutorial | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/tutorials/pubsub) · [Authentication for push subscriptions | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/authenticate-push-subscriptions)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a financial services company that operates as a stock market broker. Your company is planning to migrate to Google Cloud. You need to plan the network design in Google Cloud. Your design must:  

• Minimize the latency between all production systems.  

• Minimize costs related to your development environment.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a VPC in the Standard Tier and one in the Premium Tier. Deploy production workloads in the Standard Tier and development workloads in the Premium Tier.
Create a VPC in the Standard Tier and one in the Premium Tier. Deploy development workloads in the Standard Tier and production workloads in the Premium Tier.
Create a VPC in the Premium Tier, and deploy both production and development workloads on this VPC.
Create a VPC in the Standard Tier, and deploy both production and development workloads on this VPC.

questions.explanation: Premium Tier leverages Google's high-performance global backbone network, reducing latency for latency-sensitive production workloads typical of financial services. Standard Tier, with lower costs for internet egress, suits development environments where latency is less critical. This hybrid approach optimizes both performance and cost efficiency across environment tiers.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying an application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that needs to call an external third-party API. You need to provide the external API vendor with a list of IP addresses for their firewall to allow traffic from your application. You want to follow Google-recommended practices and avoid any risk of interrupting traffic to the API due to IP address changes. What should you do?

options.text: Configure your GKE cluster with one node, and set the node to have a static external IP address. Ensure that the GKE cluster autoscaler is off. Send the external IP address of the node to the vendor to be added to the allowlist.
Configure your GKE cluster with private nodes. Configure a Cloud NAT instance with static IP addresses. Provide these IP addresses to the vendor to be added to the allowlist.
Configure your GKE cluster with private nodes. Configure a Cloud NAT instance with dynamic IP addresses. Provide these IP addresses to the vendor to be added to the allowlist.

Configure your GKE cluster with public nodes. Write a Cloud Function that pulls the public IP addresses of each node in the cluster, Trigger the function to run every day with Cloud Scheduler. Send the list to the vendor by email every day.

questions.explanation: Cloud NAT with static IP addresses provides consistent, predictable egress IP addresses for all traffic originating from the GKE cluster. This allows you to provision a fixed allowlist with the third-party API provider without risk of IP changes during cluster scaling. Private GKE nodes combined with Cloud NAT is the recommended approach for outbound firewall integration.

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],After deploying an App Engine application with `gcloud app deploy`, you discover it was deployed to the wrong project. You need to determine why this occurred and identify which project the application was actually deployed to. What should you do?

options.text: Check the app.yaml file for your application and check project settings.
Check the web-application.xml file for your application and check project settings.
Go to Deployment Manager and review settings for deployment of applications.
Go to Cloud Shell and run gcloud config list to review the Google Cloud configuration used for deployment.

questions.explanation:
The `gcloud app deploy` command deploys to whichever project is currently active in your gcloud configuration (the `core/project` property), not necessarily the project you intended. Running `gcloud config list` in Cloud Shell (or any terminal) displays the active gcloud configuration, including the currently set project, account, and other properties used for deployments. This reveals which project was targeted and why, allowing you to correct the active project setting for future deployments. The app.yaml file only configures runtime and service behavior, not the target GCP project; web-application.xml is a Java EE artifact unrelated to gcloud project targeting; and Deployment Manager is a separate infrastructure provisioning service not involved in `gcloud app deploy` operations.

**Learn more:** [gcloud config list](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/config/list) · [Configuring the Google Cloud CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/configurations)

Your company wants to standardize the creation and management of multiple Google Cloud resources using Infrastructure as Code. You want to minimize the amount of repetitive code needed to manage the environment. What should you do?

options.text: Develop templates for the environment using Cloud Deployment Manager.
Use curl in a terminal to send a REST request to the relevant Google API for each individual resource.
Use the Cloud Console interface to provision and manage all related resources.
Create a bash script that contains all requirement steps as gcloud commands.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Deployment Manager is Google Cloud's native Infrastructure as Code service. It allows you to create reusable, parameterized templates (using Jinja2, Python, or YAML) that define configurations for Google Cloud resources. By using templates, you can define a resource configuration once and reuse it across multiple deployments or resources, significantly reducing repetitive code and standardizing resource creation and management across the environment. In contrast, manually issuing REST API calls via curl or writing sequential gcloud commands in a bash script are imperative approaches that require repeating similar code for each resource, and using the Cloud Console is a manual, non-code-based approach that does not scale or support automation/standardization.

**Learn more:** [Creating a template - Deployment Manager](https://cloud.google.com/deployment-manager/docs/configuration/templates/create-basic-template)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure permissions for a group of Compute Engine instances so that they can write data into a specific Cloud Storage bucket. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a service account with an access scope. Use the access scope 'https://www.googleapis.com/auth/devstorage.write_only'.
Create a service account with an access scope. Use the access scope 'https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform'.
Create a service account and add it to the IAM role 'storage.objectCreator' for that bucket.
Create a service account and add it to the IAM role 'storage.objectAdmin' for that bucket.

questions.explanation:
Google recommends managing access to Cloud Storage buckets through IAM roles assigned to service accounts rather than through legacy VM access scopes, and recommends granting the least-privilege role needed for the task. Because the instances only need to write (create) objects in the bucket, the appropriate least-privilege role is roles/storage.objectCreator, which permits creating objects without granting broader permissions such as reading, overwriting, or deleting existing objects (which roles/storage.objectAdmin would allow). Access scopes are considered a legacy, coarse-grained mechanism and are not the recommended way to control resource-level permissions when fine-grained IAM roles are available.

**Learn more:** [IAM roles for Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles) · [Best practices for using service accounts](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-service-accounts)

questions.question: You have just created a new project which will be used to deploy a globally distributed application. You will use Cloud Spanner for data storage. You want to create a Cloud Spanner instance. You want to perform the first step in preparation of creating the instance. What should you do?

options.text: Enable the Cloud Spanner API.
Configure your Cloud Spanner instance to be multi-regional.
Create a new VPC network with subnetworks in all desired regions.
Grant yourself the IAM role of Cloud Spanner Admin.

questions.explanation: Before creating any cloud resource, the corresponding API must be enabled. The Cloud Spanner API is not enabled by default and must be the first step. Configuring multi-regional settings, creating VPC networks, and assigning IAM roles are all downstream tasks that depend on the API being active.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: You have just created a new project which will be used to deploy a globally distributed application. You will use Cloud Spanner for data storage. You want to create a Cloud Spanner instance. You want to perform the first step in preparation of creating the instance. What should you do?

options.text: Disable the flag ג€Delete boot disk when instance is deleted.ג€
Enable delete protection on the instance.
Disable Automatic restart on the instance.
Enable Preemptibility on the instance.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine supports a deletion protection setting (the deletionProtection flag) that can be enabled on a VM instance. When this flag is set, any attempt to delete the instance—whether via the Console, gcloud, or API—fails until deletion protection is explicitly disabled, which requires the compute.instances.create permission. This safeguards production instances from accidental deletion without affecting other instance behavior such as boot disk handling, restart policy, or preemptibility.

**Learn more:** [Prevent accidental VM deletion | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/preventing-accidental-vm-deletion) · [Enable deletion protection for a new VM | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/samples/compute-delete-protection-create)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have created an application that is packaged into a Docker image. You want to deploy the Docker image as a workload on Google Kubernetes Engine. What should you do?

options.text: Upload the image to Cloud Storage and create a Kubernetes Service referencing the image.
Upload the image to Cloud Storage and create a Kubernetes Deployment referencing the image.
Upload the image to Container Registry and create a Kubernetes Service referencing the image.
Upload the image to Container Registry and create a Kubernetes Deployment referencing the image.

questions.explanation: Deploying Docker containers to GKE requires two steps: first, store the image in a container registry (Container Registry or Artifact Registry), then create a Kubernetes Deployment that references that image. A Deployment manages the lifecycle of pods running the container. Cloud Storage is not appropriate for container images; a Service provides only networking, not deployment management.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using Container Registry to centrally store your company's container images in a separate project. In another project, you want to create a Google  

Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You want to ensure that Kubernetes can download images from Container Registry. What should you do?

options.text: In the project where the images are stored, grant the Storage Object Viewer IAM role to the service account used by the Kubernetes nodes.
When you create the GKE cluster, choose the Allow full access to all Cloud APIs option under 'Access scopes'.
Create a service account, and give it access to Cloud Storage. Create a P12 key for this service account and use it as an imagePullSecrets in Kubernetes.
Configure the ACLs on each image in Cloud Storage to give read-only access to the default Compute Engine service account.

questions.explanation: To allow a GKE cluster in one project to pull images from Container Registry in another project, grant the Storage Object Viewer IAM role to the GKE service account in the project where images are stored. Container Registry uses Cloud Storage buckets, and the Storage Object Viewer role provides the minimum necessary permissions to read and pull container images. Full API access is excessive; P12 keys and ACLs are outdated approaches.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has a Google Cloud Platform project that uses BigQuery for data warehousing. Your data science team changes frequently and has few members.  
  
You need to allow members of this team to perform queries, following Google-recommended practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create an IAM entry for each data scientist's user account. 2. Assign the BigQuery jobUser role to the group.
1. Create an IAM entry for each data scientist's user account. 2. Assign the BigQuery dataViewer user role to the group.
1. Create a dedicated Google group in Cloud Identity. 2. Add each data scientist's user account to the group. 3. Assign the BigQuery jobUser role to the group.
1. Create a dedicated Google group in Cloud Identity. 2. Add each data scientist's user account to the group. 3. Assign the BigQuery dataViewer user role to the group.

questions.explanation:
Because group membership changes often, Google recommends creating a dedicated Google group (in Cloud Identity) and adding the data scientists to it, then granting IAM roles to the group rather than to individual user accounts. This avoids having to modify IAM policies each time a team member joins or leaves. To let members actually run queries (BigQuery jobs), the group must be granted the roles/bigquery.jobUser role, which grants permission to run jobs, including queries, within the project. The dataViewer role only provides read access to data and metadata and does not include permission to execute query jobs.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery IAM roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/access-control) · [Grant roles to groups instead of individual users](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/using-iam-securely#use_groups)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are running multiple microservices in a Kubernetes Engine cluster. One microservice is rendering images. The microservice responsible for the image rendering requires a large amount of CPU time compared to the memory it requires. The other microservices are workloads that are optimized for n1-standard machine types. You need to optimize your cluster so that all workloads are using resources as efficiently as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the pods of the image rendering microservice a higher pod priority than the other microservices.
Create a node pool with compute-optimized machine type nodes for the image rendering microservice. Use the node pool with general-purpose machine type nodes for the other microservices.
Use the node pool with general-purpose machine type nodes for the image rendering microservice. Create a node pool with compute-optimized machine type nodes for the other microservices.

Configure the required amount of CPU and memory in the resource requests specification of the image rendering microservice deployment. Keep the resource requests for the other microservices at the default.

questions.explanation: To optimize resource utilization, create a dedicated node pool with compute-optimized machine types for the CPU-intensive image rendering workload. Use the existing general-purpose node pool (n1-standard) for the other microservices. This approach ensures each workload runs on hardware tailored to its resource profile, maximizing efficiency and cost-effectiveness.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are operating several VPC-native Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters that all share the same subnet. The node IP addresses available in that subnet have been used up, and you need to make sure the clusters are still able to scale up in node count when required. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new subnet in the same region as the subnet being used.
Add an alias IP range to the subnet used by the GKE clusters.
Create a new VPC, and set up VPC peering with the existing VPC.
Expand the CIDR range of the relevant subnet for the cluster.

questions.explanation:
When the primary IP range of a subnet used for GKE node IPs is exhausted, Google Cloud allows you to expand that subnet's primary CIDR range to a larger block without recreating the subnet or disrupting running resources — you can only grow it, never shrink it, and the new range must not overlap with other subnets or peered networks. This directly provides the additional node IP addresses needed for the clusters to scale, without requiring new subnets, new VPCs, or peering, and without affecting the existing cluster configuration.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot IP address management in VPC clusters | GKE networking | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/vpc-clusters) · [VPC-native clusters | GKE networking | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs a variety of applications and workloads on Google Cloud, and you are responsible for managing cloud costs. You need to identify a solution that enables you to perform detailed cost analysis. You also must be able to visualize the cost data in multiple ways on the same dashboard. What should you do?

options.text: Use the cost breakdown report with the available filters from Cloud Billing to visualize the data.
Enable the Cloud Billing export to BigQuery, and use Looker Studio to visualize the data.
Run queries in Cloud Monitoring. Create dashboards to visualize the billing metrics.
Enable Cloud Monitoring metrics export to BigQuery, and use Looker to visualize the data.

questions.explanation:
Exporting Cloud Billing data to BigQuery captures granular, itemized cost and usage records that can be queried flexibly, and connecting Looker Studio to that BigQuery dataset enables building a single dashboard with multiple custom visualizations and cross-filtering of the same underlying cost data. The built-in Cloud Billing reports UI only offers a fixed set of filters and chart types on one report at a time, and Cloud Monitoring is designed for operational metrics, not detailed billing/cost line-item analysis.

**Learn more:** [Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the organization and billing administrator for your company. The engineering team currently holds the Project Creator role at the organization level. You want to prevent the engineering team from being able to link projects to the billing account. Only the finance team should be permitted to link a project to a billing account, and the finance team should not be able to make any other changes to projects.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Assign the finance team only the Billing Account User role on the billing account.
Assign the engineering team only the Billing Account User role on the billing account.
Assign the finance team the Billing Account User role on the billing account and the Project Billing Manager role on the organization.
Assign the engineering team the Billing Account User role on the billing account and the Project Billing Manager role on the organization.

questions.explanation:
Linking a project to a billing account in Google Cloud requires permissions from two separate IAM policies: billing.resourceAssociations.create on the billing account (granted by the Billing Account User role) and resourcemanager.projects.createBillingAssignment on the project (granted by the Project Billing Manager role). The Project Billing Manager role grants no rights over project resources beyond associating/disassociating billing accounts, so granting it at the organization level (so it applies to all projects through IAM inheritance) combined with Billing Account User on the billing account gives the finance team exactly the ability to link projects to billing -- and nothing more. The engineering team's Project Creator role does not include any billing permissions, so as long as they are not separately granted Billing Account User or Project Billing Manager, they remain unable to link projects to the billing account.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Billing access control and permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/billing-access) · [Enable, disable, or change billing for a project](https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/modify-project)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the Organization Administrator for your company's Google Cloud resources. Your company has strict compliance rules that require you to be notified about any modifications to files and documents hosted on Cloud Storage. In a recent incident, one of your team members was able to modify files and you did not receive any notifications, causing other production jobs to fail. You must ensure that you receive notifications for all changes to files and documents in Cloud Storage while minimizing management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: View Cloud Audit logs for all Cloud Storage files in Logs Explorer. Filter by Admin Activity logs.
Enable Cloud Storage object versioning on your bucket. Configure Pub/Sub notifications for your Cloud Storage buckets.
Enable versioning on the Cloud Storage bucket. Set up a custom script that scans versions of Cloud Storage objects being modified and alert the admin by using the script.
Configure Object change notifications on the Cloud Storage buckets. Send the events to Pub/Sub.

questions.explanation: Configuring Cloud Storage bucket notifications to publish every object create, update, and delete event to a Pub/Sub topic is a low-overhead, automated way to guarantee an alert fires for every modification, since a subscriber can immediately route the message to an alerting system. Enabling Object Versioning does not itself generate a notification—it only retains prior object generations for recovery—so pairing it with Pub/Sub adds cost and complexity that the notification requirement does not call for. **Learn more:** [Pub/Sub notifications for Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/pubsub-notifications)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution

options.text: Add a bucket lifecycle rule that archives data with newer versions after 30 days to Coldline Storage.
Add a bucket lifecycle rule that archives data with newer versions after 30 days to Nearline Storage.
Add a bucket lifecycle rule that archives data from regional storage after 30 days to Coldline Storage.
Add a bucket lifecycle rule that archives data from regional storage after 30 days to Nearline Storage.

questions.explanation:
Nearline Storage is optimized for data that is accessed less than once a month and has a 30-day minimum storage duration, aligning with both the 30-day archival threshold and the monthly access/reporting pattern described, while still allowing for the occasional updates at month-end without incurring early deletion penalties. Because the requirement concerns objects with multiple versions (previous/noncurrent versions), the lifecycle rule must be configured using a version-based condition (such as the number of newer versions present) rather than a condition based on the object's originating storage class, which is what distinguishes this from rules that simply migrate all regional/Standard storage objects. Coldline Storage, by contrast, is intended for data accessed roughly once per quarter and carries a 90-day minimum storage duration, making it less cost-effective for monthly-accessed and periodically updated archived versions.

**Learn more:** [Object Lifecycle Management | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle) · [Storage classes | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)

Your company has a large volume of unstructured data stored in various file formats. You need to perform ETL transformations on this data, and you must first make the data accessible on Google Cloud so that it can be processed by a Dataflow job. What should you do?

options.text: Upload the data to BigQuery using the bq command line tool.
Upload the data to Cloud Storage using the gsutil command line tool.
Upload the data into Cloud SQL using the import function in the console.
Upload the data into Cloud Spanner using the import function in the console.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage is Google Cloud's object storage service designed to hold data of any format, including unstructured files, and it integrates natively as a source and sink for Dataflow pipelines. The gsutil command-line tool is the standard utility for uploading data into Cloud Storage buckets. In contrast, BigQuery is optimized for structured, tabular data and requires defined schemas; Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner are relational database services intended for structured transactional data, not arbitrary unstructured files. Therefore, staging the data in Cloud Storage via gsutil is the correct way to make it accessible for a Dataflow ETL job.

**Learn more:** [Dataflow documentation - Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs) · [gsutil tool - Cloud Storage documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/gsutil)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are running an application across multiple virtual machine instances within a managed instance group, with autoscaling enabled. The autoscaling policy adds instances to the group when CPU utilization exceeds 80%, continuing to add VMs until either the group reaches its maximum size of five VMs or CPU utilization drops back to 80%. The HTTP health check configured for the instances has an initial delay of 30 seconds.  
  
You notice that the VM instances take approximately three minutes to become available to end users. When the instance group autoscales, it ends up provisioning more instances than are actually required to handle the current level of end-user traffic.  
  
You want to ensure that the instance group size is properly maintained during autoscaling. What should you do?

options.text: Set the maximum number of instances to 1.
Decrease the maximum number of instances to 3.
Use a TCP health check instead of an HTTP health check.
Increase the initial delay of the HTTP health check to 200 seconds.

questions.explanation:
The autoscaler needs accurate signals about which instances are fully operational before factoring their utilization data into scaling decisions. Because the VMs take about three minutes (180 seconds) to become ready, but the health check's initial delay is only 30 seconds, the autoscaler can act on data from instances that have not yet finished initializing, causing it to over-provision the group with more VMs than are actually needed. Google Cloud recommends configuring the initial delay of the health check to be longer than the actual startup/warm-up time of the instances so the autoscaler properly excludes not-yet-ready instances from its scaling calculations. Setting the initial delay to 200 seconds exceeds the observed three-minute boot time, allowing the autoscaler to correctly assess instance health and utilization and maintain an appropriately sized group. Simply lowering the maximum instance count only masks the symptom and limits legitimate scaling capacity, while switching to a TCP health check does not address the underlying initialization-timing issue.

**Learn more:** [Understand autoscaler decisions | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler/understanding-autoscaler-decisions) · [Autoscaling groups of instances | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler)

You are working with a user to set up an application in a new VPC that sits behind a firewall. The user is concerned about data egress, and you want to configure the fewest open egress ports possible. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a low-priority (65534) rule that blocks all egress and a high-priority rule (1000) that allows only the appropriate ports.
Set up a high-priority (1000) rule that pairs both ingress and egress ports.
Set up a high-priority (1000) rule that blocks all egress and a low-priority (65534) rule that allows only the appropriate ports.
Set up a high-priority (1000) rule to allow the appropriate ports.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud VPC firewall rules are evaluated in order of priority, where a lower numeric value indicates higher precedence. Every VPC network also has an implied allow-all-egress rule at priority 65535. To minimize open egress ports, you should create a high-priority rule (priority 1000, which is evaluated first) that explicitly allows only the specific ports required by the application, combined with a low-priority rule (priority 65534) that denies all other egress traffic. Because the allow rule at priority 1000 is evaluated before the deny rule at priority 65534, only the specified ports remain open, while the deny rule blocks everything else that isn't explicitly permitted, effectively overriding the network's implied allow-all-egress default and enforcing least-privilege network access.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules | Cloud Next Generation Firewall | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) · [Use VPC firewall rules | Cloud Next Generation Firewall | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewalls)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are working with a Cloud SQL MySQL database at your company. You need to retain a month-end copy of the database for three years for audit purposes.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set up an export job for the first of the month. Write the export file to an Archive class Cloud Storage bucket.
Save the automatic first-of-the-month backup for three years. Store the backup file in an Archive class Cloud Storage bucket.
Set up an on-demand backup for the first of the month. Write the backup to an Archive class Cloud Storage bucket.
Convert the automatic first-of-the-month backup to an export file. Write the export file to a Coldline class Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL automated and on-demand backups are managed as part of the instance's backup lifecycle and cannot be exported directly or retained independently as a standalone artifact for a fixed multi-year period — you cannot export a backup, only instance data. To create a durable, independently controlled month-end copy of the database for a 3-year audit retention requirement, you should schedule a Cloud SQL export job to run on the first of each month, writing the resulting SQL dump file to a Cloud Storage bucket. Using the Archive storage class is appropriate because it offers the lowest cost per GB among Cloud Storage classes and is intended for data that is accessed less than once a year, such as long-term compliance and audit archives, while still meeting durability requirements over a multi-year retention period.

**Learn more:** [Export and import using SQL dump files | Cloud SQL for MySQL | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/import-export/import-export-sql) · [Cloud SQL backups overview | Cloud SQL for MySQL | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backups)

Because the VMs take about three minutes (180 seconds) to become ready, but the health check's initial delay is only 30 seconds, the autoscaler can act on data from instances that have not yet finished initializing, causing it to over-provision the group with more VMs than are actually needed. Google Cloud recommends configuring the initial delay of the health check to be longer than the actual startup/warm-up time of the instances so the autoscaler properly excludes not-yet-ready instances from its scaling calculations. Setting the initial delay to 200 seconds exceeds the observed three-minute boot time, allowing the autoscaler to correctly assess instance health and utilization and maintain an appropriately sized group. Google Cloud VPC firewall rules are evaluated in order of priority, where a lower numeric value indicates higher precedence. Every VPC network also has an implied allow-all-egress rule at priority 65535. To minimize open egress ports, you should create a high-priority rule (priority 1000, which is evaluated first) that explicitly allows only the specific ports required by the application, combined with a low-priority rule (priority 65534) that denies all other egress traffic. Because the allow rule at priority 1000 is evaluated before the deny rule at priority 65534, only the specified ports remain open, while the deny rule blocks everything else that isn't explicitly permitted, effectively overriding the network's implied allow-all-egress default and enforcing least-privilege network access.

Your organization follows a hybrid cloud strategy, with some applications running on Google Cloud. A VPN tunnel links your VPC in Google Cloud to your company's on-premises network. Several applications hosted in Google Cloud must connect to an on-premises database server, and you want to avoid having to update the IP configuration across all of your applications whenever the database's IP address changes.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure Cloud NAT for all subnets of your VPC to be used when egressing from the VM instances.
Create a private zone on Cloud DNS, and configure the applications with the DNS name.
Configure the IP of the database as custom metadata for each instance, and query the metadata server.
Query the Compute Engine internal DNS from the applications to retrieve the IP of the database.

questions.explanation:
Creating a Cloud DNS private zone lets you map a stable DNS hostname to the on-premises database's IP address. Applications are then configured to reference the DNS name rather than a hard-coded IP. If the database's IP address changes, you simply update the single DNS record in the private zone, and every application automatically resolves the new IP the next time it performs a DNS lookup — no per-application reconfiguration is required. Cloud NAT only affects outbound egress translation for instances without external IPs and does not provide name resolution for on-premises resources. Custom instance metadata would still require manual updates on every instance whenever the IP changes, providing no abstraction benefit. Compute Engine's internal DNS resolves only internal Google Cloud VM names, not external on-premises hosts, so it cannot be used to reach the on-premises database.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/best-practices) · [Cloud DNS overview](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/overview)

You have deployed an application on a single Compute Engine instance. The application writes its logs to disk. Users are now reporting errors with the application, and you need to diagnose the problem. What should you do?

options.text: Navigate to Cloud Logging and view the application logs.
Connect to the instance's serial console and read the application logs.
Configure a Health Check on the instance and set a Low Healthy Threshold value.
Install and configure the Cloud Logging Agent and view the logs from Cloud Logging.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine VM images do not include a logging agent by default, so log files written to local disk by an application are not automatically forwarded to Cloud Logging. To view and analyze these logs centrally in Cloud Logging, you must install and configure the Cloud Logging agent (or the Ops Agent) on the instance, specifying the application's log file paths so the agent tails and streams the entries into Cloud Logging, where you can then search and diagnose the errors. Simply navigating to Cloud Logging without an agent configured would not surface these disk-based application logs, and the serial console or health check settings are not designed for retrieving or centralizing custom application log data.

**Learn more:** [Installing the Cloud Logging agent on individual VMs](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging/installation) · [Troubleshoot the Logging agent](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging/troubleshooting)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run an application that accepts SSL-encrypted TCP traffic on port 443. Its clients are distributed worldwide, and you want to minimize the latency they experience. Which load balancing option should you choose?

options.text: HTTPS Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
SSL Proxy Load Balancer
Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer. Add a firewall rule allowing ingress traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on the target instances.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud's SSL Proxy Load Balancer is a global, external load balancer built for encrypted, non-HTTP(S) TCP traffic on standard ports such as 443. It terminates SSL/TLS at Google's globally distributed edge locations (Google Front Ends) nearest each client and then forwards traffic over Google's private backbone to the closest available healthy backend, which minimizes the round-trip latency experienced by geographically dispersed clients. This makes it the appropriate choice when the workload is SSL-encrypted TCP (not HTTP/HTTPS) and clients are spread across the globe, unlike regional pass-through load balancers or internal load balancers, which do not provide global edge termination.

**Learn more:** [Proxy Network Load Balancer overview | Cloud Load Balancing | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/proxy-network-load-balancer) · [Choose a load balancer | Cloud Load Balancing | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/choosing-load-balancer)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have virtual machines running in a subnet whose subnet mask is 255.255.255.240. This subnet currently has no available IP addresses left, and you need 10 more IP addresses for new VMs. Both the existing VMs and the new VMs must be able to communicate with each other without requiring any additional routes. What should you do?

options.text: Use gcloud to expand the IP range of the current subnet.
Delete the subnet, and recreate it using a wider range of IP addresses.
Create a new project. Use Shared VPC to share the current network with the new project.
Create a new subnet with the same starting IP but a wider range to overwrite the current subnet.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud allows you to expand the primary IP range of an existing subnet in place (for example, with `gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range`), as long as the new range is a superset of the current one and doesn't overlap with other subnets in the network. This preserves the subnet's identity and existing VM configurations while providing additional IP addresses, and because all VMs remain within the same subnet/VPC network, they can reach each other directly without any extra routes being configured.

**Learn more:** [Expand a subnet's primary IP range](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/create-modify-vpc-networks#expand-subnet)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Management has selected Google Cloud as the company’s strategic cloud provider. You must provision Google Cloud identities for every employee in the IT and Data departments, but not for employees in other departments. This access must update automatically when employees move departments, join, or leave the company. All employees are centrally managed in an LDAP directory, with one organizational unit (OU) per department. What should you do?

options.text: Develop a containerized application that reads user information from the relevant OUs in the LDAP directory. Use the Directory API to create accounts in Cloud Identity for new users. Deploy the application as a scheduled Cloud Run job.

Develop a containerized application that reads user information from the relevant OUs in the LDAP directory. Use the Admin SDK to synchronize user accounts in Identity Platform with the LDAP directory. Deploy the application as a scheduled Cloud Run job.
Create a CSV file with the users from the relevant OUs. Upload the CSV file to Cloud Identity. Instruct your Human Resources department to repeat this process for any employee changes.
Configure Google Cloud Directory Sync to synchronize the relevant OUs between the LDAP directory and Cloud Identity. Set up a scheduled task that triggers a provisioning run.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS) synchronizes users from LDAP directories to Cloud Identity and can be configured to include the relevant organizational units. A scheduled provisioning run keeps Cloud Identity aligned with employee joiner, mover, and leaver changes in the LDAP source of truth. [Cloud Identity editions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity/docs/editions)

**Learn more:** [Cloud Identity editions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity/docs/editions) · [Active Directory user account provisioning](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/identity/federating-gcp-with-active-directory-synchronizing-user-accounts)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning to migrate the following on-premises data management solutions to Google Cloud:  
  
• One MySQL cluster for your main database  

• Apache Kafka for your event streaming platform  

• One Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database for your analytical and reporting needs  
  
You want to implement Google-recommended solutions for the migration. You need to ensure that the new solutions provide global scalability and require minimal operational and infrastructure management. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate from MySQL to Cloud SQL, from Kafka to Pub/Sub, and from Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to BigQuery.
Migrate from MySQL to Cloud Spanner, from Kafka to Pub/Sub, and from Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to BigQuery.
Migrate from MySQL to Cloud Spanner, from Kafka to Memorystore, and from Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to Cloud SQL.
Migrate from MySQL to Cloud SQL, from Kafka to Memorystore, and from Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to Cloud SQL.

questions.explanation: For global scalability and minimal management, Cloud Spanner is the only viable option for the MySQL workload—Cloud SQL is single-region and lacks horizontal scale. Cloud Pub/Sub replaces Kafka for event streaming, and BigQuery serves analytics with auto-scaling. This architecture meets both scalability and operational simplicity requirements.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company's security vulnerability management policy wants a member of the security team to have visibility into vulnerabilities and other OS metadata for a specific Compute Engine instance. This Compute Engine instance hosts a critical application in your Google Cloud project. You need to implement your company's security vulnerability management policy. What should you do?

options.text: • Ensure that the Ops Agent is installed on the Compute Engine instance.• Create a custom metric in the Cloud Monitoring dashboard.• Provide the security team member with access to this dashboard.
• Ensure that the Ops Agent is installed on the Compute Engine instance.• Provide the security team member roles/osconfig.inventoryViewer permission.
• Ensure that the OS Config agent is installed on the Compute Engine instance.• Provide the security team member roles/osconfig.vulnerabilityReportViewer permission.
• Ensure that the OS Config agent is installed on the Compute Engine instance.• Create a log sink to BigQuery dataset.• Provide the security team member with access to this dataset.

questions.explanation: OS Config agent is specifically designed for OS-level vulnerability scanning and inventory management, providing the visibility required for security vulnerability management. The Ops Agent focuses on metrics and logs for performance monitoring, not vulnerability assessment. The correct IAM role (roles/osconfig.vulnerabilityReportViewer) grants granular access to vulnerability reports without broader permissions.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are running a web application on Cloud Run for a few hundred users. Some of your users complain that the initial web page of the application takes much longer to load than the following pages. You want to follow Google’s recommendations to mitigate the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Set the minimum number of instances for your Cloud Run service to 3.
Set the concurrency number to 1 for your Cloud Run service.
Set the maximum number of instances for your Cloud Run service to 100.
Update your web application to use the protocol HTTP/2 instead of HTTP/1.1.

questions.explanation: Setting a minimum number of instances (e.g., 3) for Cloud Run keeps instances warm and ready to handle requests immediately, eliminating cold-start delays on initial requests. Cold starts occur when the platform must instantiate new containers. Setting concurrency to 1 (B) reduces throughput; maximum instances (C) don't prevent cold starts; HTTP/2 (D) has minimal impact on the initial page load problem.

You deployed an application on a managed instance group in Compute Engine. The application accepts Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) traffic on port 389 and requires you to preserve the IP address of the client who is making a request. You want to expose the application to the internet by using a load balancer. What should you do?

options.text: Expose the application by using an external TCP Network Load Balancer.
Expose the application by using a TCP Proxy Load Balancer.
Expose the application by using an SSL Proxy Load Balancer.
Expose the application by using an internal TCP Network Load Balancer.

questions.explanation: An External TCP Network Load Balancer is a passthrough (non-proxy) load balancer that preserves the client's source IP address, which is essential for this application. TCP Proxy Load Balancers (B) are proxy-based and do not natively preserve client IP without additional configuration. SSL Proxy (C) is for HTTPS/SSL. Internal (D) would not expose to the internet.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning to deploy an application to Google Cloud. Your application processes asynchronous events from Google services and must be accessible from the public Internet. You need to identify how to deploy your application. You want to follow a standardized process while minimizing development costs. You also want to have no costs when your workloads are not in use. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy your code to GKE. Use Pub/Sub for event delivery.
Deploy your code to Compute Engine. Use Pub/Sub for event delivery.
Deploy your code to GKE. Use Eventarc for event delivery.
Deploy your code to Cloud Run. Use Eventarc for event delivery.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run provides a fully serverless environment that scales to zero when idle, incurring no costs during periods of inactivity. Eventarc handles event delivery from Google Cloud services and integrates natively with Cloud Run. Together, they provide a standardized serverless event-driven architecture requiring minimal development and operational overhead.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying an application to a Compute Engine VM that belongs to a managed instance group. The application must always be running, but only one instance of the VM should run per GCP project. How should you configure the instance group?

options.text: Set autoscaling to On, set the minimum number of instances to 1, and then set the maximum number of instances to 1.
Set autoscaling to Off, set the minimum number of instances to 1, and then set the maximum number of instances to 1.
Set autoscaling to On, set the minimum number of instances to 1, and then set the maximum number of instances to 2.
Set autoscaling to Off, set the minimum number of instances to 1, and then set the maximum number of instances to 2.

questions.explanation:
A managed instance group provides self-healing so that if the single VM instance fails or is deleted, the group automatically recreates it, keeping the application always running. To guarantee that exactly one instance runs (never scaling beyond one), autoscaling must be turned Off, and both the minimum and maximum number of instances should be set to 1. This fixes the group's target size at exactly one instance per project while still benefiting from the group's automatic instance recreation behavior.

**Learn more:** [Basic scenarios for creating managed instance groups (MIGs) | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/creating-groups-of-managed-instances) · [Autoscaling groups of instances | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your digital media company stores a large number of video files on-premises. Each video file ranges from 100 MB to 100 GB. You are currently storing 150 TB of video data in your on-premises network, with no room for expansion. You need to migrate all infrequently accessed video files older than one year to Cloud Storage to ensure that on-premises storage remains available for new files. You must also minimize costs and control bandwidth usage. What should you do?

options.text: Use Storage Transfer Service to move the data from the selected on-premises file storage systems to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Use Transfer Appliance to request an appliance. Load the data locally, and ship the appliance back to Google for ingestion into Cloud Storage.

Set up a Cloud Interconnect connection between the on-premises network and Google Cloud. Establish a private endpoint for Filestore access. Transfer the data from the existing Network File System (NFS) to Filestore.

Create a Cloud Storage bucket. Establish an Identity and Access Management (IAM) role with write permissions to the bucket. Use the gsutil tool to directly copy files over the network to Cloud Storage.

questions.explanation: Storage Transfer Service is Google's managed path for on-premises-to-Cloud-Storage migrations; run with an on-premises transfer agent, it lets you schedule the copy and cap network bandwidth so the transfer does not saturate the link, at no extra service cost. Transfer Appliance is reserved for situations where available network bandwidth is too limited to move the data online within a reasonable time, and it does not offer the fine-grained bandwidth throttling the requirement asks for. **Learn more:** [Storage Transfer Service overview](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage Google Cloud infrastructure using Terraform, and the Terraform configuration files are kept in a Git repository. You need to implement a solution that lets multiple team members work on the Terraform configurations concurrently without conflicts, while ensuring sensitive values are not stored on local machines. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a local backend in Terraform, and deploy all changes by using a shared account on a bastion server.
Configure a Cloud Storage backend in Terraform.
Configure a local backend in Terraform, and store the state file in a Git repository.
Configure a local backend in Terraform, and manually share the Terraform state file with team members after every change.

questions.explanation: Terraform’s Cloud Storage backend keeps the shared state remotely in a Google Cloud Storage bucket and supports state locking, which prevents concurrent Terraform operations from conflicting. It also avoids using a local state file as the authoritative shared state, reducing persistence of sensitive state values on team members’ machines.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a single binary application that you want to run on Google Cloud Platform. You have decided to automatically scale the application based on the underlying infrastructure's CPU usage. Your organization's policies require you to use virtual machines directly.  
  
You need to ensure that the application scaling is operationally efficient and completed as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster, and use horizontal pod autoscaling to scale the application.
Create an instance template, and use the template in a managed instance group with autoscaling configured.
Create an instance template, and use the template in a managed instance group that scales up and down based on the time of day.
Use a set of third-party tools to build automation around scaling the application up and down, based on Stackdriver CPU usage monitoring.

questions.explanation:
Managed instance groups (MIGs) built from an instance template provide built-in autoscaling based on CPU utilization (or other metrics) without requiring any custom tooling or scripts. This is the native, fully-managed GCP mechanism for scaling VM-based workloads, satisfying the requirement to use VMs directly (as opposed to GKE) while being the fastest and most operationally efficient approach, since Google Cloud handles the scaling logic automatically once the autoscaling policy is configured on the MIG.

**Learn more:** [Autoscaling groups of instances](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a website hosted on the App Engine standard environment. You want 1% of your users to see a new test version of the website, and you want to minimize complexity. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the new version in the same application and use the --migrate option.
Deploy the new version in the same application and use the --splits option to give a weight of 99 to the current version and a weight of 1 to the new version.
Create a new App Engine application in the same project. Deploy the new version in that application. Use the App Engine library to proxy 1% of the requests to the new version.
Create a new App Engine application in the same project. Deploy the new version in that application. Configure your network load balancer to send 1% of the traffic to that new application.

questions.explanation:
App Engine lets you deploy multiple versions of a service within the same application and then split traffic among them by percentage using the `--splits` option (or `gcloud app services set-traffic`). This built-in traffic-splitting feature is the simplest way to route a small percentage of requests—such as 1%—to a new version while keeping the rest on the current version, with no need for a separate application, custom proxy code, or an external load balancer.

**Learn more:** [Splitting Traffic | App Engine documentation](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/splitting-traffic)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is running a three-tier web application on virtual machines that use a MySQL database. You need to create an estimated total cost of cloud infrastructure to run this application on Google Cloud instances and Cloud SQL. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google spreadsheet with multiple Google Cloud resource combinations. On a separate sheet, import the current Google Cloud prices and use these prices for the calculations within formulas.
Use the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator and select the Cloud Operations template to define your web application with as much detail as possible.

Implement a similar architecture on Google Cloud, and run a reasonable load test on a smaller scale. Check the billing information, and calculate the estimated costs based on the real load your system usually handles.

Use the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator to determine the cost of every Google Cloud resource you expect to use. Use similar size instances for the web server, and use your current on-premises machines as a comparison for Cloud SQL.

questions.explanation: The Google Cloud Pricing Calculator is the standard tool for estimating cloud costs. You input your planned resources (compute instances similar to on-premises sizes, Cloud SQL for the database) and the calculator returns accurate pricing. A spreadsheet approach is error-prone; 'Cloud Operations template' does not exist as a Pricing Calculator feature.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure 10 Compute Engine instances so they remain available during maintenance events. The requirements specify that:  
  
- The instances should attempt to automatically restart if they crash.  
- The instances should be highly available, including during system maintenance.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create an instance template for the instances. Set the 'Automatic Restart' to on. Set the 'On-host maintenance' to Migrate VM instance. Add the instance template to an instance group.
Create an instance template for the instances. Set 'Automatic Restart' to off. Set 'On-host maintenance' to Terminate VM instances. Add the instance template to an instance group.
Create an instance group for the instances. Set the 'Autohealing' health check to healthy (HTTP).
Create an instance group for the instance. Verify that the 'Advanced creation options' setting for 'do not retry machine creation' is set to off.

questions.explanation:
In Compute Engine, the 'Automatic Restart' setting controls whether a VM is automatically restarted if it crashes or is terminated for a reason other than a user-initiated action, and the 'On-host maintenance' setting controls what happens to the VM when Google performs infrastructure maintenance on the host. Setting 'On-host maintenance' to 'Migrate VM instance' enables live migration, which transparently moves the running VM to another host during maintenance without requiring a reboot, keeping it available. Combining 'Automatic Restart: on' with 'On-host maintenance: Migrate VM instance' in an instance template, then applying that template to an instance group, satisfies both requirements—automatic recovery from crashes and continuous availability during host maintenance—for all 10 instances consistently. Autohealing health checks (choice C) address application-level failures, not host maintenance, and instance-group creation retry settings (choice D) address VM creation failures, not ongoing availability during maintenance.

**Learn more:** [Setting instance scheduling options - Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/setting-instance-scheduling-options) · [Live migration of VM instances](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/live-migration-process)

You are building an application that will store relational data from users located around the world. Your CTO is concerned about scaling requirements because the eventual size of the user base is unknown. You need to implement a database solution that can scale along with your user growth while requiring minimal configuration changes. Which storage solution should you use?

options.text: Cloud SQL
Cloud Spanner
Cloud Firestore
Cloud Datastore

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a fully managed, horizontally scalable relational database service that supports SQL semantics and strong global consistency. Unlike Cloud SQL, which is limited by the resources of a single instance and requires manual intervention (such as adding read replicas or sharding) to scale beyond that, Cloud Spanner can scale horizontally by adding compute capacity/nodes with minimal configuration changes, making it well suited for relational workloads with unpredictable, potentially massive global growth. Cloud Firestore and Cloud Datastore, while highly scalable, are NoSQL document databases and do not fit the requirement for storing relational data.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner overview](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/overview) · [Choosing a storage option - Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/products/databases)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application that is currently processing transactions by using a group of managed VM instances. You need to migrate the application so that it is serverless and scalable. You want to implement an asynchronous transaction processing system, while minimizing management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Install Kafka on VM instances to acknowledge incoming transactions. Use Cloud Run to process transactions.
Use Pub/Sub to acknowledge incoming transactions. Use VM instances to process transactions.
Use Pub/Sub to acknowledge incoming transactions. Use Cloud Run to process transactions.
Install Kafka on VM instances to acknowledge incoming transactions. Use VM instances to process transactions.

questions.explanation: Pub/Sub provides a fully managed, serverless message queue for asynchronous transaction handling, while Cloud Run offers serverless compute for processing those transactions with automatic scaling. This architecture eliminates infrastructure management overhead and scales smoothly from zero to high throughput, meeting the requirement for serverless, asynchronous processing with minimal management.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Bigtable instance that consists of three nodes that store personally identifiable information (PII) data. You need to log all read or write operations, including any metadata or configuration reads of this database table, in your company’s Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. What should you do?

options.text: • Navigate to Cloud Monitoring in the Google Cloud console, and create a custom monitoring job for the Bigtable instance to track all changes.• Create an alert by using webhook endpoints, with the SIEM endpoint as a receiver.

• Navigate to the Audit Logs page in the Google Cloud console, and enable Admin Write logs for the Bigtable instance.• Create a Cloud Functions instance to export logs from Cloud Logging to your SIEM.

• Navigate to the Audit Logs page in the Google Cloud console, and enable Data Read, Data Write and Admin Read logs for the Bigtable instance.• Create a Pub/Sub topic as a Cloud Logging sink destination, and add your SIEM as a subscriber to the topic.

• Install the Ops Agent on the Bigtable instance during configuration.• Create a service account with read permissions for the Bigtable instance.• Create a custom Dataflow job with this service account to export logs to the company’s SIEM system.

questions.explanation: Audit logging for Bigtable requires enabling Data Read, Data Write, and Admin Read logs in Cloud Logging. Creating a Pub/Sub topic as a sink destination allows secure forwarding of logs to external SIEM systems as subscribers. Cloud Monitoring is for metrics, not audit logs; Cloud Functions would add operational overhead for log export.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution

options.text: Provision a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot cluster.
Provision a fleet of Compute Engine instances and install Kubernetes.
Provision a Standard regional Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster.
Provision a Standard zonal Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster.

questions.explanation: GKE Autopilot offloads node provisioning, scaling, and patching to Google, leaving teams to simply deploy their containerized microservices with minimal operational effort; deploying the cluster privately keeps workloads unreachable from the public internet. Compute Engine with self-managed Kubernetes and standard GKE clusters both require ongoing node and infrastructure management that Autopilot removes. **Learn more:** [GKE Autopilot overview](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/autopilot-overview)

You are in charge of provisioning access for all Google Cloud users in your organization. Your company recently acquired a startup company that has their own Google Cloud organization. You need to ensure that your Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) have the same project permissions in the startup company's organization as in your own organization. What should you do?

options.text: In the Google Cloud console for your organization, select Create role from selection, and choose destination as the startup company's organization.
In the Google Cloud console for the startup company, select Create role from selection and choose source as the startup company's Google Cloud organization.
Use the gcloud iam roles copy command, and provide the Organization ID of the startup company's Google Cloud Organization as the destination.
Use the gcloud iam roles copy command, and provide the project IDs of all projects in the startup company's organization as the destination.

questions.explanation: The gcloud iam roles copy command is designed to copy custom IAM roles between organizations, preserving permissions exactly. Specifying the destination organization ID ensures roles are replicated to the acquired startup's organization. This maintains consistent access control for SREs across both organizations without manual recreation.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Every employee in your company has a Google account. Your operations team must manage a large number of Compute Engine instances, and each team member only needs administrative access to these servers. Your security team wants the credential deployment process to be operationally efficient, while also being able to determine who accessed any given instance. What should you do?

options.text: Generate a new SSH key pair. Give the private key to each member of your team. Configure the public key in the metadata of each instance.
Ask each member of the team to generate a new SSH key pair and to send you their public key. Use a configuration management tool to deploy those keys on each instance.
Ask each member of the team to generate a new SSH key pair and to add the public key to their Google account. Grant the ג€compute.osAdminLoginג€ role to the Google group corresponding to this team.

Generate a new SSH key pair. Give the private key to each member of your team. Configure the public key as a project-wide public SSH key in your Cloud Platform project and allow project-wide public SSH keys on each instance.

questions.explanation:
OS Login is designed for exactly this use case: it lets each user register their own SSH public key on their personal Google account, and grants server access by assigning IAM roles (such as roles/compute.osAdminLogin for admin/sudo-level access) to a Google Group rather than distributing or copying keys to every instance individually. This scales efficiently to large fleets of instances since access is centrally managed through IAM/group membership and automatically updated or revoked when group membership changes, eliminating manual key deployment. Additionally, OS Login integrates with Cloud Audit Logs, recording login events tied to each user's Google identity, satisfying the requirement to determine who accessed a given instance — something plain metadata-based SSH keys (project-wide or per-instance) cannot reliably provide.

**Learn more:** [About OS Login | Compute Engine Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/oslogin) · [Manage OS Login in an organization | Compute Engine Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/oslogin/manage-oslogin-in-an-org)

You are performing a monthly security check of your Google Cloud environment and want to know who has access to view data stored in your Google Cloud  

Project. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Audit Logs for all APIs that are related to data storage.
Review the IAM permissions for any role that allows for data access.
Review the Identity-Aware Proxy settings for each resource.
Create a Data Loss Prevention job.

questions.explanation: To determine who currently has access to view data, you must review the IAM permissions for the project. IAM is the authoritative source for current access rights. Audit logs show historical access patterns, but do not directly answer the question of who is currently authorized. Identity-Aware Proxy and Data Loss Prevention are not relevant to determining current IAM permissions.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question:
You are performing a monthly security check of your Google Cloud environment and want to know who has access to view data stored in your Google Cloud  

Project. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Logging sink and configure BigQuery as the destination. Configure the SaaS tool to query BigQuery to retrieve the logs.
Create a Cloud Logging sink and configure Pub/Sub as the destination. Configure the SaaS tool to subscribe to the Pub/Sub topic to retrieve the logs.
Create a Cloud Logging sink and configure Cloud Storage as the destination. Configure the SaaS tool to read the Cloud Storage bucket to retrieve the logs.
Use a Cloud Scheduler cron job to trigger a Cloud Function that queries Cloud Logging and sends the logs to the SaaS tool.

questions.explanation: Pub/Sub provides near-real-time message delivery with minimal latency, ideal for time-sensitive centralization of logs. The SaaS tool subscribes to the Pub/Sub topic and receives logs immediately as they arrive. This is superior to batch-oriented approaches like BigQuery or Cloud Storage for minimizing export delays.
