You need to migrate multiple PostgreSQL databases from your on-premises data center to Google Cloud. You want to significantly improve the performance of your databases while minimizing changes to your data schema and application code. You expect to exceed 150 TB of data per geographical region. You want to follow Google-recommended practices and minimize your operational costs. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate your data to AlloyDB.
Migrate your data to Spanner.
Migrate your data to Firebase.
Migrate your data to Bigtable.

questions.explanation: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is wire-compatible with PostgreSQL, so migrating preserves the existing schema and application code while delivering substantially better performance through its columnar engine and intelligent caching layer. Because the workload consists of multiple separate PostgreSQL databases, they can be distributed across multiple AlloyDB clusters to exceed 150 TB per region in aggregate, avoiding the schema and query rewrites that Spanner, Firestore, or Bigtable would impose. **Learn more:** [AlloyDB for PostgreSQL overview](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/overview)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are managing a project for the Business Intelligence (BI) department in your company. A data pipeline streams data into BigQuery. You want members of the BI department to be able to run custom SQL queries against the latest data in BigQuery. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Data Studio dashboard that uses the related BigQuery tables as a source and give the BI team view access to the Data Studio dashboard.
Create a Service Account for the BI team and distribute a new private key to each member of the BI team.
Use Cloud Scheduler to schedule a batch Dataflow job to copy the data from BigQuery to the BI team's internal data warehouse.
Assign the IAM role of BigQuery User to a Google Group that contains the members of the BI team.

questions.explanation:
Running custom SQL queries directly against BigQuery tables requires users to have query execution permissions in BigQuery, which is provided by the predefined IAM role roles/bigquery.user (BigQuery User). This role grants the ability to run jobs, including queries, within the project, and can be combined with dataset-level read access to the underlying tables. Assigning this role to a Google Group containing the BI team is the recommended IAM best practice for managing access to a group of users rather than granting permissions individually or via service account keys, which is discouraged for interactive human access and poses security risks. A Data Studio dashboard only supports pre-built reports/visualizations and does not allow arbitrary custom SQL querying, and copying data via a scheduled Dataflow batch job introduces staleness and unnecessary complexity, conflicting with the requirement to query the latest streamed data directly in BigQuery.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery predefined IAM roles](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/access-control) · [Best practices for using service accounts](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-service-accounts)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has adopted BigQuery as its enterprise data warehouse, and users across several business units run queries against it. You have observed that BigQuery query costs are very high, and you need to bring these costs under control. Which two methods should you use? (Choose two.)

options.text: Split the users from business units to multiple projects.
Apply a user- or project-level custom query quota for BigQuery data warehouse.
Create separate copies of your BigQuery data warehouse for each business unit.
Split your BigQuery data warehouse into multiple data warehouses for each business unit.
Change your BigQuery query model from on-demand to flat rate. Apply the appropriate number of slots to each Project.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery on-demand pricing charges based on the amount of data scanned by each query, so uncontrolled or inefficient queries from many users can quickly drive up costs. Google recommends setting custom query quotas at the user or project level to cap how much data (or how many queries) can be processed, preventing runaway costs from any single user or project. Additionally, switching from on-demand pricing to flat-rate pricing lets you purchase a fixed number of slots and allocate them across projects, which provides predictable, capped compute costs regardless of query volume—ideal for high, steady query workloads across an enterprise. Simply splitting users, warehouses, or data copies across projects does not limit the underlying cost drivers (bytes scanned or compute usage) and instead increases operational complexity.

**Learn more:** [Custom quotas | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/custom-quotas) · [Introduction to BigQuery editions and slots pricing](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reservations-intro)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization already has three Google Cloud projects. You must charge the Marketing department only for its Google Cloud services used by a new initiative within that group. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Verify that you are assigned the Billing Administrator IAM role for your organization's Google Cloud Project for the Marketing department. 2. Link the new project to a Marketing Billing Account.

1. Verify that you are assigned the Billing Administrator IAM role for your organization's Google Cloud account. 2. Create a new Google Cloud Project for the Marketing department. 3. Set the default key-value project labels to department:marketing for all services in this project.

1. Verify that you are assigned the Organization Administrator IAM role for your organization's Google Cloud account. 2. Create a new Google Cloud Project for the Marketing department. 3. Link the new project to a Marketing Billing Account.

1. Verify that you are assigned the Organization Administrator IAM role for your organization's Google Cloud account. 2. Create a new Google Cloud Project for the Marketing department. 3. Set the default key-value project labels to department:marketing for all services in this project.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Billing account defines the payer for the resources in its linked projects, and usage incurred by a project is charged to that linked billing account. Creating a dedicated project for the Marketing initiative and linking it to the Marketing Billing account therefore isolates the initiative’s services for Marketing billing. Project labels can help analyze or allocate costs, but they do not make a billing account responsible for a project’s charges.

**Learn more:** [Enable, disable, or change billing for a project](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/modify-project) · [Manage your Cloud Billing account](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/manage-billing-account)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage all your service accounts in a single project named proj-sa. You want to use a service account from this project to take snapshots of VMs that run in a different project, called proj-vm. What should you do?

options.text: Download the private key from the service account, and add it to each VMs custom metadata.
Download the private key from the service account, and add the private key to each VM's SSH keys.
Grant the service account the IAM Role of Compute Storage Admin in the project called proj-vm.
When creating the VMs, set the service account's API scope for Compute Engine to read/write.

questions.explanation:
IAM permissions in Google Cloud are granted on resources (such as a project) via IAM policy bindings, and a service account from one project can be granted a role on another project's resources. Granting the service account the predefined Compute Storage Admin role (roles/compute.storageAdmin) on the proj-vm project gives it the permissions needed to create and manage Compute Engine storage resources, including disk snapshots, for the VMs in that project. Downloading and embedding a private key in VM metadata or SSH keys is not a supported or secure way to grant a service account access, and setting API access scopes on a VM only controls what the VM's own attached service account can do from inside the instance — it does not grant an external service account access to resources in another project.

**Learn more:** [Compute Engine IAM roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/iam) · [Compute Engine roles and permissions | IAM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/compute)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for a web application on Compute Engine. You want your support team to be notified automatically if users experience high latency for at least 5 minutes. You need a Google-recommended solution with no development cost. What should you do?

options.text: Export Cloud Monitoring metrics to BigQuery and use a Looker Studio dashboard to monitor your web application’s latency.
Create an alert policy to send a notification when the HTTP response latency exceeds the specified threshold.
Implement an App Engine service which invokes the Cloud Monitoring API and sends a notification in case of anomalies.
Use the Cloud Monitoring dashboard to observe latency and take the necessary actions when the response latency exceeds the specified threshold.

questions.explanation: Cloud Monitoring alert policies provide automatic, zero-development-cost alerting when metrics exceed thresholds. They can notify support teams via email, SMS, or webhooks without custom code. BigQuery dashboards and manual monitoring require developer effort; Cloud Functions adds operational overhead.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to send all logs from all of your Compute Engine instances to a BigQuery dataset named platform-logs for analysis purposes. The Cloud Logging agent has already been installed on all the instances. You want to minimize cost. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Give the BigQuery Data Editor role on the platform-logs dataset to the service accounts used by your instances. 2. Update your instances' metadata to add the following value: logs-destination: bq://platform-logs.

1. In Cloud Logging, create a logs export with a Cloud Pub/Sub topic called logs as a sink. 2. Create a Cloud Function that is triggered by messages in the logs topic. 3. Configure that Cloud Function to drop logs that are not from Compute Engine and to insert Compute Engine logs in the platform-logs dataset.
1. In Cloud Logging, create a filter to view only Compute Engine logs. 2. Click Create Export. 3. Choose BigQuery as Sink Service, and the platform-logs dataset as Sink Destination.

1. Create a Cloud Function that has the BigQuery User role on the platform-logs dataset. 2. Configure this Cloud Function to create a BigQuery Job that executes this query: INSERT INTO dataset.platform-logs (timestamp, log) SELECT timestamp, log FROM compute.logs WHERE timestamp > DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 DAY) 3. Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger this Cloud Function once a day.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging provides a native log sink/export feature that lets you route logs directly to a BigQuery dataset without any custom code or additional infrastructure. By creating a filter in Cloud Logging to select only Compute Engine logs, then using the 'Create Export' (log sink) option with BigQuery as the Sink Service and the platform-logs dataset as the Sink Destination, logs are streamed directly and continuously into BigQuery at no extra operational cost beyond BigQuery storage/query costs. This built-in mechanism avoids the added complexity and cost of building custom Pub/Sub-triggered Cloud Functions, scheduled batch jobs, or relying on non-existent instance metadata keys to achieve the same result.

**Learn more:** [Configure and manage sinks - Cloud Logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2) · [Export logs to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery)

You are responsible for Google Cloud governance at your company and recently introduced a new automated process for provisioning Google Cloud projects. You have found several projects that were created manually before this new process was implemented. You need to identify the creators of these projects so you can notify them about the new process. What should you do?

Use Resource Manager to identify the responsible department from the folder and project hierarchy.
Review the Cloud Billing account linked to the project, and then contact the owner of that billing account.
Use the IAM page in the Google Cloud console to identify the user with the Owner role.

When a user creates a Google Cloud project, the initial IAM policy grants that user the Owner role on the project. Reviewing the project IAM policy therefore identifies the project creator.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning to migrate your containerized workloads to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You need to determine which GKE option to use. Your solution must have high availability, minimal downtime, and the ability to promptly apply security updates to your nodes. You also want to pay only for the compute resources that your workloads use without managing nodes. You want to follow Google-recommended practices and minimize operational costs. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a Standard regional GKE duster.
Configure a Standard zonal GKE duster.
Configure a Standard multi-zonal GKE cluster.
Configure an Autopilot GKE cluster.

questions.explanation: Autopilot GKE is Google's fully managed, serverless Kubernetes offering that automatically handles node lifecycle, security patches, and auto-scaling. It aligns with all stated requirements: high availability through automatic node management, minimal downtime with automated updates, no node management overhead, and pay-per-pod consumption without infrastructure costs. This is the recommended practice for customers seeking operational simplicity.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s accounting department needs to run an overnight batch workload every day. You must implement a solution that minimizes the cost to run this workload and automatically retries the batch if an execution fails. What should you do?

options.text: Develop an application that runs the batch workload, and deploy the application as a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) CronJob.
Develop a web application that listens for incoming requests, and deploy the application as a Cloud Run service. Use Cloud Scheduler to call the HTTP endpoint.
Develop an application that runs the batch workload, and deploy the application as a Cloud Run job. Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger the job.
Develop a web application that listens for incoming requests, and deploy the application as a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Deployment. Use Cloud Scheduler to call the HTTP endpoint.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run jobs are purpose-built for finite batch workloads: they run to completion, support configurable automatic retries on failure, and incur cost only while executing, and Cloud Scheduler can trigger the job once nightly with no idle infrastructure to pay for. A GKE CronJob requires a continuously running cluster/node pool, and the web-service options (B, D) are designed for persistent request-serving rather than a scheduled batch task.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Run jobs overview](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/create-jobs) · [Schedule a job execution](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/execute/jobs-on-schedule)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a large 5-TB AVRO file stored in a Cloud Storage bucket. Your analysts know only SQL and need to access the data in this file. You want the most cost-effective way to fulfill their request as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Load data in Cloud Datastore and run a SQL query against it.
Create a BigQuery table and load data in BigQuery. Run a SQL query on this table and drop this table after you complete your request.
Create external tables in BigQuery that point to Cloud Storage buckets and run a SQL query on these external tables to complete your request.
Create a Hadoop cluster and copy the AVRO file to NDFS by compressing it. Load the file in a hive table and provide access to your analysts so that they can run SQL queries.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery lets you create external (federated) tables that reference data files—including Avro—residing directly in Cloud Storage, without needing to load or copy the data into BigQuery storage. Because Avro is a self-describing format, BigQuery can automatically infer the schema, so analysts can immediately run standard SQL queries against the external table. This approach avoids the time and expense of loading 5 TB into a native table (and later deleting it), avoids duplicate storage costs, and requires no infrastructure provisioning as would be needed with a Hadoop/Hive cluster, making it the fastest and most cost-effective option that also matches the analysts' SQL-only skill set.

**Learn more:** [Create Cloud Storage external tables | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/external-data-cloud-storage) · [Load Avro data from Cloud Storage | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/loading-data-cloud-storage-avro)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has a rapidly growing social media platform and a user base primarily located in North America. Due to increasing demand, your current on-premises PostgreSQL database, hosted in your United States headquarters data center, no longer meets your needs. You need to identify a cloud-based database solution that offers automatic scaling, multi-region support for future expansion, and maintains low latency. What should you do?

options.text: Use BigQuery.
Use Spanner.
Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.
Use Bigtable.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a fully managed, horizontally scalable relational database that natively supports the PostgreSQL interface, and it is purpose-built for automatic scaling and synchronous multi-region replication with low latency for globally growing workloads. Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL only scales vertically and with read replicas, so it cannot meet the multi-region, auto-scaling requirement.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner overview](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/overview) · [PostgreSQL interface](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/postgresql-interface)

questions.question: You want to permanently delete a Pub/Sub topic managed by Config Connector in your Google Cloud project. What should you do?

options.text: Use kubectl to create the label deleted-by-cnrm and to change its value to true for the topic resource.
Use kubectl to delete the topic resource.
Use gcloud CLI to delete the topic.
Use gcloud CLI to update the topic label managed-by-cnrm to false.

questions.explanation: Resources managed by Config Connector are Kubernetes manifests. Deletion must occur through kubectl, which syncs the deletion back to the Google Cloud resource. Using gcloud or labels would bypass the Config Connector management contract.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud VPC firewall rules can use service accounts as both the target and source filters, which is a more secure and manageable way to identify instances than IP ranges or network tags, since service account assignment is controlled through IAM and cannot be changed on a running instance. To meet the stated requirement with least-privilege access, you should create two ingress firewall rules: one targeting instances that use the tier #2 service account, allowing ingress only from instances using the tier #1 service account, restricted to TCP port 8080; and a second rule targeting instances that use the tier #3 service account, allowing ingress only from instances using the tier #2 service account, also restricted to TCP port 8080. This precisely satisfies the tier-to-tier communication requirement without opening unnecessary broader access (as 'allow all' protocol rules or IP-range-based rules would do), and correctly uses ingress rules since the goal is to control what traffic each tier's instances accept from the prior tier.

Your company requires that Google Cloud products are created with a specific configuration to comply with your company’s security policies. You need to implement a mechanism that will allow software engineers at your company to deploy and update Google Cloud products in a preconfigured and approved manner. What should you do?

options.text: Create Java packages that utilize the Google Cloud Client Libraries for Java to configure Google Cloud products. Store and share the packages in a source code repository.
Create bash scripts that utilize the Google Cloud CLI to configure Google Cloud products. Store and share the bash scripts in a source code repository.
Use the Google Cloud APIs by using curl to configure Google Cloud products. Store and share the curl commands in a source code repository.
Create Terraform modules that utilize the Google Cloud Terraform Provider to configure Google Cloud products. Store and share the modules in a source code repository.

questions.explanation: Terraform modules using the Google Cloud Terraform Provider represent the industry-standard Infrastructure as Code approach for managing preconfigured, approved deployments at scale. Terraform ensures consistency, enables version control, supports modular design for security policies, and follows Google-recommended practices for enterprise infrastructure deployment.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have successfully set up a development environment within a project for an application that relies on Compute Engine and Cloud SQL. You now need to build out a production environment for this same application. The security team has mandated that no network routes may exist between these two environments, and they want you to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new project, enable the Compute Engine and Cloud SQL APIs in that project, and replicate the setup you have created in the development environment.
Create a new production subnet in the existing VPC and a new production Cloud SQL instance in your existing project, and deploy your application using those resources.

Create a new project, modify your existing VPC to be a Shared VPC, share that VPC with your new project, and replicate the setup you have in the development environment in that new project in the Shared VPC.

Ask the security team to grant you the Project Editor role in an existing production project used by another division of your company. Once they grant you that role, replicate the setup you have in the development environment in that project.

questions.explanation:
Google recommends isolating environments such as development and production into separate projects, each with its own VPC network. Since VPC networks are isolated from one another by default (no implicit routes between separate VPC networks unless explicitly connected via VPC peering, Cloud VPN, or Shared VPC), creating a new project and replicating the setup there — without linking the two VPCs — satisfies the requirement that no routes exist between the environments. Using a Shared VPC (option C) or keeping resources in the same VPC (option B) would create routable connectivity between the environments, violating the security team's mandate. Requesting elevated access to an unrelated project (option D) is not a recommended isolation practice.

**Learn more:** [Decide a resource hierarchy for your Google Cloud landing zone](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/landing-zones/decide-resource-hierarchy) · [VPC network overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are monitoring an application and receive user feedback that a particular error is spiking. You determine that the error is caused by a Service Account having insufficient permissions. You are able to resolve the issue, but you also want to be notified automatically if the same problem happens again. What should you do?

options.text: In the Log Viewer, filter the logs on severity 'Error' and the name of the Service Account.
Create a sink to BigQuery to export all the logs. Create a Data Studio dashboard on the exported logs.
Create a custom log-based metric for the specific error to be used in an Alerting Policy.
Grant Project Owner access to the Service Account.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging allows you to create a custom log-based metric that counts occurrences of a specific error pattern in your logs. This metric can then be referenced in a Cloud Monitoring Alerting Policy, which will automatically notify you (via email, Slack, PagerDuty, etc.) whenever the error condition recurs. This is the standard proactive monitoring approach in Google Cloud, as opposed to manually filtering logs (reactive only), exporting logs to BigQuery/Data Studio for dashboards (no automated notification), or granting excessive permissions to the Service Account (a security risk that doesn't address the notification requirement).

**Learn more:** [Logs-based metrics overview](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics) · [Creating alerting policies](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/using-alerting-ui)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure Object Lifecycle Management for objects stored in storage buckets. The objects are written once and then accessed frequently for the first 30 days. After that 30-day period, the objects are not read again unless there is a special need. The objects must be retained for a total of three years, and you want to minimize cost.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set up a policy that uses Nearline storage for 30 days and then moves to Archive storage for three years.
Set up a policy that uses Standard storage for 30 days and then moves to Archive storage for three years.
Set up a policy that uses Nearline storage for 30 days, then moves the Coldline for one year, and then moves to Archive storage for two years.
Set up a policy that uses Standard storage for 30 days, then moves to Coldline for one year, and then moves to Archive storage for two years.

questions.explanation:
Standard storage is intended for data accessed more than once a month, which fits the frequent access pattern during the first 30 days. After that point, the objects are rarely accessed and only for special needs, and they must be retained long-term (three years total), which matches the use case for Archive storage — the lowest-cost Cloud Storage class, intended for data accessed less than once a year with a 365-day minimum storage duration. Moving directly from Standard to Archive after 30 days avoids paying the higher storage costs of an intermediate Coldline stage, since Coldline offers no benefit here given the described (rare, special-need only) access pattern — it would simply add unnecessary storage expense compared to Archive for the same data over the same retention period.

**Learn more:** [Storage classes | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has created hundreds of service accounts for different applications hosted on-premises and in other clouds that use Google Cloud APIs. You need to audit the service account keys that were created and identify keys older than 90 days.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Execute the gcloud asset search-all-resources--scope=
Execute the gcloud iam service-accounts list--filter=
Execute the gcloud tans keys list--filter=
Execute the gcloud asset search-all-resources--scope=

questions.explanation:
Cloud Asset Inventory can search an organization’s resources by `createTime`. Service account keys have the asset type `iam.googleapis.com/ServiceAccountKey`, so filtering that type for creation times earlier than the 90-day cutoff and ordering by `createTime` identifies the required keys.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: You are building an application that stores relational data from users. Users across the globe will use this application. Your CTO is concerned about the scaling requirements because the size of the user base is unknown. You need to implement a database solution that can scale with your user growth with minimum configuration changes. Which storage solution should you use?

options.text: Cloud SQL
Firestore
Cloud Spanner
Bigtable

questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed, horizontally scalable relational database designed for applications requiring strong consistency and multi-region deployment. It automatically handles scaling without configuration changes. Cloud SQL lacks horizontal scaling across regions; Firestore and Bigtable are NoSQL and incompatible with relational data requirements.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: You are building an application that stores relational data from users. Users across the globe will use this application. Your CTO is concerned about the scaling requirements because the size of the user base is unknown. You need to implement a database solution that can scale with your user growth with minimum configuration changes. Which storage solution should you use?

options.text: Configure an SSL Proxy load balancer in front of the application servers.
Configure an Internal UDP load balancer in front of the application servers.
Configure an External HTTP(s) load balancer in front of the application servers.
Configure an External Network load balancer in front of the application servers.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud's External TCP/UDP Network Load Balancer is a regional, passthrough load balancer that supports both TCP and UDP traffic originating from clients on the Internet, and it distributes that traffic across a backend service made up of multiple VMs behind a single external IP address (a forwarding rule). Since the requirement is UDP traffic from external (Internet-based) clients, and neither the SSL Proxy nor HTTP(S) load balancers support UDP, and the Internal UDP load balancer only serves internal clients, the External Network Load Balancer is the appropriate choice.

**Learn more:** [Network Load Balancer overview | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/network) · [Choosing a load balancer | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/choosing-load-balancer)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application that runs on Compute Engine VM instances in a custom Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Your company’s security policies only allow the use of internal IP addresses on VM instances and do not let VM instances connect to the internet. You need to ensure that the application can access a file hosted in a Cloud Storage bucket within your project. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Private Service Access on the Cloud Storage Bucket.
Add storage.googleapis.com to the list of restricted services in a VPC Service Controls perimeter and add your project to the list of protected projects.
Enable Private Google Access on the subnet within the custom VPC.
Deploy a Cloud NAT instance and route the traffic to the dedicated IP address of the Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation: Private Google Access allows VM instances with only internal IP addresses to reach the external IP addresses of Google APIs and services, including Cloud Storage. Private Service Access (A) does not support Cloud Storage. VPC Service Controls (B) is for access restrictions, not enablement. Cloud NAT (D) adds unnecessary complexity and cost.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You ate managing an application deployed on Cloud Run. The development team has released a new version of the application. You want to deploy and redirect traffic to this new version of the application. To ensure traffic to the new version of the application is served with no startup time, you want to ensure that there are two idle instances available for incoming traffic before adjusting the traffic flow. You also want to minimize administrative overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Ensure the checkbox “Serve this revision immediately” is unchecked when deploying the new revision. Before changing the traffic rules, use a traffic simulation tool to send load to the new revision.
Configure service autoscaling and set the minimum number of instances to 2.
Configure revision autoscaling for the new revision and set the minimum number of instances to 2.
Configure revision autoscaling for the existing revision and set the minimum number of instances to 2.

questions.explanation:
Minimum instance counts in Cloud Run are configured per revision, so setting revision-level autoscaling with two minimum instances on the newly deployed revision (before shifting traffic to it) warms up two idle instances that are ready to serve without cold-start latency. Configuring it on the existing revision or via a nonexistent "service-level" setting would not prepare the new revision, and simulating traffic manually adds administrative overhead.

**Learn more:** [Set minimum instances | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/min-instances)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating a shell script that contains several gcloud CLI commands to access Google Cloud resources. You want to test the script in your local development environment using a service account in the most secure manner. What should you do?

options.text: Generate an ID token for the service account. Use the token with the gcloud CLI commands.
Enable service account impersonation, and use the gcloud config set command to use it by default.
Download the service account key file and save it in a secure location. Set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable to the key file.
Download the service account key file, and use it to generate an access token. Use the token with the gcloud CLI commands.

questions.explanation:
Service account impersonation lets an authenticated principal obtain short-lived credentials for the service account without downloading or managing a long-lived service account key. The gcloud CLI supports making impersonation the default by setting the `auth/impersonate_service_account` configuration property.

**Learn more:** [Authenticate for the gcloud CLI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/authenticate) · [Use service account impersonation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/use-service-account-impersonation)

You have a developer laptop running Ubuntu with the Cloud SDK installed, where the Cloud SDK was installed from the Google Cloud Ubuntu package repository. You want to test your application locally on your laptop using Cloud Datastore. What should you do?

options.text: Export Cloud Datastore data using gcloud datastore export.
Create a Cloud Datastore index using gcloud datastore indexes create.
Install the google-cloud-sdk-datastore-emulator component using the apt get install command.
Install the cloud-datastore-emulator component using the gcloud components install command.

questions.explanation:
Because the Cloud SDK was installed from the Google Cloud apt repository rather than through the standalone/interactive installer, gcloud's internal component manager is disabled for that installation method, so `gcloud components install` cannot be used to add the emulator. Instead, additional components such as the Datastore emulator must be installed as separate apt packages. The correct package to install in this case is `google-cloud-sdk-datastore-emulator` via `sudo apt-get install google-cloud-sdk-datastore-emulator`, which provides the local Datastore emulator needed for local application testing.

**Learn more:** [Quickstart: Install the Google Cloud CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install) · [Installing the Cloud Datastore Emulator](https://cloud.google.com/datastore/docs/tools/datastore-emulator)

The DevOps group in your organization needs full control of Compute Engine resources in your development project. However, they should not have permission to create or update any other resources in the project. You want to follow Google’s recommendations for setting permissions for the DevOps group. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the basic role roles/viewer and the predefined role roles/compute.admin to the DevOps group.
Create an IAM policy and grant all compute.instanceAdmin.* permissions to the policy. Attach the policy to the DevOps group.
Create a custom role at the folder level and grant all compute.instanceAdmin.* permissions to the role. Grant the custom role to the DevOps group.
Grant the basic role roles/editor to the DevOps group.

questions.explanation:
roles/compute.admin is the predefined role for full control of Compute Engine resources, and pairing it with the basic roles/viewer role gives the group read-only visibility into the rest of the project without any ability to create or modify non-Compute Engine resources. Google's IAM guidance favors predefined roles over custom ones when they fit the need; compute.instanceAdmin.* permissions alone do not amount to full control of Compute Engine (they omit permissions like network and firewall management), and roles/editor is far broader than the DevOps group requires.

**Learn more:** [Understanding roles - compute.admin](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/understanding-roles#compute.admin)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You host a website on Compute Engine. The number of global users accessing your website is expanding rapidly. You need to minimize latency and accommodate user growth across multiple geographical regions. You also want to follow Google-recommended practices while minimizing operational costs. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use an external Application Load Balancer in Regional mode.
Deploy your VMs in multiple Google Cloud regions closest to your user’s geographical locations.
Use a Network Load Balancer.
Use an external Application Load Balancer in Global mode.
Deploy all of your VMs in a single Google Cloud region with the largest available CIDR range.

questions.explanation:
For global HTTP(S) workloads, a global external Application Load Balancer provides multi-region load balancing and directs users toward the closest healthy backend with available capacity. Placing Compute Engine VMs in multiple regions near the users they serve reduces network latency and supports regional growth. Google Cloud documents both multi-region backends near clients and the global external Application Load Balancer as the appropriate design for globally dispersed users.

**Learn more:** [External Application Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https) · [External Application Load Balancer performance best practices](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https/http-load-balancing-best-practices)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has developed a new application that consists of multiple microservices. You want to deploy the application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), and you want to ensure that the cluster can scale as more applications are deployed in the future. You want to avoid manual intervention when each new application is deployed. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the application on GKE, and add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler to the deployment.
Deploy the application on GKE, and add a VerticalPodAutoscaler to the deployment.
Create a GKE cluster with autoscaling enabled on the node pool. Set a minimum and maximum for the size of the node pool.
Create a separate node pool for each application, and deploy each application to its dedicated node pool.

questions.explanation:
The requirement is that the cluster itself — its node capacity — scales automatically as new, unrelated applications are deployed over time, with zero manual intervention per new workload. Enabling cluster autoscaling on the node pool with a defined minimum and maximum size lets GKE add or remove nodes to fit whatever aggregate demand future deployments create; a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (A) only resizes replicas of one specific Deployment and would need to be configured again for each new application, which is exactly the manual step the requirement rules out.

**Learn more:** [About cluster autoscaling | GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/cluster-autoscaler)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to create a copy of a custom Compute Engine virtual machine (VM) in order to accommodate an anticipated increase in application traffic resulting from a business acquisition.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a Compute Engine snapshot of your base VM. Create your images from that snapshot.
Create a Compute Engine snapshot of your base VM. Create your instances from that snapshot.
Create a custom Compute Engine image from a snapshot. Create your images from that image.
Create a custom Compute Engine image from a snapshot. Create your instances from that image.

questions.explanation:
The recommended pattern in Google Cloud for replicating a custom VM configuration is to first create a snapshot of the source VM's persistent disk, then create a custom (reusable) image from that snapshot. Custom images serve as templates that can be used to create multiple new VM instances with the same configuration, which is exactly what's needed to scale out capacity for increased traffic. Images are the correct source for creating instances (not directly for creating other images), so the workflow of snapshot → custom image → new instances aligns with Compute Engine's documented best practices for creating copies of a VM.

**Learn more:** [Create custom images | Compute Engine Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/images/create-custom) · [Create and manage disk snapshots](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/create-snapshots)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to migrate invoice documents stored on-premises to Cloud Storage. The documents have the following storage requirements:  
  
• Documents must be kept for five years.  

• Up to five revisions of the same invoice document must be stored, to allow for corrections.  

• Documents older than 365 days should be moved to lower cost storage tiers.  
  
You want to follow Google-recommended practices to minimize your operational and development costs. What should you do?

options.text: Enable retention policies on the bucket, and use Cloud Scheduler to invoke a Cloud Function to move or delete your documents based on their metadata.
Enable retention policies on the bucket, use lifecycle rules to change the storage classes of the objects, set the number of versions, and delete old files.
Enable object versioning on the bucket, and use Cloud Scheduler to invoke a Cloud Functions instance to move or delete your documents based on their metadata.
Enable object versioning on the bucket, use lifecycle conditions to change the storage class of the objects, set the number of versions, and delete old files.

questions.explanation: Object versioning enables storage of multiple revisions for corrections, while lifecycle conditions automatically transition objects to lower-cost storage tiers (Nearline, Coldline, Archive) after 365 days and can delete old versions after the retention period. This approach balances the 5-year retention requirement with cost optimization. Retention policies in option B would prevent deletion even after 365 days, reducing flexibility.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently received a new Google Cloud project with an attached billing account where you will work. You need to create instances, set firewalls, and store data in Cloud Storage. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use the gcloud CLI services enable cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com command to enable all resources.
Use the gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com command to enable Compute Engine and the gcloud services enable storage-api.googleapis.com command to enable the Cloud Storage APIs.
Open the Google Cloud console and enable all Google Cloud APIs from the API dashboard.
Open the Google Cloud console and run gcloud init --project in a Cloud Shell.

questions.explanation: To follow Google-recommended practices, specific APIs must be enabled only when needed. Option B enables exactly the required APIs: compute.googleapis.com (for instances and firewalls, which are part of Compute Engine) and storage-api.googleapis.com (for Cloud Storage). Enabling all APIs or using the cloud resource manager API introduces unnecessary services and broadens the attack surface.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a product on top of Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You have a single GKE cluster. For each of your customers, a Pod is running in that cluster, and your customers can run arbitrary code inside their Pod. You want to maximize the isolation between your customers' Pods. What should you do?

options.text: Use Binary Authorization and whitelist only the container images used by your customers' Pods.
Use the Container Analysis API to detect vulnerabilities in the containers used by your customers' Pods.
Create a GKE node pool with a sandbox type configured to gvisor. Add the parameter runtimeClassName: gvisor to the specification of your customers' Pods.
Use the cos_containerd image for your GKE nodes. Add a nodeSelector with the value cloud.google.com/gke-os-distribution: cos_containerd to the specification of your customers' Pods.

questions.explanation: GKE Sandbox using gVisor provides kernel-level isolation for pods running untrusted or arbitrary code. gVisor is a sandboxing technology that intercepts system calls, creating a strong security boundary between each pod and the host kernel. This is the recommended approach for multi-tenant scenarios where workload isolation is critical.

You have downloaded and installed the gcloud command-line interface (CLI) and authenticated with your Google Account. Most of your Compute Engine instances in your project run in the europe-west1-d zone, and you want to avoid specifying this zone with every CLI command when managing these instances.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set the europe-west1-d zone as the default zone using the gcloud config subcommand.
In the Settings page for Compute Engine under Default location, set the zone to europeג€
In the CLI installation directory, create a file called default.conf containing zone=europeג€
Create a Metadata entry on the Compute Engine page with key compute/zone and value europeג€

questions.explanation:
The gcloud CLI allows you to set default properties, such as the default zone, using the `gcloud config` command (e.g., `gcloud config set compute/zone europe-west1-d`). Once set, gcloud compute commands automatically use this zone unless overridden with the --zone flag, eliminating the need to specify it manually every time. This is the documented, supported way to configure CLI defaults, unlike the other options, which describe non-existent configuration mechanisms (there is no CLI 'Settings page' for default location, no default.conf file read by gcloud, and instance metadata entries are not used to configure the CLI's default zone).

**Learn more:** [gcloud config set | Google Cloud CLI Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/config/set) · [Configuring default settings for the gcloud CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/configurations)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure a budget alert for the usage of Compute Engine services on one of three Google Cloud Platform projects that you manage, where all three projects are linked to a single billing account. What should you do?

options.text: Verify that you are the project billing administrator. Select the associated billing account and create a budget and alert for the appropriate project.
Verify that you are the project billing administrator. Select the associated billing account and create a budget and a custom alert.
Verify that you are the project administrator. Select the associated billing account and create a budget for the appropriate project.
Verify that you are project administrator. Select the associated billing account and create a budget and a custom alert.

questions.explanation:
Budgets and budget alerts in Google Cloud are created and managed at the billing account level, so the user must have the Billing Account Administrator role (not merely a project administrator role) to create a budget. Because the billing account is shared across three projects but the alert is needed for only one, the budget must be created with a filter scoping it to that specific project. This aligns with Google Cloud's documented process for creating budgets: select the billing account, then define the budget scope to include only the relevant project, and set the alert.

**Learn more:** [Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets) · [Cloud Billing access control](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/billing-access)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You created several resources in multiple Google Cloud projects. All projects are linked to different billing accounts. To better estimate future charges, you want to have a single visual representation of all costs incurred. You want to include new cost data as soon as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Fill all resources in the Pricing Calculator to get an estimate of the monthly cost.
Use the Reports view in the Cloud Billing Console to view the desired cost information.
Visit the Cost Table page to get a CSV export and visualize it using Looker Studio.
Configure Billing Data Export to BigQuery and visualize the data in Looker Studio.

questions.explanation: For multi-project cost visibility with different billing accounts, BigQuery Data Export combined with Looker Studio is the recommended approach. This combination allows real-time or near-real-time visualization of costs across multiple projects and billing accounts, with automatic updates as new billing data arrives. The Pricing Calculator provides estimates only, while Billing Reports work only within a single billing account.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your finance team wants to be able to view the billing report for your projects, and you need to ensure this access does not grant them any extra permissions on the project. What should you do?

options.text: Add the group for the finance team to roles/billing user role.
Add the group for the finance team to roles/billing admin role.
Add the group for the finance team to roles/billing viewer role.
Add the group for the finance team to roles/billing project/Manager role.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud's predefined billing IAM role roles/billing.viewer grants read-only access to billing account information such as cost and usage reports, without providing any ability to modify billing settings or manage project resources. Assigning the finance team's group to this role satisfies the requirement to view billing reports while ensuring no additional project permissions are granted, unlike roles/billing.user or roles/billing.admin, which include broader permissions such as linking billing accounts to projects or fully managing billing configuration.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Billing access control - Predefined roles](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/billing-access)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to deploy an application in Google Cloud using serverless technology. You want to test a new version of the application with a small percentage of production traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the application to Cloud Run. Use gradual rollouts for traffic splitting.
Deploy the application to Google Kubernetes Engine. Use Anthos Service Mash for traffic splitting.
Deploy the application to Cloud Functions. Specify the version number in the functions name.
Deploy the application to App Engine. For each new version, create a new service.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run is a serverless platform supporting gradual rollouts and traffic splitting, enabling canary deployments with minimal risk. GKE is not serverless (requires cluster management), Cloud Functions lacks versioning/traffic-splitting capabilities, and App Engine lacks the same level of traffic splitting control. Gradual rollouts on Cloud Run allow testing new versions with a small percentage of users and rollback if issues occur.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage resources in a Google Cloud project. A new service account must be able to invoke a Cloud Run service. You need permissions to modify IAM policies for service accounts while following the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: Request the roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin role for your user account.
Request the roles/run.invoker role for your user account.
Request the Editor role for your user account.
Request the Owner role for your user account.

questions.explanation:
The predefined Service Account Admin role (`roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin`) includes the permissions needed to manage a service account’s IAM policy, including `iam.serviceAccounts.getIamPolicy` and `iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy`. It is narrower than the basic Editor and Owner roles; Cloud Run Invoker grants permission to invoke a Cloud Run service but does not allow IAM-policy administration for service accounts.

**Learn more:** [Manage access to service accounts](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/manage-access-service-accounts)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to set up an autoscaling managed instance group for an HTTPS web application, and you want to ensure that any unhealthy VM instances are automatically recreated. What should you do?

options.text: Create a health check on port 443 and use that when creating the Managed Instance Group.
Select Multi-Zone instead of Single-Zone when creating the Managed Instance Group.
In the Instance Template, add the label 'health-check'.
In the Instance Template, add a startup script that sends a heartbeat to the metadata server.

questions.explanation:
Recreating unhealthy instances in a managed instance group is handled by the autohealing feature, which relies on an application-level health check rather than the simple network load balancer health check. For an HTTPS application, you create a health check that probes port 443 (the port the app serves on) and specify that health check when configuring the managed instance group's autohealing policy. If instances fail this health check for the configured unhealthy threshold, the MIG automatically deletes and recreates them. Multi-zone distribution improves fault tolerance across zones but doesn't trigger recreation of unhealthy instances; instance template labels are purely metadata; and there is no built-in GCE mechanism using a custom heartbeat script sent to the metadata server for autohealing.

**Learn more:** [Setting up an application health check and autohealing](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/creating-groups-of-managed-instances#health-check) · [About health checks for autohealing VMs in a MIG](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/autohealing-instances-in-migs)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the Google Cloud systems administrator for your organization. User A reports receiving an error while trying to access the Cloud SQL database in their Google Cloud project, whereas User B can access the database. You need to troubleshoot User A’s issue while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do first?

options.text: Confirm that network firewall rules are not blocking traffic for User A.
Verify that User A has the Identity and Access Management (IAM) Project Owner role assigned.
Review recent configuration changes that may have caused unintended modifications to permissions.
Review the error message that User A received.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL access failures can originate at the database, IAM, network, client, or Cloud SQL service layer. The error message provides the diagnostic detail needed to identify the applicable layer and choose a targeted, least-privilege remediation; granting the broad Project Owner role is not an appropriate initial troubleshooting action.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL error messages](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/error-messages)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are running a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster with autoscaling enabled to host a new application. You need to expose this application publicly over HTTPS on a public IP address. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Kubernetes Service of type NodePort for your application, and a Kubernetes Ingress to expose this Service via a Cloud Load Balancer.
Create a Kubernetes Service of type ClusterIP for your application. Configure the public DNS name of your application using the IP of this Service.

Create a Kubernetes Service of type NodePort to expose the application on port 443 of each node of the Kubernetes cluster. Configure the public DNS name of your application with the IP of every node of the cluster to achieve load-balancing.

Create a HAProxy pod in the cluster to load-balance the traffic to all the pods of the application. Forward the public traffic to HAProxy with an iptable rule. Configure the DNS name of your application using the public IP of the node HAProxy is running on.

questions.explanation:
On GKE, exposing an application externally with HTTPS and a stable public IP is achieved by creating a Service of type NodePort for the application and then defining a Kubernetes Ingress resource. The GKE Ingress controller uses this configuration to automatically provision and configure a Google Cloud external Application (HTTP/HTTPS) Load Balancer, which provides a single public IP address, terminates/handles HTTPS traffic, performs health checks, and load-balances traffic across the autoscaled backend nodes/pods referenced by the NodePort Service. This is the documented, supported pattern in GKE networking (see 'Ingress for external Application Load Balancers').

**Learn more:** [GKE Ingress for Application Load Balancers | GKE networking | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ingress) · [Set up an external Application Load Balancer with Ingress | GKE networking | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/tutorials/http-balancer)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are preparing to deploy a new Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system on Google Cloud. This application keeps the entire database in memory to enable fast data access, and you must provision the most suitable Google Cloud resources for it. What should you do?

options.text: Provision preemptible Compute Engine instances.
Provision Compute Engine instances with GPUs attached.
Provision Compute Engine instances with local SSDs attached.
Provision Compute Engine instances with M1 machine type.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud's memory-optimized machine family, which includes the M1 machine type, is purpose-built for workloads that require very large amounts of RAM relative to CPU, such as large in-memory databases (for example, SAP HANA) and memory-intensive ERP/CRM systems. M1 instances can scale up to several terabytes of memory, which directly satisfies the requirement of holding the full database in memory for fast access. Preemptible VMs optimize for cost but can be reclaimed at any time, making them unsuitable for a production ERP workload; GPUs accelerate parallel/ML computation rather than memory capacity; and local SSDs speed up disk I/O, which is not the bottleneck when the entire dataset resides in memory rather than on disk.

**Learn more:** [Memory-optimized machine family for Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/memory-optimized-machines) · [Machine families resource and comparison guide | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/machine-resource)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to host your video encoding software on Compute Engine. Your user base is growing rapidly, and users need to be able to encode their videos at any time without interruption or CPU limitations. You must ensure that your encoding solution is highly available, and you want to follow Google-recommended practices to automate operations. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy your solution on multiple standalone Compute Engine instances, and increase the number of existing instances when CPU utilization on Cloud Monitoring reaches a certain threshold.
Deploy your solution on multiple standalone Compute Engine instances, and replace existing instances with high-CPU instances when CPU utilization on Cloud Monitoring reaches a certain threshold.
Deploy your solution to an instance group, and increase the number of available instances whenever you see high CPU utilization in Cloud Monitoring.
Deploy your solution to an instance group, and set the autoscaling based on CPU utilization.

questions.explanation: For high availability and automation of a CPU-intensive workload, a Managed Instance Group with CPU-based autoscaling provides both failover and automatic scaling. Manual instance management or single-instance deployments do not meet the reliability and automation requirements.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application that uses Cloud Spanner as its backend database. The application experiences a very predictable traffic pattern. You want to automatically scale the number of Cloud Spanner nodes up or down depending on the traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Create a cron job that runs on a scheduled basis to review Cloud Monitoring metrics, and then resize the Spanner instance accordingly.
Create a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy to send an alert to oncall SRE emails when Cloud Spanner CPU exceeds the threshold. SREs would scale resources up or down accordingly.
Create a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy to send an alert to Google Cloud Support email when Cloud Spanner CPU exceeds your threshold. Google support would scale resources up or down accordingly.

Create a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy to send an alert to webhook when Cloud Spanner CPU is over or under your threshold. Create a Cloud Function that listens to HTTP and resizes Spanner resources accordingly.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner does not automatically scale its provisioned nodes or processing units in response to load; scaling must be handled by an external mechanism that monitors utilization and calls the Spanner Admin API to change instance capacity. The recommended pattern (also used by Google's open-source Cloud Spanner Autoscaler) is to create a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy on the Spanner CPU utilization metric that notifies a webhook when the metric crosses the configured upper or lower threshold, and to have a Cloud Function subscribed to that webhook automatically resize the Spanner instance's nodes/processing units accordingly. This fully automates scaling without human involvement, unlike alerting SREs (who would manually resize) or alerting Google Cloud Support (who does not manage customer instance sizing), and it reacts immediately to threshold breaches rather than relying on a periodic cron-based check.

**Learn more:** [Autoscaler tool overview | Spanner | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/autoscaler-tool-overview) · [GitHub - cloudspannerecosystem/autoscaler](https://github.com/cloudspannerecosystem/autoscaler)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution

options.text: Manually copy the error messages, and search for them in public forums and documentation.
Use Cloud Profiler to analyze the application’s performance during the time of the errors.
Use the “Explain this log entry” feature in Logs Explorer, and start a conversation with Gemini.
Search the application source code to determine the cause of the errors.

questions.explanation:
Logs Explorer can use Gemini Cloud Assist through **Explain this log entry** to generate a summary and help interpret an unfamiliar log entry. Cloud Logging sends the entry text to Gemini, making this an appropriate rapid first step when the logged content contains no PII.

**Learn more:** [Summarize log entries with Gemini assistance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/view/summarize-log-entries-gemini)

You are auditing your Google Cloud organization. You need to find every Compute Engine instance that has a public IP address. You want a solution that is straightforward to maintain and uses Google Cloud managed services. What should you do?

options.text: Enable the compute.vmExternalIpAccess organization policy at the organization level.
Use Cloud Shell and Gemini CLI to query the Compute Engine API for instances with a public IP address.
Use Cloud Asset Inventory to query for all Compute Engine instances with a public IP address.
Create a shell script using the gcloud CLI to find all instances with a public IP address.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Asset Inventory provides organization-wide managed asset search, and the `compute.googleapis.com/Instance` asset type includes the searchable `externalIPs` attribute. It can therefore query Compute Engine instances that have public IP addresses without maintaining custom scripts or interactive tooling.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Asset Inventory asset types](https://docs.cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/asset-types) · [Search for resources with Cloud Asset Inventory](https://docs.cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/search-resources)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your customer wants you to create a secure website with autoscaling based on the compute instance CPU load. You want to enhance performance by storing static content in Cloud Storage. Which resources are needed to distribute the user traffic?

options.text: An external HTTP(S) load balancer with a managed SSL certificate to distribute the load and a URL map to target the requests for the static content to the Cloud Storage backend.
An external network load balancer pointing to the backend instances to distribute the load evenly. The web servers will forward the request to the Cloud Storage as needed.
An internal HTTP(S) load balancer together with Identity-Aware Proxy to allow only HTTPS traffic.
An external HTTP(S) load balancer to distribute the load and a URL map to target the requests for the static content to the Cloud Storage backend. Install the HTTPS certificates on the instance.

questions.explanation: External HTTPS load balancer with managed SSL certificate and URL maps provides secure, cost-effective static content delivery. Managed certificates simplify certificate lifecycle management across autoscaling instances. URL maps intelligently route static content requests directly to Cloud Storage backend, bypassing compute instances for efficiency. Network load balancers lack HTTPS termination; internal load balancers are unsuitable for public traffic.

questions.question: You need to add a group of new users to Cloud Identity. Some of the users already have existing Google accounts. You want to follow one of Google's recommended practices and avoid conflicting accounts. What should you do?

options.text: Invite the user to transfer their existing account.
Invite the user to use an email alias to resolve the conflict.
Tell the user that they must delete their existing account.
Tell the user to remove all personal email from the existing account.

questions.explanation: Google's recommended practice for adding users with existing Google accounts to Cloud Identity is to invite them to transfer their existing account. This preserves access rights and data associated with their Gmail account. Using email aliases or deleting accounts are not recommended as they either fragment identity or cause data loss.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: You need to add a group of new users to Cloud Identity. Some of the users already have existing Google accounts. You want to follow one of Google's recommended practices and avoid conflicting accounts. What should you do?

options.text: Enable the Cloud Pub/Sub API in the API Library on the GCP Console.
Rely on the automatic enablement of the Cloud Pub/Sub API when the Service Account accesses it.
Use Deployment Manager to deploy your application. Rely on the automatic enablement of all APIs used by the application being deployed.
Grant the App Engine Default service account the role of Cloud Pub/Sub Admin. Have your application enable the API on the first connection to Cloud Pub/ Sub.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud APIs, including the Cloud Pub/Sub API, must be explicitly enabled for a project before any client—service account or otherwise—can call them; there is no automatic enablement triggered by an API call, by Deployment Manager deployments, or by granting an IAM role. Enabling the API through the API Library in the GCP Console (or an equivalent method such as `gcloud services enable pubsub.googleapis.com`) is the required step, after which the service account (already granted appropriate Pub/Sub IAM permissions) can successfully authenticate and use the API.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Pub/Sub API – APIs & Services – Google Cloud console](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/pubsub.googleapis.com) · [Authenticate to Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/authentication)

Your application stores files on Cloud Storage by using the Standard Storage class. The application only requires access to files created in the last 30 days. You want to automatically save costs on files that are no longer accessed by the application. What should you do?

options.text: Create an object lifecycle on the storage bucket to change the storage class to Archive Storage for objects with an age over 30 days.
Create a cron job in Cloud Scheduler to call a Cloud Functions instance every day to delete files older than 30 days.
Create a retention policy on the storage bucket of 30 days, and lock the bucket by using a retention policy lock.
Enable object versioning on the storage bucket and add lifecycle rules to expire non-current versions after 30 days.

questions.explanation:
Object Lifecycle Management is the native, fully automatic way to cut storage cost as data ages: a rule that transitions objects older than 30 days to Archive storage keeps the files available at much lower cost without any custom code. Building a scheduled function to delete files requires maintaining custom infrastructure and permanently destroys data the application no longer touches but may still need for other purposes; a retention policy only prevents early deletion, and object versioning addresses overwritten or deleted objects rather than aging of the current version.

**Learn more:** [Object Lifecycle Management](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle)

questions.question: You are running out of primary internal IP addresses in a subnet for a custom mode VPC. The subnet has the IP range 10.0.0.0/20, and the IP addresses are primarily used by virtual machines in the project. You need to provide more IP addresses for the virtual machines. What should you do?

options.text: Add a secondary IP range 10.1.0.0/20 to the subnet.
Change the subnet IP range from 10.0.0.0/20 to 10.0.0.0/18.
Change the subnet IP range from 10.0.0.0/20 to 10.0.0.0/22.
Convert the subnet IP range from IPv4 to IPv6.

questions.explanation: Expanding the primary subnet range from 10.0.0.0/20 to 10.0.0.0/18 directly increases available IP addresses for primary VM instances. The /18 range provides four times the address space. Secondary ranges (A) are designed for alias IP addresses, not primary instance addresses. Changing to /22 (C) reduces address space. IPv6 (D) is incompatible with existing IPv4 infrastructure.

questions.question: You are running out of primary internal IP addresses in a subnet for a custom mode VPC. The subnet has the IP range 10.0.0.0/20, and the IP addresses are primarily used by virtual machines in the project. You need to provide more IP addresses for the virtual machines. What should you do?

options.text: Create a single budget for all projects and configure budget alerts on this budget.
Create a separate billing account per sandbox project and enable BigQuery billing exports. Create a Data Studio dashboard to plot the spending per billing account.
Create a budget per project and configure budget alerts on all of these budgets.
Create a single billing account for all sandbox projects and enable BigQuery billing exports. Create a Data Studio dashboard to plot the spending per project.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Budgets can be scoped to specific projects within a billing account, and each budget can have its own alert thresholds that trigger email notifications (via Cloud Monitoring/Pub/Sub) when spending crosses the defined amount. To be notified when any individual developer's sandbox exceeds $500/month, you need a distinct budget scoped to each project (not a single combined budget, which would only reflect aggregate spend across all 10 projects and wouldn't identify which developer exceeded the threshold). Billing export to BigQuery with a Looker Studio (Data Studio) dashboard only supports visualization/reporting after the fact and does not provide proactive alerting/notifications, so it doesn't satisfy the requirement to be notified.

**Learn more:** [Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets)
