lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You create a Deployment with 2 replicas in a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster that has a single preemptible node pool. After a few minutes, you use `kubectl` to check the status of your Pods and notice that one of them is still showing a Pending status:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783718295874-0wmei56q.jpg)  
  
What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The pending Pod's resource requests are too large to fit on a single node of the cluster.
Too many Pods are already running in the cluster, and there are not enough resources left to schedule the pending Pod.
The node pool is configured with a service account that does not have permission to pull the container image used by the pending Pod.

The pending Pod was originally scheduled on a node that has been preempted between the creation of the Deployment and your verification of the Pods' status. It is currently being rescheduled on a new node.

questions.explanation:
Preemptible VM instances in Compute Engine (and therefore GKE nodes built on them) can be terminated by Google Cloud at any time, with the node receiving only a short termination notice before it is reclaimed. When a node running one of the Deployment's Pods is preempted, GKE evicts the Pod from that node, and the Deployment's ReplicaSet controller immediately creates a replacement Pod to maintain the desired replica count. That replacement Pod remains in Pending status until a new node becomes available and the scheduler places it there. Since the cluster's node pool consists entirely of preemptible nodes, and only a short time has passed since the Deployment was created, the most likely explanation for the temporarily Pending Pod is that its original node was preempted in the interim and it is now waiting to be rescheduled onto a new node — a normal and expected behavior of preemptible-based node pools, as described in GKE's guidance on using preemptible VMs for fault-tolerant workloads.

**Learn more:** [Use preemptible VMs to run fault-tolerant workloads | GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/preemptible-vms)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to manage a Cloud Spanner instance for best query performance. Your instance in production runs in a single Google Cloud region. You need to improve performance in the shortest amount of time. You want to follow Google best practices for service configuration. What should you do?

options.text: Create an alert in Cloud Monitoring to alert when the percentage of high priority CPU utilization reaches 45%. If you exceed this threshold, add nodes to your instance.

Create an alert in Cloud Monitoring to alert when the percentage of high priority CPU utilization reaches 45%. Use database query statistics to identify queries that result in high CPU usage, and then rewrite those queries to optimize their resource usage.
Create an alert in Cloud Monitoring to alert when the percentage of high priority CPU utilization reaches 65%. If you exceed this threshold, add nodes to your instance.

Create an alert in Cloud Monitoring to alert when the percentage of high priority CPU utilization reaches 65%. Use database query statistics to identify queries that result in high CPU usage, and then rewrite those queries to optimize their resource usage.

questions.explanation: For single-region Cloud Spanner instances, Google's best practice documentation specifies a maximum recommended CPU utilization threshold of 65% for high-priority traffic (not 45%, which applies only to multi-region instances). When this threshold is exceeded, you should add nodes to the instance. Setting alerts at the correct threshold enables proactive scaling before performance degradation occurs.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a new application and need a Jenkins installation to build and deploy your source code. You want to automate the installation as quickly and easily as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy Jenkins through the Google Cloud Marketplace.
Create a new Compute Engine instance. Run the Jenkins executable.
Create a new Kubernetes Engine cluster. Create a deployment for the Jenkins image.
Create an instance template with the Jenkins executable. Create a managed instance group with this template.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Marketplace offers a click-to-deploy Jenkins solution that automatically provisions a properly configured Compute Engine VM with Jenkins installed, along with the required firewall rules, disks, and startup scripts. This lets you get a fully functional Jenkins server running in minutes without manually installing software, writing deployment manifests, or configuring instance templates and managed instance groups, making it the fastest and easiest path to automate the installation.

**Learn more:** [Jenkins on Google Cloud Marketplace](https://console.cloud.google.com/marketplace/product/click-to-deploy-images/jenkins)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an application intended to run on Google Kubernetes Engine. You have determined that MongoDB is the best-suited database for this application, and you want to deploy a managed MongoDB environment that comes with a support SLA. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Bigtable cluster, and use the HBase API.
Deploy MongoDB Atlas from the Google Cloud Marketplace.
Download a MongoDB installation package, and run it on Compute Engine instances.
Download a MongoDB installation package, and run it on a Managed Instance Group.

questions.explanation:
MongoDB Atlas, available directly from the Google Cloud Marketplace, is the officially managed MongoDB-as-a-service offering. It provides an industry-standard uptime SLA (99.995%) along with end-to-end vendor support for the database service, and it integrates with Google Cloud billing and networking so it can be consumed by applications running on GKE. In contrast, running MongoDB yourself on Compute Engine instances or a Managed Instance Group makes you responsible for installation, patching, scaling, and availability with no vendor SLA, and Cloud Bigtable with the HBase API is an entirely different database technology, not MongoDB.

**Learn more:** [MongoDB Atlas | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/mongodb) · [MongoDB Atlas (pay-as-you-go) – Google Cloud Marketplace](https://console.cloud.google.com/marketplace/product/mongodb/mdb-atlas-self-service)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster with the cluster autoscaler feature enabled. You need to ensure that every node in the cluster runs a monitoring pod that sends container metrics to a third-party monitoring solution. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the monitoring pod in a StatefulSet object.
Deploy the monitoring pod in a DaemonSet object.
Reference the monitoring pod in a Deployment object.
Reference the monitoring pod in a cluster initializer at the GKE cluster creation time.

questions.explanation:
A DaemonSet guarantees that a copy of a specified pod runs on every node in the cluster, and automatically schedules a pod onto any new nodes that are added — including nodes added by the cluster autoscaler — making it the correct object type for deploying per-node monitoring/logging agents. StatefulSets are designed for stateful workloads requiring stable identities and persistent storage, not for ensuring one instance per node. Deployments manage a desired replica count independent of node count, so they cannot guarantee coverage on every node as the cluster scales. Cluster initializers were an alpha admission-control mechanism for intercepting resource creation and are unrelated to per-node pod scheduling.

**Learn more:** [DaemonSet | Kubernetes Documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/daemonset/)

You are building an application that processes data files uploaded from thousands of suppliers. Your primary goals for the application are data security and the expiration of aged data. You need to design the application so that it:  
  
- Restricts access so that suppliers can access only their own data.  
- Gives suppliers write access to data only for 30 minutes.  
- Deletes data that is over 45 days old.  
  
You have a very short development cycle, and you need to ensure that the application requires minimal maintenance. Which two strategies should you use? (Choose two.)

options.text: Build a lifecycle policy to delete Cloud Storage objects after 45 days.
Use signed URLs to allow suppliers limited time access to store their objects.
Set up an SFTP server for your application, and create a separate user for each supplier.
Build a Cloud function that triggers a timer of 45 days to delete objects that have expired.
Develop a script that loops through all Cloud Storage buckets and deletes any buckets that are older than 45 days.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage signed URLs provide time-limited, scoped access to a specific object without requiring you to build or maintain custom authentication infrastructure — you can set the expiration to 30 minutes and issue a unique URL per supplier so each supplier can only write to their own designated object/path. Object Lifecycle Management rules let you configure a Delete action with an Age condition (45 days) directly on the Cloud Storage bucket; Google Cloud automatically evaluates and enforces this rule daily with no custom code or servers to maintain, satisfying the aged-data-deletion requirement with minimal ongoing maintenance. Standing up an SFTP server with per-user accounts, writing a custom Cloud Function timer, or scripting bucket deletion all require building and maintaining custom infrastructure or code, which conflicts with the short development cycle and minimal-maintenance requirements.

**Learn more:** [Object Lifecycle Management | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle) · [Signed URLs | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls)

A team of data scientists only occasionally needs to use a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster that you manage. They require GPUs for some long-running jobs that cannot be restarted. You want to minimize cost. What should you do?

options.text: Enable node auto-provisioning on the GKE cluster.
Create a VerticalPodAutscaler for those workloads.
Create a node pool with preemptible VMs and GPUs attached to those VMs.
Create a node pool of instances with GPUs, and enable autoscaling on this node pool with a minimum size of 1.

questions.explanation:
Because the jobs are long-running and cannot be restarted, they must run on stable, non-preemptible compute — ruling out preemptible VMs, which can be terminated at any time by Google Cloud. To minimize cost while still meeting this reliability requirement, you create a dedicated node pool with GPU-attached instances and enable autoscaling with a minimum node count of 1. GKE's cluster autoscaler will scale the GPU node pool up when GPU-requesting pods are scheduled and scale it back down when demand drops, so you only pay for GPU nodes when they are actually needed, without risking interruption of jobs that cannot tolerate preemption.

**Learn more:** [About GKE cluster autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/cluster-autoscaler) · [Run GPUs in GKE Standard node pools](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/gpus)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You just installed the Google Cloud CLI on your new corporate laptop. You need to list the existing instances of your company on Google Cloud. What must you do before you run the gcloud compute instances list command? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run gcloud auth login, enter your login credentials in the dialog window, and paste the received login token to gcloud CLI.
Create a Google Cloud service account, and download the service account key. Place the key file in a folder on your machine where gcloud CLI can find it.
Download your Cloud Identity user account key. Place the key file in a folder on your machine where gcloud CLI can find it.
Run gcloud config set compute/zone $my_zone to set the default zone for gcloud CLI.
Run gcloud config set project $my_project to set the default project for gcloud CLI.

questions.explanation: Before gcloud can make any authenticated API call, you must sign in with gcloud auth login so the CLI has credentials tied to your account, and you must set a default project with gcloud config set project, since resource-listing commands run against whichever project is currently configured. A default zone is unrelated to a project-wide instances list, and downloading service account or Cloud Identity user keys is not how an interactive human administrator authenticates with gcloud.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company closely monitors its cloud spending. You need to enable different teams to monitor their Google Cloud costs. Ensure that team members receive notifications when cloud spend reaches specified thresholds, and allow them to create dashboards for further insights using detailed billing data. You want to follow Google-recommended practices while minimizing engineering costs. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy Grafana to Compute Engine. Create a dashboard for each team that uses the data from the Cloud Billing API. Ask each team to create their own alerts in Cloud Monitoring.
Set up alerts for each team based on required thresholds. Create a shell script to read data from the Cloud Billing API, and push the results to BigQuery. Grant team members access to BigQuery.
Deploy Grafana to Compute Engine. Create a dashboard for each team that uses the data from the Cloud Billing Budget API. Ask each team to create their own alerts in Grafana.
Set up alerts for each team based on required thresholds. Set up billing exports to BigQuery. Grant team members access to BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Billing budgets and budget alerts provide managed spend-threshold notifications. Cloud Billing export to BigQuery automatically exports detailed usage-cost data, including resource-level information, so authorized team members can query it and build custom dashboards without operating Grafana or maintaining scripts.

**Learn more:** [Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets) · [Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have built an application composed of multiple microservices, with each microservice packaged as its own Docker container image. You want to deploy the whole application on Google Kubernetes Engine in a way that lets each microservice be scaled independently. What should you do?

options.text: Create and deploy a Custom Resource Definition per microservice.
Create and deploy a Docker Compose File.
Create and deploy a Job per microservice.
Create and deploy a Deployment per microservice.

questions.explanation:
In Kubernetes/GKE, a Deployment is the standard resource for running and managing long-lived, scalable sets of container replicas. By creating a separate Deployment for each microservice, you can independently set and adjust the replica count (or attach a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) for each service without affecting the others. Jobs are intended for run-to-completion batch workloads rather than continuously running, independently scalable services. Docker Compose files are not a native Kubernetes/GKE deployment mechanism. Custom Resource Definitions extend the Kubernetes API for custom controllers/operators but are not required or standard for simply deploying and independently scaling containerized microservices.

**Learn more:** [Deployments | Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has developed a stateless application which requires it to be run directly on virtual machines. The application is expected to receive a fluctuating amount of traffic and needs to scale automatically. You need to deploy the application. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the application on a managed instance group and configure autoscaling.
Deploy the application on a Kubernetes Engine cluster and configure node pool autoscaling.
Deploy the application on Cloud Functions and configure the maximum number instances.
Deploy the application on Cloud Run and configure autoscaling.

questions.explanation: Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) are purpose-built for running stateless applications on VMs with automatic scaling. MIGs provide auto-healing, load balancing, and configurable autoscaling policies based on CPU, HTTP traffic, or custom metrics. This satisfies both the requirement to run on VMs and the need for automatic scaling in response to traffic fluctuations.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: You are migrating your company’s on-premises compute resources to Google Cloud. You need to deploy batch processing jobs that run every night. The jobs require significant CPU and memory for several hours but can tolerate interruptions. You must ensure that the deployment is cost-effective. What should you do?

options.text: Use the M1 machine series on Compute Engine.
Containerize the batch processing jobs and deploy them on Compute Engine.
Use Spot VMs on Compute Engine.
Use custom machine types on Compute Engine.

questions.explanation: Spot VMs offer up to 70% cost savings compared to standard on-demand instances, making them ideal for fault-tolerant batch workloads. Because the nightly batch jobs can tolerate interruptions and run for limited durations, Spot VMs provide the most cost-effective solution without requiring architectural complexity or custom VM sizing.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: You are migrating your company’s on-premises compute resources to Google Cloud. You need to deploy batch processing jobs that run every night. The jobs require significant CPU and memory for several hours but can tolerate interruptions. You must ensure that the deployment is cost-effective. What should you do?

options.text: Cold Storage
Nearline Storage
Regional Storage
Multi-Regional Storage

questions.explanation:
Coldline Storage (referred to here as Cold Storage) is the Google Cloud Storage class designed for data that is accessed at most once every 90 days (roughly quarterly). It offers very low storage costs while charging retrieval fees, making it the most cost-effective choice for infrequently accessed archival data with a quarterly access pattern. Nearline Storage is optimized for data accessed about once a month, making it less cost-efficient than Coldline for quarterly access. Regional and Multi-Regional Storage are location/availability configurations for the Standard storage class, intended for frequently accessed data, and are not designed as low-cost archival tiers.

**Learn more:** [Storage classes | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an object stored in a Cloud Storage bucket that contains sensitive data, and you want to share it with an external company. You want access to the content to be revoked after four hours. The external company does not have a Google account that you could use to grant specific user-based access privileges. You want to use the most secure method that requires the fewest steps. What should you do?

options.text: Create a signed URL with a four-hour expiration and share the URL with the company.
Set object access to 'public' and use object lifecycle management to remove the object after four hours.
Configure the storage bucket as a static website and furnish the object's URL to the company. Delete the object from the storage bucket after four hours.
Create a new Cloud Storage bucket specifically for the external company to access. Copy the object to that bucket. Delete the bucket after four hours have passed.

questions.explanation:
A signed URL grants time-limited read (or other) access to a specific Cloud Storage object without requiring the recipient to have a Google account or any IAM permissions. You generate the URL with an expiration set to four hours, and after that time the URL becomes invalid automatically, revoking access without further action. This approach is more secure than making the object public (which exposes the sensitive data to anyone with the link indefinitely until manually cleaned up) and requires far fewer steps than creating a separate bucket, copying the object, and deleting the bucket afterward. Google Cloud's documentation specifically recommends signed URLs for providing temporary access to private objects to users who lack Google accounts.

**Learn more:** [Signed URLs | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a virtual machine that is currently configured with 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of memory. It is running out of memory. You want to upgrade the virtual machine to have 8 GB of memory. What should you do?

options.text: Rely on live migration to move the workload to a machine with more memory.
Use gcloud to add metadata to the VM. Set the key to required-memory-size and the value to 8 GB.
Stop the VM, change the machine type to n1-standard-8, and start the VM.
Stop the VM, increase the memory to 8 GB, and start the VM.

questions.explanation: To increase VM memory in Google Cloud, stop the instance first (live migration only moves VMs between hosts without changing properties), then increase the memory to the desired size via the machine configuration, and restart. Custom machine types can be created with exact memory specifications without requiring a predefined instance type like n1-standard-8, which may have excess resources. Metadata and live migration alone cannot change compute resources.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring Cloud DNS. You want to create DNS records to point home.mydomain.com, mydomain.com, and www.mydomain.com to the IP address of your Google Cloud load balancer. What should you do?

options.text: Create one CNAME record to point mydomain.com to the load balancer, and create two A records to point WWW and HOME to mydomain.com respectively.
Create one CNAME record to point mydomain.com to the load balancer, and create two AAAA records to point WWW and HOME to mydomain.com respectively.
Create one A record to point mydomain.com to the load balancer, and create two CNAME records to point WWW and HOME to mydomain.com respectively.
Create one A record to point mydomain.com to the load balancer, and create two NS records to point WWW and HOME to mydomain.com respectively.

questions.explanation: DNS best practice requires an A record for the root domain (mydomain.com pointing to the load balancer IP) and CNAME records for subdomains (www and home pointing back to mydomain.com). CNAME cannot be used for the root domain as it conflicts with other record types. Options A and B violate this fundamental DNS principle.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to enable your development team to deploy new features to an existing Cloud Run service in production. To minimize the risk associated with a new revision, you want to reduce the number of customers who might be affected by an outage without introducing any development or operational costs to your customers. You want to follow Google-recommended practices for managing revisions to a service. What should you do?

options.text: Ask your customers to retry access to your service with exponential backoff to mitigate any potential problems after the new revision is deployed.
Gradually roll out the new revision and split customer traffic between the revisions to allow rollback in case a problem occurs.
Send all customer traffic to the new revision, and roll back to a previous revision if you witness any problems in production.
Deploy your application to a second Cloud Run service, and ask your customers to use the second Cloud Run service.

questions.explanation: Gradual traffic rollout is the Google-recommended practice for reducing blast radius during deployments. This approach allows monitoring the new revision with a small percentage of customers while maintaining the ability to rollback instantly to the previous revision if problems occur. No development or operational changes are required on the customer side, and no additional infrastructure costs are introduced.

options.text: Assign the auditor the IAM role roles/logging.privateLogViewer. Perform the export of logs to Cloud Storage.
Assign the auditor the IAM role roles/logging.privateLogViewer. Direct the auditor to also review the logs for changes to Cloud IAM policy.
Assign the auditor's IAM user to a custom role that has logging.privateLogEntries.list permission. Perform the export of logs to Cloud Storage.
Assign the auditor's IAM user to a custom role that has logging.privateLogEntries.list permission. Direct the auditor to also review the logs for changes to Cloud IAM policy.

questions.explanation:
The predefined role roles/logging.privateLogViewer includes all the permissions of roles/logging.viewer (which covers standard Admin Activity audit logs, including entries for changes to Cloud IAM policy) plus the additional permissions required to view Data Access audit logs stored in the _Default log bucket. Granting this single predefined role to the auditor, and instructing them to also review the Admin Activity logs for IAM policy changes, satisfies both stated requirements without needing to export logs or build a fragile custom role around a single list permission, which would not provide full log-viewing access equivalent to the predefined role.

**Learn more:** [Access control with IAM | Cloud Logging | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/access-control) · [Cloud Audit Logs overview | Cloud Logging | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit)

Your organization uses G Suite for communication and collaboration, and every user in the organization already has a G Suite account. You want to grant some of these G Suite users access to your Cloud Platform project. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud Identity in the GCP Console for your domain.
Grant them the required IAM roles using their G Suite email address.
Create a CSV sheet with all users' email addresses. Use the gcloud command line tool to convert them into Google Cloud Platform accounts.
In the G Suite console, add the users to a special group called [email protected]. Rely on the default behavior of the Cloud Platform to grant users access if they are members of this group.

questions.explanation:
G Suite accounts are Google identities managed through Cloud Identity, and Google Cloud IAM natively supports granting roles to any existing Google Account, including G Suite email addresses, without any additional account creation or conversion step. To grant access, an administrator simply adds an IAM policy binding for each user's G Suite email address with the appropriate role(s) at the project (or higher) level, as described in Google Cloud's IAM documentation on granting roles to users, groups, and domains.

**Learn more:** [Grant an IAM role to users - Google Cloud IAM documentation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/granting-changing-revoking-access) · [Overview of Cloud Identity - Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/identity/docs/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a batch workload that runs every night and uses a large number of virtual machines (VMs). It is fault-tolerant and can tolerate some of the VMs being terminated. The current cost of VMs is too high. What should you do?

options.text: Run a test using simulated maintenance events. If the test is successful, use preemptible N1 Standard VMs when running future jobs.
Run a test using simulated maintenance events. If the test is successful, use N1 Standard VMs when running future jobs.
Run a test using a managed instance group. If the test is successful, use N1 Standard VMs in the managed instance group when running future jobs.
Run a test using N1 standard VMs instead of N2. If the test is successful, use N1 Standard VMs when running future jobs.

questions.explanation:
Because the batch workload is fault-tolerant and can tolerate VM termination, it is well suited to Google Cloud preemptible VMs, which cost significantly less than standard VMs (up to 80% cheaper) but can be reclaimed by Compute Engine at any time. Google recommends first running a test using simulated maintenance events (via the Compute Engine API) to verify that the application correctly handles preemption/termination signals before relying on preemptible VMs in production. Once validated, switching future nightly batch jobs to preemptible N1 Standard VMs reduces cost while remaining appropriate for a fault-tolerant workload.

**Learn more:** [Preemptible VM instances | Compute Engine Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/preemptible) · [Testing preemption behavior with simulated maintenance events](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/simulating-host-maintenance)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a large company that has recently acquired three smaller startups. All Google Cloud resources belonging to the startups must be managed centrally under one Google Cloud organization. However, every startup has its own budget and financial-reporting structure. You need to make sure each startup gets a separate monthly invoice for its Google Cloud usage. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google Cloud organization with a folder for each startup. Share a single Cloud Billing account, and use the detailed billing export to allocate costs.
Create a Google Cloud organization with a folder for each startup. Configure each startup to have its own Cloud Billing account.
Create a Google Cloud organization for each startup. Configure each startup to have its own Cloud Billing account.

questions.explanation:
A single Google Cloud organization centrally manages its folders and projects. questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have received a JSON file containing the private key of a Service Account, which grants access to several resources in a Google Cloud project. After downloading and installing the Cloud SDK, you want to use this private key to authenticate and authorize when running gcloud commands. What should you do?

options.text: Use the command gcloud auth login and point it to the private key.
Use the command gcloud auth activate-service-account and point it to the private key.
Place the private key file in the installation directory of the Cloud SDK and rename it to ג€credentials.jsonג€.
Place the private key file in your home directory and rename it to ג€GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALSג€.

questions.explanation:
The `gcloud auth activate-service-account` command is specifically designed to authorize gcloud (and other SDK tools) using a service account's private key JSON file. Running this command with the `--key-file` flag pointing to the downloaded JSON key activates the service account as the active identity for subsequent gcloud commands. In contrast, `gcloud auth login` is used for interactive user account authentication (via browser-based OAuth flow), not for service account keys. Renaming the key file to 'credentials.json' and placing it in the SDK installation directory is not a supported mechanism. GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS is an environment variable (not a filename) that points to a credentials file for use by Application Default Credentials in client libraries — it is not something you rename a file to.

**Learn more:** [gcloud auth activate-service-account | Google Cloud CLI Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/auth/activate-service-account)

You are deploying an application to App Engine. You want the number of instances to scale based on request rate, and you need at least 3 unoccupied (idle) instances available at all times. Which scaling type should you use?

options.text: Manual Scaling with 3 instances.
Basic Scaling with min_instances set to 3.
Basic Scaling with max_instances set to 3.
Automatic Scaling with min_idle_instances set to 3.

questions.explanation:
Automatic Scaling adjusts the number of running instances dynamically according to request rate, latency, and other traffic metrics, and it supports a min_idle_instances setting in the automatic_scaling block of app.yaml that reserves a specified number of idle instances so incoming requests are served immediately without cold-start delay. Setting min_idle_instances to 3 satisfies the requirement of always having at least 3 unoccupied instances while still allowing the total instance count to scale up and down based on request rate. In contrast, Basic Scaling only creates instances when requests arrive and does not support a min_instances/min_idle setting (it uses max_instances to cap scaling), and Manual Scaling keeps a fixed set of instances running at all times without scaling based on request load.

**Learn more:** [How instances are managed | App Engine standard environment](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/how-instances-are-managed)

questions.domain: Setting up a cloud solution environment
questions.question:
You have created a new project in Google Cloud through the gcloud command line interface (CLI) and linked a billing account. You need to create a new Compute  

Engine instance using the CLI. You need to perform the prerequisite steps. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Monitoring Workspace.
Create a VPC network in the project.
Enable the compute googleapis.com API.
Grant yourself the IAM role of Computer Admin.

questions.explanation: The Compute Engine API (compute.googleapis.com) must be enabled before you can create Compute Engine instances via CLI. Google Cloud requires services to be explicitly enabled before use. Monitoring workspaces, VPC networks, and IAM roles are important but come after API enablement.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question:
You have created a new project in Google Cloud through the gcloud command line interface (CLI) and linked a billing account. You need to create a new Compute  

Engine instance using the CLI. You need to perform the prerequisite steps. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the size of the disk to 1 TB.
Increase the allocated CPU to the instance.
Migrate to use a Local SSD on the instance.
Migrate to use a Regional SSD on the instance.

questions.explanation:
Local SSDs are physically attached to the host and deliver far higher IOPS and throughput than any zonal SSD persistent disk configuration, at a lower cost than continually resizing the persistent disk. Since the workload is read-heavy on large files rather than CPU-bound, migrating those reads to a Local SSD directly relieves the throttling instead of paying for more capacity (A), more CPU (B), or a regional disk that trades performance for cross-zone replication (D).

**Learn more:** [About Local SSD-backed disks | Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/local-ssd)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has decided to deploy all its compute workloads to Kubernetes on Google Cloud and two other cloud providers. You want to build an Infrastructure-as-code solution to automate the provisioning process for all cloud resources. What should you do?

options.text: Build the solution by using Config Connector, and provision the resources.
Build the solution by using Terraform, and provision the resources.
Build solution by using Python and the cloud SDKs from all providers to provision the resources.
Build the solution by using YAML manifests, and provision the resources.

questions.explanation:
Terraform is a cloud-agnostic infrastructure-as-code tool with providers for Google Cloud, AWS, Azure, and Kubernetes, making it the standard choice for provisioning workloads consistently across multiple cloud providers from a single codebase. Config Connector only manages Google Cloud resources, and hand-rolled scripts using each provider's SDK or raw YAML manifests would require far more custom engineering to replicate what Terraform already provides.

**Learn more:** [Terraform on Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],After a recent security incident, your startup company wants better insight into what is happening in the Google Cloud environment. You need to monitor unexpected firewall changes and instance creation. Your company prefers simple solutions. What should you do?

options.text: Create a log sink to forward Cloud Audit Logs filtered for firewalls and compute instances to Cloud Storage. Use BigQuery to periodically analyze log events in the storage bucket.
Use Cloud Logging filters to create log-based metrics for firewall and instance actions. Monitor the changes and set up reasonable alerts.

Install Kibana on a compute instance. Create a log sink to forward Cloud Audit Logs filtered for firewalls and compute instances to Pub/Sub. Target the Pub/Sub topic to push messages to the Kibana instance. Analyze the logs on Kibana in real time.
Turn on Google Cloud firewall rules logging, and set up alerts for any insert, update, or delete events.

questions.explanation: Cloud Logging filters with log-based metrics and alerts provide a simple, native solution for monitoring specific events without additional tools or infrastructure. This approach directly monitors Cloud Audit Logs for firewall and instance creation events. Log sinks to BigQuery add complexity for periodic analysis, while custom Kibana installations introduce operational overhead contrary to the stated preference for simplicity.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a single file containing 32 GB of data that needs to be uploaded to a Nearline Storage bucket. The WAN connection being used is rated at 1 Gbps, and you are the only user on that connection. You want to maximize use of the rated 1 Gbps bandwidth so the file transfers as quickly as possible.  
  
How should you upload the file?

options.text: Use the GCP Console to transfer the file instead of gsutil.
Enable parallel composite uploads using gsutil on the file transfer.
Decrease the TCP window size on the machine initiating the transfer.
Change the storage class of the bucket from Nearline to Multi-Regional.

questions.explanation:
gsutil supports parallel composite uploads, which break a large file into multiple chunks that are uploaded concurrently over separate connections and then composed into the final object once all chunks arrive. This parallelism allows a single large file transfer to make much better use of available WAN bandwidth than a single-stream upload, which is especially useful for large files like a 32 GB object on a fast (1 Gbps) link. Using the GCP Console would not provide this parallel chunking benefit, decreasing the TCP window size would lower throughput rather than increase it, and changing the bucket's storage class only affects storage tier/pricing behavior, not upload transfer speed.

**Learn more:** [Parallel composite uploads | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/parallel-composite-uploads)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to monitor resources that are distributed across different projects in Google Cloud Platform, and you want to consolidate reporting under the same Stackdriver Monitoring dashboard. What should you do?

options.text: Use Shared VPC to connect all projects, and link Stackdriver to one of the projects.
For each project, create a Stackdriver account. In each project, create a service account for that project and grant it the role of Stackdriver Account Editor in all other projects.
Configure a single Stackdriver account, and link all projects to the same account.
Configure a single Stackdriver account for one of the projects. In Stackdriver, create a Group and add the other project names as criteria for that Group.

questions.explanation:
Stackdriver Monitoring (Cloud Monitoring) organizes monitoring data using a Workspace (formerly known as a metrics scope), which can span multiple GCP projects. By configuring a single Stackdriver account and linking the other projects to it as monitored projects, all their metrics, dashboards, and alerting policies become visible and consolidated within that one workspace, satisfying the requirement to report on resources from different projects in a single dashboard. Shared VPC (A) only addresses network connectivity, not monitoring data aggregation. Creating separate Stackdriver accounts per project with cross-project IAM roles (B) does not merge reporting into a single dashboard. Stackdriver Groups (D) are used to organize resources like VM instances, databases, and load balancers within an existing workspace, not to add entire additional projects as monitored projects.

**Learn more:** [Workspaces | Stackdriver Monitoring | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/workspaces/) · [Using Stackdriver Workspaces to help manage your hybrid and multicloud environment | Google Cloud Blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/management-tools/using-stackdriver-workspaces-help-manage-your-hybrid-and-multicloud-environment)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an application that will be deployed on Google Cloud. The application will use a service account to retrieve data from BigQuery. Before you deploy your application, you want to test the permissions of this service account from your local machine to ensure there will be no authentication issues. You want to ensure that you use the most secure method while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Generate a service account key, and configure the gcloud CLI to use this key. Issue a relevant BigQuery request through the gdoud CLI to test the access.
Grant the service account the BigQuery Administrator IAM role to ensure the service account has all required access.
Configure the gcloud CLI to use service account impersonation. Issue a relevant BigQuery request through the gcloud CLI to test the access.
Configure the gcloud CLI with Application Default Credentials using your user account. Issue a relevant BigQuery request through the gcloud CLI to test the access.

questions.explanation: Service account impersonation is the most secure method for testing service account permissions because it avoids storing long-lived service account keys locally. Using your own credentials to impersonate the service account follows Google-recommended security practices and reduces the risk of key compromise.

You need to set up an SSH connection to a single Compute Engine instance for the users in the dev1 group. This instance is the only resource in this particular Google Cloud Platform project that dev1 users should be able to connect to. What should you do?

options.text: Set metadata to enable-oslogin=true for the instance. Grant the dev1 group the compute.osLogin role. Direct them to use the Cloud Shell to ssh to that instance.
Set metadata to enable-oslogin=true for the instance. Set the service account to no service account for that instance. Direct them to use the Cloud Shell to ssh to that instance.
Enable block project wide keys for the instance. Generate an SSH key for each user in the dev1 group. Distribute the keys to dev1 users and direct them to use their third-party tools to connect.

Enable block project wide keys for the instance. Generate an SSH key and associate the key with that instance. Distribute the key to dev1 users and direct them to use their third-party tools to connect.

questions.explanation:
OS Login provides centralized, IAM-based management of SSH access to Compute Engine instances without requiring manual SSH key distribution. Setting the enable-oslogin=true metadata key on the specific instance (rather than at the project level) ensures that only that instance uses OS Login for access control, leaving other instances unaffected. Granting the dev1 group the compute.osLogin IAM role tied to that instance allows those users to authenticate and connect via SSH (including through Cloud Shell using gcloud compute ssh) while keeping access scoped to just that one resource, satisfying the requirement that dev1 users can reach only this instance in the project.

**Learn more:** [Set up OS Login](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/oslogin/set-up-oslogin) · [Manage OS Login in an organization](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/oslogin/set-up-oslogin#configure_users)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Company management has asked an external auditor to review all the resources in a specific project. The security team has enabled the Organization Policy called Domain Restricted Sharing on the organization node, specifying only your Cloud Identity domain. You want the auditor to be able to only view — not modify — the resources in that project.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Ask the auditor for their Google account, and give them the Viewer role on the project.
Ask the auditor for their Google account, and give them the Security Reviewer role on the project.
Create a temporary account for the auditor in Cloud Identity, and give that account the Viewer role on the project.
Create a temporary account for the auditor in Cloud Identity, and give that account the Security Reviewer role on the project.

questions.explanation:
With Domain Restricted Sharing enforced to allow only the organization's Cloud Identity domain, no principal outside that domain (such as the auditor's personal Google account) can be granted an IAM role on the project — this rules out simply adding the auditor's own Google account. Instead, a temporary account must be created for the auditor within the Cloud Identity domain so it complies with the policy. That account should then be granted the basic Viewer role (roles/viewer), which provides broad read-only access to view the configuration and details of resources across the project without allowing any modifications. The Security Reviewer role (roles/iam.securityReviewer) is not appropriate here because it only grants permission to view IAM policies and grantable roles, not general read access to the project's resources.

**Learn more:** [Restrict identities with domain-restricted sharing | Organization Policy | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/organization-policy/restrict-domains) · [Domain-restricted sharing | Organization Policy | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/organization-policy/domain-restricted-sharing)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You operate a data warehouse on BigQuery. A partner company wants to build a recommendation engine using data from your data warehouse. This partner company also runs its own workloads on Google Cloud, managing its resources within its own separate project, but it needs access to the BigQuery dataset that resides in your project.  
  
What should you do to provide the partner company with access to the dataset?

options.text: Create a Service Account in your own project, and grant this Service Account access to BigQuery in your project.
Create a Service Account in your own project, and ask the partner to grant this Service Account access to BigQuery in their project.
Ask the partner to create a Service Account in their project, and have them give the Service Account access to BigQuery in their project.
Ask the partner to create a Service Account in their project, and grant their Service Account access to the BigQuery dataset in your project.

questions.explanation:
Following BigQuery's dataset access-control model, the data owner should grant IAM roles (such as BigQuery Data Viewer) at the dataset level to a specific principal — in this case, a service account. Since the partner runs its recommendation engine in its own project, it should create and manage that service account itself. You, as the data owner, then grant that partner-owned service account the appropriate role directly on your BigQuery dataset. This lets the partner's application authenticate as its own service account and query your dataset cross-project, without needing project-level access to your environment, while you retain full control over which resource (the dataset) is shared and at what permission level.

**Learn more:** [Controlling access to datasets](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/dataset-access-controls) · [Securing and Sharing BigQuery Datasets and Tables | Google Skills for Partners](https://partner.skills.google/focuses/58504?parent=catalog)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a development project that already has the appropriate IAM roles configured. You are creating a new production project and want that project to have the same IAM roles, using the fewest possible steps. What should you do?

options.text: Use gcloud iam roles copy and specify the production project as the destination project.
Use gcloud iam roles copy and specify your organization as the destination organization.
In the Google Cloud Platform Console, use the 'create role from role' functionality.
In the Google Cloud Platform Console, use the 'create role' functionality and select all applicable permissions.

questions.explanation:
The `gcloud iam roles copy` command lets you copy an existing custom IAM role directly to a new destination, which can be either a project or an organization. Because the roles exist on the development project and need to be replicated on the production project (a project-to-project copy, not project-to-organization), you specify the production project as the destination project using the `--dest-project` flag (with `--source-project` identifying the development project). This is a single command per role and is far fewer steps than manually recreating each role through the Console via 'create role from role' or by selecting permissions individually in 'create role'.

**Learn more:** [gcloud iam roles copy | Google Cloud SDK | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/iam/roles/copy)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure a policy so that video files kept in a specific Regional Cloud Storage bucket are transitioned to Coldline storage after 90 days, and then deleted one year after their creation date. Which approach should you use to set up this policy?

options.text: Use Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management using Age conditions with SetStorageClass and Delete actions. Set the SetStorageClass action to 90 days and the Delete action to 275 days (365 ג€
Use Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management using Age conditions with SetStorageClass and Delete actions. Set the SetStorageClass action to 90 days and the Delete action to 365 days.
Use gsutil rewrite and set the Delete action to 275 days (365-90).
Use gsutil rewrite and set the Delete action to 365 days.

questions.explanation:
In Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management, an Age-based condition is always calculated as the number of days since the object was created, regardless of any prior lifecycle actions applied to it. This means each rule operates independently against the object's creation timestamp. To achieve the described behavior, you configure a lifecycle rule with an Age condition of 90 days paired with a SetStorageClass action targeting Coldline, and a separate rule with an Age condition of 365 days paired with a Delete action — both measured from the object's creation date. There's no need to subtract 90 from 365, since the deletion rule's age condition is independent of the storage class change and still measures from creation date.

**Learn more:** [Object Lifecycle Management | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage an App Engine service that aggregates and visualizes data from BigQuery. The application is deployed using the default App Engine service account.  
  
The data that needs to be visualized resides in a different project managed by another team. You do not have access to this project, but you want your application to be able to read data from the BigQuery dataset in it.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Ask the other team to grant your default App Engine Service account the role of BigQuery Job User.
Ask the other team to grant your default App Engine Service account the role of BigQuery Data Viewer.
In Cloud IAM of your project, ensure that the default App Engine service account has the role of BigQuery Data Viewer.
In Cloud IAM of your project, grant a newly created service account from the other team the role of BigQuery Job User in your project.

questions.explanation:
Reading data from a BigQuery dataset owned by another project requires the reader's identity (here, the default App Engine service account) to be granted read access on that dataset/project — specifically the BigQuery Data Viewer role (roles/bigquery.dataViewer). Because this IAM grant must be made on the resource being accessed, and you do not have access to the other project, the only viable action is to ask the owning team to add your App Engine service account with the BigQuery Data Viewer role. Running the query job itself uses the job-runner's own project quota, which the default App Engine service account already has via its existing project role, so no changes are needed there.

**Learn more:** [Controlling access to datasets](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/dataset-access-controls) · [BigQuery IAM roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/access-control)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are working for a startup that was officially registered as a business 6 months ago. As your customer base grows, your use of Google Cloud increases. You want to allow all engineers to create new projects without asking them for their credit card information. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Billing account, associate a payment method with it, and provide all project creators with permission to associate that billing account with their projects.
Grant all engineers permission to create their own billing accounts for each new project.
Apply for monthly invoiced billing, and have a single invoice for the project paid by the finance team.
Create a billing account, associate it with a monthly purchase order (PO), and send the PO to Google Cloud.

questions.explanation: Creating a central billing account with a payment method and granting project creators the billing.user permission allows engineers to link new projects to the shared billing account without providing personal credit cards. Option C (invoiced billing) requires the business to be registered for at least one year and meet minimum spending thresholds, disqualifying the 6-month-old startup.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises data analytics set of binaries that processes data files in memory for about 45 minutes every midnight. The sizes of those data files range from 1 gigabyte to 16 gigabytes. You want to migrate this application to Google Cloud with minimal effort and cost. What should you do?

options.text: Create a container for the set of binaries. Use Cloud Scheduler to start a Cloud Run job for the container.
Create a container for the set of binaries. Deploy the container to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and use the Kubernetes scheduler to start the application.
Upload the code to Cloud Functions. Use Cloud Scheduler to start the application.
Lift and shift to a VM on Compute Engine. Use an instance schedule to start and stop the instance.

questions.explanation: A 45-minute, late-night batch job with 1–16 GB data files is ideally suited to lift-and-shift onto a Compute Engine VM. Instance scheduling automatically starts and stops the VM at midnight, eliminating idle costs. Containerization (Cloud Run or GKE) adds unnecessary complexity and development overhead for a simple batch job.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Google Cloud Platform project that contains an App Engine application. The application was originally set up to serve from the us-central region. You now need the application to be served from the asia-northeast1 region instead. What should you do?

options.text: Change the default region property setting in the existing GCP project to asia-northeast1.
Change the region property setting in the existing App Engine application from us-central to asia-northeast1.
Create a second App Engine application in the existing GCP project and specify asia-northeast1 as the region to serve your application.
Create a new GCP project and create an App Engine application inside this new project. Specify asia-northeast1 as the region to serve your application.

questions.explanation: In App Engine, the region selected when the application is created is permanent and cannot be modified later — there is no setting to change an existing App Engine app's region. Additionally, each GCP project can host only one App Engine application, so a second App Engine app cannot be added to the same project. To serve an application from asia-northeast1, you must create a new GCP project and create a new App Engine application within it, specifying asia-northeast1 as the region during creation.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring service accounts for an application that spans multiple projects. Virtual machines (VMs) running in the web-applications project need access to BigQuery datasets in the crm-databases project. You want to follow Google-recommended practices to grant access to the service account in the web-applications project. What should you do?

options.text: Grant
Grant
Grant
Grant roles/bigquery.dataViewer role to crm-databases and appropriate roles to web-applications.

questions.explanation:
Google's least-privilege guidance for cross-project service accounts is to grant the account the specific role it needs directly on the resource's own project — here, roles/bigquery.dataViewer on the crm-databases project — and to grant only the permissions it actually needs within its home project. Granting a broad Owner role on either project exposes far more access than reading BigQuery datasets requires.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for using service accounts](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-for-using-and-managing-service-accounts)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Some employees at your organization have been creating projects on Google Cloud Platform and paying for them using their own personal credit cards, which the company later reimburses. The company now wants to consolidate all of these projects under one new, centralized billing account. What should you do?

options.text: Contact [email protected] with your bank account details and request a corporate billing account for your company.
Create a ticket with Google Support and wait for their call to share your credit card details over the phone.
In the Google Platform Console, go to the Resource Manage and move all projects to the root Organizarion.
In the Google Cloud Platform Console, create a new billing account and set up a payment method.

questions.explanation:
To centralize billing for existing Google Cloud projects, you create a new Cloud Billing account through the Google Cloud Console and configure a valid payment method (such as a corporate credit card) on it. Once the billing account exists, you can link each of the existing projects to that single billing account, allowing all charges to be consolidated and paid through the company's official payment method instead of individual employees' personal cards. This is the standard, documented workflow for managing billing in Google Cloud — there is no process involving emailing a special address with bank details or providing credit card information over the phone to support, and moving projects into an Organization resource hierarchy addresses resource management/organization structure, not billing consolidation.

**Learn more:** [Create, modify, or close your self-serve Cloud Billing account](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/manage-billing-account) · [Enable, disable, or change billing for a project](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/modify-project)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a pipeline to process time-series data. Based on the architecture diagram below, which Google Cloud Platform services belong in boxes 1, 2, 3, and 4?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783718309206-9l7biwqd.jpg)

options.text: Cloud Pub/Sub, Cloud Dataflow, Cloud Datastore, BigQuery
Firebase Messages, Cloud Pub/Sub, Cloud Spanner, BigQuery
Cloud Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Pub/Sub, Cloud Dataflow, Cloud Bigtable, BigQuery

questions.explanation:
In Google's standard IoT/time-series data processing architecture, device data flows from constrained and standard devices through a gateway into Cloud Pub/Sub (box 1), which ingests and buffers the incoming messages. Cloud Dataflow (box 2) then consumes and processes/transforms this streaming data, forking the output to two destinations: a storage sink and an analytics sink. Cloud Bigtable (box 3) is used as the storage destination because it is optimized for high-throughput, low-latency reads/writes typical of time-series and IoT workloads. BigQuery (box 4) is used as the analytics destination because it provides serverless SQL-based analytics over large processed datasets. This flow (Pub/Sub → Dataflow → Bigtable for storage, BigQuery for analytics) is documented in Google's reference IoT architecture.

**Learn more:** [IoT platform product architecture on Google Cloud | Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/connected-devices/iot-platform-product-architecture) · [Bigtable overview | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution

options.text: Deploy the web application on Google Kubernetes Engine standard edition with an internal ingress.
Deploy the web application on Cloud Run with Private Google Access configured.
Deploy the web application on Cloud Run with Private Service Connect configured.
Deploy the web application to GKE Autopilot with Private Google Access configured.

questions.explanation: Private Service Connect for Cloud Run publishes the service as an internal endpoint that is reachable from the VPC and, together with VPN or Interconnect, from the on-premises network, while Cloud Run itself stays fully serverless with nothing to provision or patch. Private Google Access only allows resources without external IPs to reach Google APIs and services outbound; it does not expose a Cloud Run service for inbound access from on-premises networks. **Learn more:** [Private Service Connect](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/private-service-connect)

You have an application that uses Cloud Spanner as a database backend to keep current state information about users. Cloud Bigtable logs all events triggered by users. You export Cloud Spanner data to Cloud Storage during daily backups.  
  
An analyst asks you to join data from Cloud Spanner and Cloud Bigtable for specific users. You want to complete this ad hoc request as efficiently as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a dataflow job that copies data from Cloud Bigtable and Cloud Storage for specific users.
Create a dataflow job that copies data from Cloud Bigtable and Cloud Spanner for specific users.
Create a Cloud Dataproc cluster that runs a Spark job to extract data from Cloud Bigtable and Cloud Storage for specific users.
Create two separate BigQuery external tables on Cloud Storage and Cloud Bigtable. Use the BigQuery console to join these tables through user fields, and apply appropriate filters.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery lets you create external tables that query data residing in Cloud Storage and in Cloud Bigtable without first loading or copying that data into BigQuery-managed storage. By creating one external table over the Cloud Storage export of the Spanner backup and another external table over the Bigtable data, an analyst can run a standard SQL join across both sources directly in the BigQuery console, filtering for the specific users needed. This approach requires no pipeline development, cluster provisioning, or data movement, making it the fastest and most efficient way to satisfy a one-time ad hoc analytical request compared to building a Dataflow job or standing up a Dataproc/Spark cluster.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to external tables | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/external-tables) · [Query and analyze Bigtable data with BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/bigquery-analysis)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to host an application on a Compute Engine instance within a project that is shared with other teams. You want to prevent those other teams from accidentally causing downtime on that application. Which feature should you use?

options.text: Use a Shielded VM.
Use a Preemptible VM.
Use a sole-tenant node.
Enable deletion protection on the instance.

questions.explanation:
Google Compute Engine allows you to set a deletion protection flag on a VM instance. When this flag is enabled, any attempt to delete the instance—whether via the console, gcloud, or the API—will fail until the flag is explicitly disabled by a user with the compute.instances.create permission. This adds a deliberate safeguard against accidental deletion in shared or multi-team projects, directly addressing the risk of another team unintentionally deleting the instance and causing application downtime. Shielded VM addresses boot integrity and rootkit protection, preemptible VMs are short-lived, cost-optimized instances that Google can terminate at any time (making them unsuitable for uptime protection), and sole-tenant nodes provide dedicated physical hardware for compliance or licensing needs, none of which prevent accidental deletion.

**Learn more:** [Prevent accidental VM deletion | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/preventing-accidental-vm-deletion)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Last month your project costs were higher than expected. After investigating, you discovered that a development GKE container generated an unusually large volume of logs, driving up the cost. You want to quickly disable these logs using the fewest possible steps. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Go to the Logs ingestion window in Stackdriver Logging, and disable the log source for the GKE container resource.
1. Go to the Logs ingestion window in Stackdriver Logging, and disable the log source for the GKE Cluster Operations resource.
1. Go to the GKE console, and delete existing clusters. 2. Recreate a new cluster. 3. Clear the option to enable legacy Stackdriver Logging.
1. Go to the GKE console, and delete existing clusters. 2. Recreate a new cluster. 3. Clear the option to enable legacy Stackdriver Monitoring.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging lets you exclude or disable log ingestion for a specific monitored resource type directly from the Logs ingestion settings, without needing to delete or recreate any GKE clusters. Since the excessive logs originate from the GKE container resource type, disabling ingestion for that resource type immediately stops the high-volume logs with a single configuration change, which is far fewer steps than deleting and recreating a cluster to change legacy logging/monitoring agent settings. The 'GKE Cluster Operations' resource type covers different (administrative) log data, not the container's own log stream, so it would not resolve the cost issue caused by container log volume.

**Learn more:** [Excluding logs from routing in the Logs Router](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview#exclusions) · [Kubernetes Engine monitored resources](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/resources#tag_k8s_container)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to deploy a new containerized application into Google Cloud by using a Kubernetes manifest. You want to have full control over the Kubernetes deployment, and at the same time, you want to minimize configuring infrastructure. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the application on GKE Autopilot.
Deploy the application on Cloud Run.
Deploy the application on GKE Standard.
Deploy the application on Cloud Functions.

questions.explanation: GKE Autopilot still exposes the full standard Kubernetes API, so any manifest (Deployments, Services, StatefulSets, etc.) can be applied and full control over the workload's configuration is retained; Google manages only the node infrastructure, which is exactly the piece you want to minimize. Cloud Run and Cloud Functions cannot consume Kubernetes manifests, and GKE Standard would require managing node pools and cluster infrastructure yourself. **Learn more:** [GKE Autopilot overview](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/autopilot-overview)

Google Compute Engine allows you to set a deletion protection flag on a VM instance. When this flag is enabled, any attempt to delete the instance—whether via the console, gcloud, or the API—will fail until the flag is explicitly disabled by a user with the compute.instances.create permission. This adds a deliberate safeguard against accidental deletion in shared or multi-team projects, directly addressing the risk of another team unintentionally deleting the instance and causing application downtime. Shielded VM addresses boot integrity and rootkit protection, preemptible VMs are short-lived, cost-optimized instances that Google can terminate at any time (making them unsuitable for uptime protection), and sole-tenant nodes provide dedicated physical hardware for compliance or licensing needs, none of which prevent accidental deletion.

You need to set up a landing zone in Google Cloud before migrating the VMs. You must ensure that all VM in your production environment can communicate with each other through private IP addresses. You need to allow all VMs in your Google Cloud organization to accept connections on specific TCP ports. You want to follow Google-recommended practices, and you need to minimize your operational costs. What should you do?

options.text: Create individual VPCs per Google Cloud project. Peer all he VPC together. Apply organization policies on the organization level.
Create individual VPCs for each Google Cloud project. Peer ail ne VPCs together. Apply hierarchical firewall policies on the organization level.
Create a host VPC project with each production project as its service project. Apply organization policies on the organization level.
Create a host VPC project with each production project as its service project. Apply hierarchical firewall policies on the organization level.

questions.explanation: Shared VPC (with the landing zone as host project and production projects as service projects) centralizes network management, enabling all VMs to communicate over private IPs within a unified network. This design follows Google-recommended practices for multi-project landing zones and minimizes operational overhead compared to VPC peering.

Your Dataproc cluster runs in a single Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network in a single subnetwork with range 172.16.20.128/25. There are no private IP addresses available in the subnetwork. You want to add new VMs to communicate with your cluster using the minimum number of steps. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the existing subnet range to 172.16.20.0/24.
Create a new Secondary IP Range in the VPC and configure the VMs to use that range.
Create a new VPC network for the VMs. Enable VPC Peering between the VMs'VPC network and the Dataproc cluster VPC network.
Create a new VPC network for the VMs with a subnet of 172.32.0.0/16. Enable VPC network Peering between the Dataproc VPC network and the VMs VPC network. Configure a custom Route exchange.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine lets you expand a subnet's primary IP range in place, for example with gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range, as long as the new, larger CIDR still contains the existing range and doesn't collide with other subnets — moving from a /25 to a /24 here frees the unused lower half of the block for new VMs in a single step. Adding a secondary range only provides alias IP ranges rather than usable primary addresses for new VM interfaces, and standing up a separate peered VPC network is far more steps than necessary.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs its Linux workloads on Compute Engine instances. The company is about to start working with a new operations partner that does not use Google Accounts. Access to the instances needs to be granted to this operations partner so they can maintain the installed tooling. What should be done?

options.text: Enable Cloud IAP for the Compute Engine instances, and add the operations partner as a Cloud IAP Tunnel User.
Tag all the instances with the same network tag. Create a firewall rule in the VPC to grant TCP access on port 22 for traffic from the operations partner to instances with the network tag.
Set up Cloud VPN between your Google Cloud VPC and the internal network of the operations partner.
Ask the operations partner to generate SSH key pairs, and add the public keys to the VM instances.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine supports authenticating SSH connections using key pairs stored in project or instance metadata, independent of any Google Account or IAM identity. Because the operations partner has no Google Account, they cannot be granted IAM roles (such as the IAP-Secured Tunnel User role needed for Cloud IAP, or any other Google Cloud IAM binding), so mechanisms that rely on Google identities are not viable. Instead, the partner should generate their own SSH key pair, and the public key should be added to the target VM instance's metadata (or project-wide metadata). Compute Engine's guest agent reads these metadata-stored keys and grants SSH access to anyone holding the corresponding private key, entirely bypassing the need for a Google identity, while still allowing scoped, per-instance access control.

**Learn more:** [Add SSH keys to VMs that use metadata-based SSH keys](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/connect/add-ssh-keys) · [About SSH connections | Compute Engine Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/ssh)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are assigned to maintain a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster named 'dev' that was deployed on Google Cloud. You want to manage the GKE configuration using the command line interface (CLI). You have just downloaded and installed the Cloud SDK. You want to ensure that future CLI commands by default address this specific cluster What should you do?

options.text: Use the command gcloud config set container/cluster dev.
Use the command gcloud container clusters update dev.
Create a file called gke.default in the ~/.gcloud folder that contains the cluster name.
Create a file called defaults.json in the ~/.gcloud folder that contains the cluster name.

questions.explanation: The gcloud config set command configures local settings for gcloud CLI. Using `gcloud config set container/cluster dev` sets the default cluster for all future container-related commands in that configuration profile. This is the standard, documented way to set default values for CLI tool parameters.
