lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a new frontend service for an online game. The service uses a micro-frontend architecture and comprises multiple containers that communicate through a service mesh.  
  
You need to control how many compute instances run at any given time. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Compute Engine instance template using a container-optimized virtual machine (VM) instance, and create a startup script that installs Istio service mesh. Deploy the service, and create a managed instance group with a fixed number of instances to run the service.
Create a Cloud Run service specifying the minimum and maximum number of instances, and configure the service to use Cloud Service Mesh. Deploy all the containers to the service.
Create a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot cluster, and enable Cloud Service Mesh. Deploy the service, and use vertical and horizontal Pod autoscaling to control the cluster size.
Create a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Standard cluster with a node pool that has a fixed number of nodes. Enable the Cloud Service Mesh add-on, and deploy the service.

questions.explanation:
A GKE Standard node pool can be configured with a fixed number of nodes, which fixes the number of underlying Compute Engine instances available for the workload. GKE Standard also supports Cloud Service Mesh for communication among the containerized micro-frontends. GKE Autopilot automatically manages and resizes node capacity, while horizontal and vertical Pod autoscaling control Pods or resource requests rather than maintaining a fixed node count.

**Learn more:** [Resize a Standard cluster by adding or removing nodes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/resizing-a-cluster) · [Supported platforms — Cloud Service Mesh](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/supported-platforms)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Linux virtual machine that must connect to Cloud SQL. You have already created a service account with the necessary permissions. You want to ensure that the VM uses this service account instead of the default Compute Engine service account. What should you do?

options.text: When creating the VM via the web console, specify the service account under the 'Identity and API Access' section.
Download a JSON Private Key for the service account. On the Project Metadata, add that JSON as the value for the key compute-engine-service- account.
Download a JSON Private Key for the service account. On the Custom Metadata of the VM, add that JSON as the value for the key compute-engine- service-account.
Download a JSON Private Key for the service account. After creating the VM, ssh into the VM and save the JSON under ~/.gcloud/compute-engine-service- account.json.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine lets you attach a specific service account to a VM instance at creation time. In the Google Cloud Console, this is configured under the 'Identity and API access' section when creating the VM, where you select the desired service account instead of using the default Compute Engine service account. The VM then automatically obtains short-lived credentials for that service account via the instance metadata server, with no need to download, distribute, or store a JSON private key file. Manually downloading and placing a JSON key in project or custom metadata, or copying it onto the VM's filesystem, is not the supported method for assigning VM identity and is discouraged due to the security risks of managing long-lived key files.

**Learn more:** [Create a VM that uses a user-managed service account](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/create-enable-service-accounts-for-instances)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are running multiple microservices in a Kubernetes Engine cluster. One microservice is rendering images. The microservice responsible for the image rendering requires a large amount of CPU time compared to the memory it requires. The other microservices are workloads that are optimized for n2-standard machine types. You need to optimize your cluster so that all workloads are using resources as efficiently as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the pods of the image rendering microservice a higher pod priority than the other microservices.
Create a node pool with compute-optimized machine type nodes for the image rendering microservice. Use the node pool with general-purpose machine type nodes for the other microservices.
Use the node pool with general-purpose machine type nodes for the image rendering microservice. Create a node pool with compute-optimized machine type nodes for the other microservices.

Configure the required amount of CPU and memory in the resource requests specification of the image rendering microservice deployment. Keep the resource requests for the other microservices at the default.

questions.explanation: For heterogeneous workloads in GKE, machine types should match workload characteristics. The image rendering microservice requires substantial CPU but less memory, making compute-optimized machines ideal for this workload. Other microservices optimized for n2-standard machines (general purpose) should run on general-purpose node pools. This segregation ensures efficient resource utilization and cost optimization. Pod priority or resource requests alone cannot address the fundamental mismatch between workload needs and node capabilities.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your development team needs a new Jenkins server for their project. You need to deploy the server using the fewest steps possible. What should you do?

options.text: Download and deploy the Jenkins Java WAR to App Engine Standard.
Create a new Compute Engine instance and install Jenkins through the command line interface.
Create a Kubernetes cluster on Compute Engine and create a deployment with the Jenkins Docker image.
Use GCP Marketplace to launch the Jenkins solution.

questions.explanation:
GCP Marketplace (Cloud Marketplace) provides a curated, pre-configured Jenkins solution that automates provisioning of the underlying Compute Engine VM, installation of Jenkins, and configuration of networking/firewall rules in a single guided deployment flow. This requires far fewer manual steps than manually creating a Compute Engine instance and installing Jenkins via the CLI, standing up a Kubernetes cluster and writing a deployment manifest for the Jenkins Docker image, or manually downloading and deploying the Jenkins WAR file to App Engine Standard (which also has compatibility issues since Jenkins isn't officially supported on App Engine Standard's sandboxed environment).

**Learn more:** [Jenkins | Google Cloud Marketplace](https://console.cloud.google.com/marketplace/product/click-to-deploy-images/jenkins)

Your customer has implemented a solution that uses Cloud Spanner and notices some read latency-related performance issues on one table. This table is accessed only by their users using a primary key. The table schema is shown below.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783720872504-kn1tyjxh.png)  
  
You want to resolve the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the profile_picture field from the table.
Add a secondary index on the person_id column.
Change the primary key to not have monotonically increasing values.
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783720875514-uvs1x6dx.png)

questions.explanation:
The schema defines person_id as a sequential, monotonically increasing INT64 primary key. In Cloud Spanner, a strictly increasing key concentrates all recent reads and writes on a single split at the "end" of the keyspace, creating a hotspot that limits throughput and drives up latency even though queries already use the primary key. Since the table is only ever queried by that same key, adding a secondary index (B or the DDL shown in D, which still leads with person_id) does not relieve the hotspot; the fix is to redesign the primary key itself — e.g., using a UUID, bit-reversed sequence, or hashed prefix — so writes and the associated reads spread evenly across splits.

**Learn more:** [Choose a primary key that prevents hotspots | Cloud Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-design#primary-key-prevent-hotspots)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using Deployment Manager to provision a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. Within that same Deployment Manager deployment, you also need to create a DaemonSet in the cluster's kube-system namespace. You want to accomplish this using the fewest possible services. What should you do?

options.text: Add the cluster's API as a new Type Provider in Deployment Manager, and use the new type to create the DaemonSet.
Use the Deployment Manager Runtime Configurator to create a new Config resource that contains the DaemonSet definition.
With Deployment Manager, create a Compute Engine instance with a startup script that uses kubectl to create the DaemonSet.
In the cluster's definition in Deployment Manager, add a metadata that has kube-system as key and the DaemonSet manifest as value.

questions.explanation:
Deployment Manager's Type Provider feature allows you to register any RESTful API—including the Kubernetes API exposed by the GKE cluster you just created—as a custom resource type within the same Deployment Manager project. After registering the cluster's API as a Type Provider, you can define a resource of that new type in the same deployment configuration to create the DaemonSet directly in kube-system. This approach relies solely on Deployment Manager itself, requiring no additional Google Cloud services such as Compute Engine instances, startup scripts, or the Runtime Configurator, satisfying the requirement to use the fewest possible services. Metadata key/value pairs on the cluster resource have no mechanism for provisioning Kubernetes API objects, so that approach is not viable.

**Learn more:** [Adding an API as a type provider | Cloud Deployment Manager | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deployment-manager/docs/configuration/type-providers/creating-type-provider) · [deploymentmanager-samples/examples/v2/gke/daemonsets](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/deploymentmanager-samples/tree/master/examples/v2/gke/daemonsets)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage multiple Google Cloud Platform (GCP) projects and need access to all logs from the past 60 days. You want to be able to explore and quickly analyze the log contents. Following Google-recommended practices, what should you do to obtain the combined logs for all projects?

options.text: Navigate to Stackdriver Logging and select resource.labels.project_id=
Create a Stackdriver Logging Export with a Sink destination to a BigQuery dataset. Configure the table expiration to 60 days.
Create a Stackdriver Logging Export with a Sink destination to Cloud Storage. Create a lifecycle rule to delete objects after 60 days.
Configure a Cloud Scheduler job to read from Stackdriver and store the logs in BigQuery. Configure the table expiration to 60 days.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging (formerly Stackdriver Logging) provides log sinks that can export logs to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, or Pub/Sub. For combined logs across multiple projects that need to be explored and analyzed quickly, Google recommends exporting logs to a BigQuery dataset via a sink, since BigQuery supports fast, interactive SQL-based querying and analysis of large volumes of log data. Setting the BigQuery table expiration to 60 days automatically manages retention to meet the stated requirement without needing to build custom deletion logic. Cloud Storage sinks are better suited for long-term archival rather than interactive analysis, and using a Cloud Scheduler job to manually pull logs is unnecessary and non-standard since Logging sinks continuously and natively export logs to the destination.

**Learn more:** [Overview of logs export - BigQuery destination](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery) · [Design patterns for exporting Cloud Logging data](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/exporting-stackdriver-logging-for-splunk)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a Google Cloud project containing a critical marketing application. You need to give an external vendor read-only access to the objects stored in one specific Cloud Storage bucket. The vendor must not be able to view any other resources in the project. What should you do?

options.text: Create a custom IAM role with the storage.objects.get permission, and grant the vendor this role on the project.
Grant the vendor the Storage Object User role on the project.
Grant the vendor the Storage Object User role on the bucket.
Grant the vendor the Storage Object Viewer role on the bucket.

questions.explanation:
The Storage Object Viewer role (`roles/storage.objectViewer`) grants permission to view and list objects and their metadata, while assigning it on a bucket limits that access to the bucket and its contained objects. Bucket-level IAM provides the required least-privilege scope without granting access across the project.

**Learn more:** [IAM roles for Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles) · [Identity and Access Management for Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You hold a Google Cloud Platform account that has access to both a production project and a development project. You want to set up an automated process that lists all Compute Engine instances in both the development and production projects every day. What should you do?

options.text: Create two configurations using gcloud config. Write a script that sets configurations as active, individually. For each configuration, use gcloud compute instances list to get a list of compute resources.

Create two configurations using gsutil config. Write a script that sets configurations as active, individually. For each configuration, use gsutil compute instances list to get a list of compute resources.
Go to Cloud Shell and export this information to Cloud Storage on a daily basis.
Go to GCP Console and export this information to Cloud SQL on a daily basis.

questions.explanation:
gcloud supports multiple named configurations, each of which can store a distinct project (and account) context. By creating one configuration for the development project and one for the production project, a script can activate each configuration in turn (gcloud config configurations activate) and then run 'gcloud compute instances list' to retrieve the compute instances for that project. This script can be scheduled to run daily (e.g., via cron or a scheduler), providing the required automated, recurring listing across both projects. gsutil does not have a 'compute instances list' command since it is scoped to Cloud Storage operations, making option B invalid. Manually using Cloud Shell or the GCP Console to export data to Cloud Storage or Cloud SQL does not constitute a reliable automated daily process and introduces unnecessary complexity for a simple instance-listing task.

**Learn more:** [gcloud topic configurations](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/topic/configurations) · [gcloud compute instances list](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/instances/list)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to choose and configure a storage and archiving solution on Google Cloud Platform. The solution must meet compliance requirements for data originating from a single geographic location. This data should be archived after 30 days, and it needs to be accessed once per year.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Select Multi-Regional Storage. Add a bucket lifecycle rule that archives data after 30 days to Coldline Storage.
Select Multi-Regional Storage. Add a bucket lifecycle rule that archives data after 30 days to Nearline Storage.
Select Regional Storage. Add a bucket lifecycle rule that archives data after 30 days to Nearline Storage.
Select Regional Storage. Add a bucket lifecycle rule that archives data after 30 days to Coldline Storage.

questions.explanation:
Because the data originates from a single geographic location, Regional Storage is the appropriate storage class, as it keeps data within one region rather than replicating it across multiple regions like Multi-Regional Storage. Since the archived data only needs to be accessed about once a year, Coldline Storage is the correct target for the lifecycle rule, as it is specifically designed for infrequently accessed data (access frequency of less than once a year), offering the lowest storage costs among the "cold" storage tiers. Nearline Storage, by contrast, is optimized for data accessed less than once a month, making it unsuitable for an annual access pattern.

**Learn more:** [Storage classes | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating your on-premises workload to Google Cloud. Your company is implementing its Cloud Billing configuration and requires access to a granular breakdown of its Google Cloud costs. You need to ensure that the Cloud Billing datasets are available in BigQuery so you can conduct a detailed analysis of costs. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud Billing data export to BigQuery when you create a Cloud Billing account.
Enable Cloud Billing on the project, and link a Cloud Billing account. Then view the billing data table in the BigQuery dataset.
Create a Cloud Billing account. Enable the BigQuery Data Transfer Service API to export pricing data.
Enable the BigQuery API, and ensure that the BigQuery User IAM role is selected. Change the BigQuery dataset to select a data location.

questions.explanation: Detailed, itemized Cloud Billing cost data is delivered into BigQuery only through the Cloud Billing BigQuery export feature, enabled on the Cloud Billing account, which automatically streams granular usage and cost records into a BigQuery dataset for analysis. Simply enabling the BigQuery API or the BigQuery Data Transfer Service does not populate billing cost data, since neither is the mechanism that exports Cloud Billing records. **Learn more:** [Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your static website is hosted on Cloud Storage, and you have recently added links to PDF files on the site. Currently, when users click these PDF links, their browsers prompt them to save the file locally instead of opening it. You want the PDF files to open and display directly within the browser window when clicked, without prompting a save dialog. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud CDN on the website frontend.
Enable 'Share publicly' on the PDF file objects.
Set Content-Type metadata to application/pdf on the PDF file objects.
Add a label to the storage bucket with a key of Content-Type and value of application/pdf.

questions.explanation:
Browsers decide whether to render a file inline or force a download based on the object's Content-Type (and Content-Disposition) HTTP response header. If PDF objects in Cloud Storage are missing the correct Content-Type or have it set to a generic type like application/octet-stream, browsers default to downloading the file rather than displaying it. By explicitly setting the Content-Type metadata to application/pdf on each PDF object, Cloud Storage serves the file with the correct MIME type, allowing browsers to use their built-in PDF viewer to render the file inline instead of prompting a save dialog. Cloud CDN only affects caching, 'Share publicly' only affects access permissions, and bucket labels are unrelated key-value pairs for resource organization/billing that do not affect how object content is served.

**Learn more:** [Editing object metadata | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/viewing-editing-metadata) · [Hosting a static website | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/hosting-static-website)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have deployed an LDAP server on Compute Engine, and it is reachable via TLS on port 636 using UDP. You need to ensure the server is reachable by clients on that port. What should you do?

options.text: Add the network tag allow-udp-636 to the VM instance running the LDAP server.
Create a route called allow-udp-636 and set the next hop to be the VM instance running the LDAP server.
Add a network tag of your choice to the instance. Create a firewall rule to allow ingress on UDP port 636 for that network tag.
Add a network tag of your choice to the instance running the LDAP server. Create a firewall rule to allow egress on UDP port 636 for that network tag.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud VPC firewall rules control both inbound (ingress) and outbound (egress) traffic to and from VM instances. Network tags by themselves have no effect on connectivity—they only become meaningful when referenced as a target in a firewall rule. To allow clients to reach the LDAP server on UDP port 636, you must attach a network tag to the instance and then create an ingress firewall rule that allows traffic on UDP port 636 for instances with that tag. Routes control the path packets take (next hops) and do not enforce port-level access, and an egress rule would only control traffic leaving the instance, not incoming client requests.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/firewalls)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have built an application on Google Cloud that uses Cloud Spanner. Your support team needs to monitor the environment but should not have access to table data.  
  
You need a streamlined solution to grant the correct permissions to your support team, following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Add the support team group to the roles/monitoring.viewer role
Add the support team group to the roles/spanner.databaseUser role.
Add the support team group to the roles/spanner.databaseReader role.
Add the support team group to the roles/stackdriver.accounts.viewer role.

questions.explanation:
The predefined role roles/monitoring.viewer provides read-only access to Cloud Monitoring resources (dashboards, metrics, alerting policies, uptime checks, etc.) across a project, allowing the support team to observe the health and performance of the Cloud Spanner environment without granting any permissions to read or modify the actual table data stored in Spanner. In contrast, roles/spanner.databaseUser and roles/spanner.databaseReader both grant direct access to Spanner database contents, which is explicitly what the support team should not have. roles/stackdriver.accounts.viewer is a legacy Stackdriver account role not intended for this use case. Using the built-in Monitoring Viewer role is the simplest, IAM-recommended way to grant monitoring-only visibility.

**Learn more:** [Access control for Cloud Monitoring](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/access-control) · [Cloud Spanner IAM roles](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/iam)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have written a code snippet that needs to run automatically whenever a new file is uploaded to a Cloud Storage bucket. You want to deploy this code snippet so that it is triggered this way. What should you do?

options.text: Use App Engine and configure Cloud Scheduler to trigger the application using Pub/Sub.
Use Cloud Functions and configure the bucket as a trigger resource.
Use Google Kubernetes Engine and configure a CronJob to trigger the application using Pub/Sub.
Use Dataflow as a batch job, and configure the bucket as a data source.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Functions supports Cloud Storage triggers, which allow a function to be invoked automatically in response to changes in a bucket, such as when an object is created (finalized), updated, archived, or deleted. By deploying the code snippet as a Cloud Function and configuring the bucket as the trigger resource, the function runs automatically on new file uploads without requiring any additional infrastructure, scheduling, or manual invocation, making it the appropriate serverless, event-driven solution for this use case.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage Triggers | Cloud Functions Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/calling/storage)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to deploy an application that is packaged as a container image into a new project. The application exposes an HTTP endpoint and receives very few requests per day. You want to minimize costs. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the container on Cloud Run.
Deploy the container on Cloud Run on GKE.
Deploy the container on App Engine Flexible.
Deploy the container on GKE with cluster autoscaling and horizontal pod autoscaling enabled.

questions.explanation:
Fully managed Cloud Run automatically scales the number of container instances based on incoming traffic and scales down to zero instances when there are no requests, so you are billed only for the compute resources used while actually handling requests. This makes it the most cost-effective option for an HTTP-based container workload with very low and infrequent traffic. In contrast, Cloud Run on GKE and GKE with autoscaling require an underlying GKE cluster with at least one running node, incurring ongoing infrastructure costs even when idle, and App Engine Flexible always keeps a minimum of one instance running, preventing scale-to-zero cost savings.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Run documentation - About instance autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-instance-autoscaling) · [Cloud Run pricing](https://cloud.google.com/run/pricing)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: You recently discovered an issue with your rolling update in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You now need to roll back a rolling update. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the deployment.
Use the kubectl rollout restart command to revert the deployment.
Use the kubectl rollout undo command.
Manually scale down the new Pods and scale up the old Pods.

questions.explanation: The kubectl rollout undo command is the Kubernetes-native mechanism for reverting a deployment to its previous revision. It automatically handles pod termination and restoration of the prior version, making it the standard and safest approach for recovering from failed rolling updates without manual intervention.

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: You recently discovered an issue with your rolling update in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You now need to roll back a rolling update. What should you do?

options.text: gcloud deployment-manager deployments create --config <deployment-config-path>
gcloud deployment-manager deployments update --config <deployment-config-path>
gcloud deployment-manager resources create --config <deployment-config-path>
gcloud deployment-manager resources update --config <deployment-config-path>

questions.explanation:
In Google Cloud Deployment Manager, deployments are updated using the `gcloud deployment-manager deployments update` command with a new or modified configuration file. This command compares the current deployment state with the new configuration and applies only the necessary changes, updating resources in place whenever possible rather than deleting and recreating them, which avoids downtime. Using `deployments create` would attempt to create a new deployment rather than modify an existing one, and the `resources` command group is not used to apply configuration-based updates to a deployment.

**Learn more:** [gcloud deployment-manager deployments update](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/deployment-manager/deployments/update)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have deployed an application on a Compute Engine instance. An external consultant needs to access the Linux-based instance. The consultant is connected to your corporate network through a VPN connection, but the consultant has no Google account. What should you do?

options.text: Instruct the external consultant to use the gcloud compute ssh command line tool by using Identity-Aware Proxy to access the instance.
Instruct the external consultant to use the gcloud compute ssh command line tool by using the public IP address of the instance to access it.

Instruct the external consultant to generate an SSH key pair, and request the public key from the consultant. Add the public key to the instance yourself, and have the consultant access the instance through SSH with their private key.

Instruct the external consultant to generate an SSH key pair, and request the private key from the consultant. Add the private key to the instance yourself, and have the consultant access the instance through SSH with their public key.

questions.explanation: Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding for SSH still authenticates the caller against a Google identity, which this external consultant does not have, so IAP is not a fit here. Because the consultant already reaches the network over the VPN, the standard approach is to have them generate their own SSH key pair, send you only the public key to add to the instance's metadata, and keep the private key on their side to authenticate — the private key must never be shared, which is why the option reversing the key roles is wrong.

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company publishes large files using an Apache web server that runs on a Compute Engine instance. The Apache web server is not the only application running in the project. You want to receive an email notification when the egress network costs for this server exceed $100 for the current month, as measured by Google Cloud.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set up a budget alert on the project with an amount of 100 dollars, a threshold of 100%, and notification type of ג€email.ג€
Set up a budget alert on the billing account with an amount of 100 dollars, a threshold of 100%, and notification type of ג€email.ג€

Export the billing data to BigQuery. Create a Cloud Function that uses BigQuery to sum the egress network costs of the exported billing data for the Apache web server for the current month and sends an email if it is over 100 dollars. Schedule the Cloud Function using Cloud Scheduler to run hourly.

Use the Cloud Logging Agent to export the Apache web server logs to Cloud Logging. Create a Cloud Function that uses BigQuery to parse the HTTP response log data in Cloud Logging for the current month and sends an email if the size of all HTTP responses, multiplied by current Google Cloud egress prices, totals over 100 dollars. Schedule the Cloud Function using Cloud Scheduler to run hourly.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud budget alerts can only be scoped to a billing account, a project, specific services, or labels — they report on aggregated spend and cannot isolate the egress network cost of a single Compute Engine instance among other resources and applications sharing the same project. To get the granularity needed (only the egress network costs of one specific server), you must export detailed billing data to BigQuery, which provides resource- and SKU-level billing line items. A Cloud Function can then query BigQuery to sum just the egress network cost entries for that Apache server for the current month, and Cloud Scheduler can trigger this function hourly, sending an email when the total exceeds $100. This approach is described in Google Cloud's guidance on billing export to BigQuery for detailed cost analysis and automation, whereas simple budget alerts (options A and B) only support coarser-grained thresholds and cannot isolate a single instance's egress cost.

**Learn more:** [Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets) · [Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery)

You store sensitive data in three Cloud Storage buckets and have turned on data access logging for them. You need to check the activity of a specific user across these buckets, using the smallest number of steps possible. Specifically, you want to confirm:  
  
- Whether metadata labels were added  
- Which files were viewed from those buckets  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Using the GCP Console, filter the Activity log to view the information.
Using the GCP Console, filter the Stackdriver log to view the information.
View the bucket in the Storage section of the GCP Console.
Create a trace in Stackdriver to view the information.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage audit logging records both Admin Activity events (such as adding metadata labels) and, when Data Access logging is enabled, Data Access events (such as viewing/reading objects). Both log types are written to Cloud Logging (formerly Stackdriver Logging), where you can use the Logs Explorer to filter by the specific user's identity and by resource (bucket) across all three buckets in a single set of filter steps, showing both the metadata label changes and the object read/view events. The Activity log view in the console does not reliably expose Data Access log entries like object views, the Storage console bucket view only shows the current state of objects/metadata rather than historical access events, and Stackdriver Trace is meant for application performance tracing rather than audit log review.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Audit Logs overview](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit) · [Cloud Storage audit logging](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/audit-logging)

Your organization has built a complex Google Cloud structure containing hundreds of folders and projects. Only a small number of team members need to be able to view this hierarchical structure. You must grant these team members the minimum permissions necessary, following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Add the users to roles/browser role.
Add the users to roles/iam.roleViewer role.
Add the users to a group, and add this group to roles/browser.
Add the users to a group, and add this group to roles/iam.roleViewer role.

questions.explanation:
The predefined role roles/browser grants read-only access to browse the resource hierarchy — including organization, folders, projects, and IAM allow policies — without exposing the actual resource contents, making it the minimal role needed to view the hierarchy. Google's IAM best practices recommend granting roles to groups rather than to individual user accounts, since managing group membership is easier and less error-prone than managing IAM bindings for each user individually, especially in large, complex hierarchies. roles/iam.roleViewer instead only grants permission to view the definitions of IAM roles (predefined and custom), not the folder/project hierarchy, so it does not satisfy the requirement.

**Learn more:** [Browser roles and permissions | IAM | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/browser) · [Using resource hierarchy for access control | IAM | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/resource-hierarchy-access-control)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has many legacy third-party applications that rely on a shared NFS server for file sharing between these workloads. You want to modernize the NFS server by using a Google Cloud managed service. You need to select the solution that requires the least amount of change to the application. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Compute Engine instance and configure an NFS server on the instance. Point all NFS mounts to the Compute Engine instance.
Deploy a Filestore instance. Replace all NFS mounts with a Filestore mount.
Configure Firestore. Configure all applications to use Firestore instead of the NFS server.
Create a Cloud Storage bucket. Configure all applications to use Cloud Storage client libraries instead of the NFS server.

questions.explanation:
Filestore is Google Cloud's fully managed NFS file server, so applications can mount it using the same NFS protocol they already use, requiring no code or configuration changes beyond repointing the mount target. Firestore and Cloud Storage use entirely different APIs and are not drop-in NFS replacements, and self-managing NFS on Compute Engine is not a managed-service modernization.

**Learn more:** [Filestore overview](https://cloud.google.com/filestore/docs/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have two subnets (subnet-a and subnet-b) in the default VPC. Your database servers are running in subnet-a. Your application servers and web servers are running in subnet-b. You want to configure a firewall rule that only allows database traffic from the application servers to the database servers. What should you do?

options.text: • Create service accounts sa-app and sa-db.• Associate service account sa-app with the application servers and the service account sa-db with the database servers.• Create an ingress firewall rule to allow network traffic from source service account sa-app to target service account sa-db.

• Create network tags app-server and db-server.• Add the app-server tag to the application servers and the db-server tag to the database servers.• Create an egress firewall rule to allow network traffic from source network tag app-server to target network tag db-server.

• Create a service account sa-app and a network tag db-server.• Associate the service account sa-app with the application servers and the network tag db-server with the database servers.• Create an ingress firewall rule to allow network traffic from source VPC IP addresses and target the subnet-a IP addresses.

• Create a network tag app-server and service account sa-db.• Add the tag to the application servers and associate the service account with the database servers.• Create an egress firewall rule to allow network traffic from source network tag app-server to target service account sa-db.

questions.explanation: Service accounts are Google Cloud's recommended method for granular firewall rule control. Using sa-app and sa-db service accounts with an ingress rule allows precise traffic control from application to database servers. Option B incorrectly uses an egress rule (wrong direction) and network tags, which are less precise than service accounts for this use case.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Compute Engine instance that hosts an application used only between 9 AM and 6 PM on weekdays. You want to back up this instance every day for disaster recovery purposes, keeping the backups for 30 days. You want to implement the Google-recommended solution while minimizing management overhead and the number of services used. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Update your instances' metadata to add the following value: snapshotג€

1. In the Cloud Console, go to the Compute Engine Disks page and select your instance's disk. 2. In the Snapshot Schedule section, select Create Schedule and configure the following parameters: - Schedule frequency: Daily - Start time: 1:00 AM ג€

1. Create a Cloud Function that creates a snapshot of your instance's disk. 2. Create a Cloud Function that deletes snapshots that are older than 30 days. 3. Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger both Cloud Functions daily at 1:00 AM.

1. Create a bash script in the instance that copies the content of the disk to Cloud Storage. 2. Create a bash script in the instance that deletes data older than 30 days in the backup Cloud Storage bucket. 3. Configure the instance's crontab to execute these scripts daily at 1:00 AM.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine provides a native, fully managed snapshot schedule feature for persistent disks. From the Compute Engine Disks page, you can select a disk and create a snapshot schedule specifying the frequency (daily), a start time window, and an autodelete/retention period (30 days). This resource-policy-based scheduling is Google's recommended approach for automated disk backups because it requires no custom code, no additional compute or serverless resources, and no extra orchestration services — Compute Engine handles snapshot creation and expiration automatically, minimizing operational overhead compared to building custom Cloud Functions, Cloud Scheduler jobs, or in-instance scripts.

**Learn more:** [About snapshot schedules for disks | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/about-snapshot-schedules) · [Create schedules for disk snapshots | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/scheduled-snapshots)

Your application development team has created Docker images for an application that will be deployed on Google Cloud. Your team does not want to manage the infrastructure associated with this application. You need to ensure that the application can scale automatically as it gains popularity. What should you do?

options.text: Create an instance template with the container image, and deploy a Managed Instance Group with Autoscaling.
Upload Docker images to Artifact Registry, and deploy the application on Google Kubernetes Engine using Standard mode.
Upload Docker images to the Cloud Storage, and deploy the application on Google Kubernetes Engine using Standard mode.
Upload Docker images to Artifact Registry, and deploy the application on Cloud Run.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run is a fully serverless platform requiring zero infrastructure management—the team does not provision or scale nodes. Autoscaling is built-in and automatic based on request volume. Options A and B require node management; option C uses non-recommended Cloud Storage as a container source.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates a single sign-on (SSO) identity provider that supports Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) integration with service providers. Your company's users exist in Cloud Identity, and you want these users to authenticate using your company's own SSO provider.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: In Cloud Identity, set up SSO with Google as an identity provider to access custom SAML apps.
In Cloud Identity, set up SSO with a third-party identity provider with Google as a service provider.
Obtain OAuth 2.0 credentials, configure the user consent screen, and set up OAuth 2.0 for Mobile & Desktop Apps.
Obtain OAuth 2.0 credentials, configure the user consent screen, and set up OAuth 2.0 for Web Server Applications.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Identity and Google Workspace support SAML 2.0 for single sign-on. When an organization already operates its own SAML-based SSO identity provider and wants its Cloud Identity users to authenticate against that provider, the correct configuration is to register the company's IdP as a third-party identity provider within Cloud Identity, with Google acting as the SAML service provider (SP). In this model, the external IdP authenticates the user and issues a signed SAML assertion, which Google/Cloud Identity (as the SP) validates via its Assertion Consumer Service to establish the user's session — Google does not manage the user's credentials directly. This is distinct from configuring "Google as an identity provider," which is used when you want users authenticated by Google to sign into external, non-Google custom SAML applications (the reverse role). OAuth 2.0 flows (Mobile & Desktop, or Web Server applications) are used for authorizing application access to APIs/resources and are unrelated to configuring organization-wide SAML-based SSO authentication.

**Learn more:** [Setting up SSO - Cloud Identity Help](https://support.google.com/cloudidentity/answer/12032922?hl=en) · [Technical overview of SAML-based SSO - Cloud Identity Help](https://support.google.com/cloudidentity/answer/6262987?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring a Windows virtual machine on Compute Engine and need to ensure you are able to log in to it using RDP. What should you do?

options.text: After the VM has been created, use your Google Account credentials to log in into the VM.
After the VM has been created, use gcloud compute reset-windows-password to retrieve the login credentials for the VM.
When creating the VM, add metadata to the instance using 'windows-password' as the key and a password as the value.
After the VM has been created, download the JSON private key for the default Compute Engine service account. Use the credentials in the JSON file to log in to the VM.

questions.explanation:
Windows VMs on Compute Engine do not come with a pre-set password; you must generate one before connecting via RDP. The supported way to do this is to run `gcloud compute reset-windows-password` (or use the equivalent Cloud Console action) after the VM is created, which creates a Windows user account if it doesn't exist and returns a new password you can then use to authenticate over RDP. Google Account credentials are not valid Windows login credentials, setting a 'windows-password' metadata key is not a supported mechanism for provisioning RDP access, and service account JSON keys are used for programmatic API authentication rather than interactive OS login.

**Learn more:** [gcloud compute reset-windows-password | Google Cloud SDK Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/reset-windows-password) · [Manage accounts and credentials on Windows VMs | Compute Engine Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/windows/generating-credentials)

Your company has an existing GCP organization with hundreds of projects and a billing account. Your company recently acquired another company that also has hundreds of projects and its own billing account. You would like to consolidate all GCP costs of both GCP organizations onto a single invoice. You would like to consolidate all costs as of tomorrow. What should you do?

options.text: Link the acquired company's projects to your company's billing account.
Configure the acquired company's billing account and your company's billing account to export the billing data into the same BigQuery dataset.
Migrate the acquired company's projects into your company's GCP organization. Link the migrated projects to your company's billing account.

Create a new GCP organization and a new billing account. Migrate the acquired company's projects and your company's projects into the new GCP organization and link the projects to the new billing account.

questions.explanation: To consolidate GCP costs onto a single invoice as of tomorrow, link the acquired company's projects to your company's existing billing account. This approach consolidates costs immediately without requiring time-consuming migrations. Exporting to BigQuery enables analysis but doesn't change billing; migrating all projects or creating a new organization would require significant effort and time. Note that cross-organization project linking has platform constraints that may affect implementation details.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your manager asks you to deploy a workload to a Kubernetes cluster. You are not sure of the workload's resource requirements or how the requirements might vary depending on usage patterns, external dependencies, or other factors. You need a solution that makes cost-effective recommendations regarding CPU and memory requirements, and allows the workload to function consistently in any situation. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for availability, and configure the cluster autoscaler for suggestions.
Configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for availability, and configure the Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendations for suggestions.
Configure the Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendations for availability, and configure the Cluster autoscaler for suggestions.
Configure the Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendations for availability, and configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for suggestions.

questions.explanation: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler ensures availability by scaling pod replicas based on CPU metrics, handling workload variation without manual intervention. Vertical Pod Autoscaler provides cost-effective recommendations for CPU and memory requests based on actual usage patterns, enabling right-sizing without guesswork. This combination addresses both availability (HPA) and optimization (VPA recommendations), following Google-recommended practices for uncertain resource requirements.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have deployed a microservice named myapp1 to a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster using the following YAML configuration file:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783717989305-tmyx6v6u.jpg)  
  
You need to refactor this configuration so that the database password is not stored in plain text. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Store the database password inside the Docker image of the container, not in the YAML file.
Store the database password inside a Secret object. Modify the YAML file to populate the DB_PASSWORD environment variable from the Secret.
Store the database password inside a ConfigMap object. Modify the YAML file to populate the DB_PASSWORD environment variable from the ConfigMap.
Store the database password in a file inside a Kubernetes persistent volume, and use a persistent volume claim to mount the volume to the container.

questions.explanation:
Kubernetes Secret objects are designed to hold sensitive data such as passwords, tokens, and keys separately from the Pod specification, and Deployments can reference a Secret's key to populate an environment variable using the env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef field, so the plain-text value never appears in the Deployment manifest. ConfigMaps are intended for non-confidential configuration data and are not treated as sensitive by Kubernetes RBAC or tooling, so they are not appropriate for credentials. Embedding the password in the container image or in a file on a persistent volume are not standard, Google-recommended mechanisms for supplying application secrets and make rotation and access control more difficult. Referencing Google Cloud's guidance on GKE secret management, using a Kubernetes Secret and populating the environment variable from it is the recommended approach for this scenario.

**Learn more:** [Secret Manager best practices](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/best-practices) · [Using Secrets to store sensitive data | Config Connector](https://cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/how-to/secrets)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a backend service for an ecommerce platform that will persist transaction data from mobile and web clients. After the platform is launched, you expect a large volume of global transactions. Your business team wants to run SQL queries to analyze the data. You need to build a highly available and scalable data store for the platform. What should you do?

options.text: Create a multi-region Cloud Spanner instance with an optimized schema.
Create a multi-region Firestore database with aggregation query enabled.
Create a multi-region Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database with optimized indexes.
Create a multi-region BigQuery dataset with optimized tables.

questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner is designed for globally distributed, mission-critical databases requiring horizontal scalability, strong consistency, and ACID compliance. Multi-region Cloud Spanner instances provide automatic replication across regions for both high availability and disaster recovery. Firestore lacks SQL support, Cloud SQL and BigQuery lack global distribution capabilities needed for multi-region transaction processing.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You built an application on your development laptop that uses Google Cloud services. Your application uses Application Default Credentials for authentication and works fine on your development laptop. You want to migrate this application to a Compute Engine virtual machine (VM) and set up authentication using Google- recommended practices and minimal changes. What should you do?

options.text: Assign appropriate access for Google services to the service account used by the Compute Engine VM.
Create a service account with appropriate access for Google services, and configure the application to use this account.
Store credentials for service accounts with appropriate access for Google services in a config file, and deploy this config file with your application.
Store credentials for your user account with appropriate access for Google services in a config file, and deploy this config file with your application.

questions.explanation:
Google's recommended practice is for each Compute Engine workload to run under a dedicated service account granted only the IAM roles it needs, rather than relying on the broad, project-wide Compute Engine default service account. Creating a purpose-built service account and configuring the application (via Application Default Credentials on the VM) to use it preserves least privilege and requires minimal application code changes, whereas storing user or service account key files in a config file (C, D) contradicts Google's guidance against distributing long-lived credentials.

**Learn more:** [Service accounts for instances | Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/create-enable-service-accounts-for-instances)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company requires all developers to have the same permissions, regardless of the Google Cloud project they are working on. Your company’s security policy also restricts developer permissions to Compute Engine, Cloud Functions, and Cloud SQL. You want to implement the security policy with minimal effort. What should you do?

options.text: • Create a custom role with Compute Engine, Cloud Functions, and Cloud SQL permissions in one project within the Google Cloud organization.• Copy the role across all projects created within the organization with the gcloud iam roles copy command.• Assign the role to developers in those projects.
• Add all developers to a Google group in Google Groups for Workspace.• Assign the predefined role of Compute Admin to the Google group at the Google Cloud organization level.

• Add all developers to a Google group in Cloud Identity.• Assign predefined roles for Compute Engine, Cloud Functions, and Cloud SQL permissions to the Google group for each project in the Google Cloud organization.

• Add all developers to a Google group in Cloud Identity.• Create a custom role with Compute Engine, Cloud Functions, and Cloud SQL permissions at the Google Cloud organization level.• Assign the custom role to the Google group.

questions.explanation: Creating a custom role at the organization level with specific permissions (Compute, Functions, SQL) and assigning it to a Cloud Identity group ensures all developers have identical permissions across all projects with minimal effort. This approach centralizes permission management and avoids redundant role assignments per project. Copy-and-paste roles (A) is error-prone; predefined roles (B, C) cannot restrict to exactly the three required services.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your managed instance group raised an alert stating that new instance creation has failed to create new instances. You need to solve the instance creation problem. What should you do?

options.text: Create an instance template that contains valid syntax which will be used by the instance group. Delete any persistent disks with the same name as instance names.
Create an instance template that contains valid syntax that will be used by the instance group. Verify that the instance name and persistent disk name values are not the same in the template.

Verify that the instance template being used by the instance group contains valid syntax. Delete any persistent disks with the same name as instance names. Set the disks.autoDelete property to true in the instance template.

Delete the current instance template and replace it with a new instance template. Verify that the instance name and persistent disk name values are not the same in the template. Set the disks.autoDelete property to true in the instance template.

questions.explanation:
Instance creation in a managed instance group fails when Compute Engine tries to attach a new boot disk that collides with a persistent disk already using the instance's name; Google's own MIG troubleshooting guidance is to keep the template syntax valid and delete the conflicting disk (optionally snapshotting it first) so a fresh one can be created. Instance templates are immutable, so modifying an existing template is not possible, and replacing the whole template is unnecessary once the disk conflict is resolved.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshooting managed instance groups](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/troubleshooting/troubleshooting-migs)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) with cluster autoscaling enabled. The application exposes a TCP endpoint, and there are several replicas of it running in the cluster.  
  
You also have a Compute Engine instance located in the same region, but in a different Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) named `gce-network`. This VPC has no overlapping IP ranges with the VPC used by the GKE cluster.  
  
This Compute Engine instance needs to connect to the application running on GKE. You want to accomplish this with minimal effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. In GKE, create a Service of type LoadBalancer that uses the application's Pods as backend. 2. Set the service's externalTrafficPolicy to Cluster. 3. Configure the Compute Engine instance to use the address of the load balancer that has been created.

1. In GKE, create a Service of type NodePort that uses the application's Pods as backend. 2. Create a Compute Engine instance called proxy with 2 network interfaces, one in each VPC. 3. Use iptables on this instance to forward traffic from gce-network to the GKE nodes. 4. Configure the Compute Engine instance to use the address of proxy in gce-network as endpoint.

1. In GKE, create a Service of type LoadBalancer that uses the application's Pods as backend. 2. Add an annotation to this service: cloud.google.com/load-balancer-type: Internal 3. Peer the two VPCs together. 4. Configure the Compute Engine instance to use the address of the load balancer that has been created.

1. In GKE, create a Service of type LoadBalancer that uses the application's Pods as backend. 2. Add a Cloud Armor Security Policy to the load balancer that whitelists the internal IPs of the MIG's instances. 3. Configure the Compute Engine instance to use the address of the load balancer that has been created.

questions.explanation:
Creating a GKE Service of type LoadBalancer with the annotation `cloud.google.com/load-balancer-type: Internal` provisions an internal TCP/UDP load balancer with a private IP address instead of a public one. Because the two VPCs (the GKE cluster's VPC and gce-network) have non-overlapping IP ranges, they can be connected via VPC Network Peering, which allows private RFC 1918 connectivity between the VPCs without requiring VPNs, proxies, or public IP exposure. Once peered, the Compute Engine instance in gce-network can reach the internal load balancer's IP directly, satisfying the requirement with minimal configuration effort compared to standing up a manual NAT/iptables proxy VM (Option B) or unnecessarily exposing the service externally (Options A and D, where Cloud Armor is designed for filtering external HTTP(S) traffic and is not the mechanism for enabling private cross-VPC connectivity).

**Learn more:** [Configuring internal load balancing to access GKE services](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/service-parameters) · [VPC Network Peering overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering)

You have a Dockerfile that needs to be deployed to Kubernetes Engine. What should you do?

options.text: Use kubectl app deploy <dockerfilename>.
Use gcloud app deploy <dockerfilename>.
Create a docker image from the Dockerfile and upload it to Container Registry. Create a Deployment YAML file to point to that image. Use kubectl to create the deployment with that file.
Create a docker image from the Dockerfile and upload it to Cloud Storage. Create a Deployment YAML file to point to that image. Use kubectl to create the deployment with that file.

questions.explanation:
Deploying a containerized application to GKE requires building a Docker image from the Dockerfile and pushing it to a container image registry such as Google Container Registry (or Artifact Registry), since Kubernetes nodes pull images from a registry, not from object storage like Cloud Storage. After the image is available in the registry, you author a Kubernetes Deployment manifest (YAML) that references the image, and then use kubectl to create/apply that Deployment on the cluster. There is no 'gcloud app deploy' or 'kubectl app deploy' command applicable to GKE deployments — 'gcloud app deploy' is used for App Engine, not GKE.

**Learn more:** [Pushing and pulling images - Container Registry documentation](https://cloud.google.com/container-registry/docs/pushing-and-pulling) · [Creating a Deployment - Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/deploying-workloads-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using Looker Studio to visualize a table from your data warehouse that is built on top of BigQuery. Data is appended to the data warehouse during the day. At night, the daily summary is recalculated by overwriting the table. You just noticed that the charts in Looker Studio are broken, and you want to analyze the problem. What should you do?

options.text: In Cloud Logging, create a filter for your Looker Studio report.
Use the open source CLI tool, Snapshot Debugger, to find out why the data was not refreshed correctly.
Review the Error Reporting page in the Google Cloud console to find any errors.
Use the BigQuery interface to review the nightly job and look for any errors.

questions.explanation: When Looker Studio charts break after a data refresh, the root cause is typically in the data pipeline—here, the nightly BigQuery job that overwrites the table. The BigQuery interface shows job execution history, errors, and data changes. Cloud Logging and Error Reporting are less relevant for data pipeline diagnosis.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is a financial company that must retain audit log files for 3 years. Your organization has hundreds of Google Cloud projects. You need to implement a cost-effective approach for retaining these log files. What should you do?

options.text: Create an export to the sink that saves logs from Cloud Audit to BigQuery.
Create an export to the sink that saves logs from Cloud Audit to a Coldline Storage bucket.
Write a custom script that uses logging API to copy the logs from Stackdriver logs to BigQuery.
Export these logs to Cloud Pub/Sub and write a Cloud Dataflow pipeline to store logs to Cloud SQL.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage's Coldline storage class is built for infrequently accessed data with a minimum storage duration well suited to multi-year archival needs, and it is substantially cheaper per GB than BigQuery storage or Cloud SQL. By creating an aggregated log sink (e.g., at the organization or folder level) that exports Cloud Audit Logs to a Coldline Storage bucket, you can centrally and cost-effectively retain the required audit trail across all projects for the mandated 3-year period, optionally combined with Object Lifecycle Management and Bucket Lock for compliance. Using BigQuery incurs higher storage and query costs suited for active analysis rather than passive archival, writing a custom script to copy logs adds unnecessary operational overhead, and routing logs through Pub/Sub and Dataflow into Cloud SQL is both costly and not designed for large-scale log archival.

**Learn more:** [Storage classes | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes) · [Configure and manage sinks | Cloud Logging | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An employee was terminated, but their access to Google Cloud was not removed until 2 weeks later. You need to find out if this employee accessed any sensitive customer information after their termination. What should you do?

options.text: View System Event Logs in Cloud Logging. Search for the user's email as the principal.
View System Event Logs in Cloud Logging. Search for the service account associated with the user.
View Data Access audit logs in Cloud Logging. Search for the user's email as the principal.
View the Admin Activity log in Cloud Logging. Search for the service account associated with the user.

questions.explanation: Data Access audit logs specifically capture API calls that read user-provided resource data, including access to sensitive customer information. These logs are essential for compliance and security auditing. System Event Logs and Admin Activity logs do not provide the detailed data access information needed to determine if sensitive data was accessed.

You are planning to migrate a database and a backend application to a Standard Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You need to prevent data loss and make sure there are enough nodes available for your backend application based on the demands of your workloads. You want to follow Google-recommended practices and minimize the amount of manual work required. What should you do?

options.text: Run your database as a StatefulSet. Configure cluster autoscaling to handle changes in the demands of your workloads.
Run your database as a single Pod. Run the resize command when you notice changes in the demands of your workloads.
Run your database as a DaemonSet. Run the resize command when you notice changes in the demands of your workloads.
Run your database as a Deployment. Configure cluster autoscaling to handle changes in the demands of your workloads.

questions.explanation: StatefulSet is the Kubernetes resource for stateful workloads like databases—it provides persistent storage, ordered pod naming, and stable network identity, preventing data loss. Cluster autoscaling automatically adjusts node capacity based on workload demands, minimizing manual intervention. This combination addresses both resilience and operational efficiency.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has a dedicated person who creates and manages all service accounts for Google Cloud projects. You need to assign this person the minimum role for projects. What should you do?

options.text: Add the user to roles/iam.roleAdmin role.
Add the user to roles/iam.securityAdmin role.
Add the user to roles/iam.serviceAccountUser role.
Add the user to roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin role.

questions.explanation:
The roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin predefined role grants exactly the permissions needed to create, update, delete, undelete, and list service accounts within a project, making it the minimum role required for someone whose job is to create and manage service accounts. roles/iam.roleAdmin is for managing custom IAM roles, roles/iam.securityAdmin grants broader permissions to view and set IAM policies on any resource (more than needed), and roles/iam.serviceAccountUser only allows a principal to use (impersonate/attach) existing service accounts rather than create or manage them.

**Learn more:** [Service accounts overview - IAM predefined roles](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-overview) · [Understanding roles - IAM predefined roles (roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin)](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/understanding-roles#iam-roles)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to choose and configure a cost-effective solution for relational data on Google Cloud Platform. You are working with a small set of operational data located in a single geographic region, and you need to support point-in-time recovery. What should you do?

options.text: Select Cloud SQL (MySQL). Verify that the enable binary logging option is selected.
Select Cloud SQL (MySQL). Select the create failover replicas option.
Select Cloud Spanner. Set up your instance with 2 nodes.
Select Cloud Spanner. Set up your instance as multi-regional.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL is the cost-effective managed relational database option for small, single-region operational workloads, whereas Cloud Spanner is designed for large-scale, globally distributed data and is not cost-effective for this use case. In Cloud SQL for MySQL, point-in-time recovery depends on binary logging being enabled, since binary logs record data changes that can be replayed to restore the database to a specific moment in time, in combination with automated backups. Enabling failover replicas provides high availability but does not by itself enable point-in-time recovery.

**Learn more:** [About point-in-time recovery | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/pitr)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your preview application, deployed on a single-zone Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster in us-central1, has gained popularity. You are now ready to make the application generally available. You need to deploy the application to production while ensuring high availability and resilience. You also want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use the gcloud container clusters create command with the options --enable-multi-networking and --enable-autoscaling to create an autoscaling zonal cluster and deploy the application to it.
Use the gcloud container clusters create-auto command to create an autopilot cluster and deploy the application to it.
Use the gcloud container clusters update command with the option --region us-central1 to update the cluster and deploy the application to it.
Use the gcloud container clusters update command with the option --node-locations us-central1-a,us-central1-b to update the cluster and deploy the application to the nodes.

questions.explanation: GKE Autopilot clusters are Google's recommended practice for managed Kubernetes—they handle infrastructure provisioning, scaling, and management automatically. Autopilot provides built-in high availability and resilience features across zones and nodes. The create-auto command simplifies cluster creation compared to managing zonal clusters or node locations manually.

You are deploying a new internal web application behind an internal Application Load Balancer. The application must be reachable from both the VPC network and the on-premises network by using the domain name `internal.altostrat.com`. This name must not be resolvable from the public internet. Your on-premises network is connected to the VPC network using Cloud VPN, and you have configured an inbound server policy. You need to resolve the domain name with the least administrative overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Create an A record on the on-premises DNS server that points to the load balancer’s IP address.
Create a Cloud DNS managed private zone, authorize the VPC network to use it, and add an A record that points to the load balancer’s IP address.
Create a Cloud DNS managed public zone, and add an A record that points to the load balancer’s IP address.
On each employee’s workstation, edit the local HOSTS file to map the domain name to the load balancer’s IP address.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud DNS managed private zone, authorized for the VPC network, provides private DNS records that are not exposed to the public internet. An inbound server policy lets on-premises resolvers connected through Cloud VPN query the VPC’s Cloud DNS name-resolution service, so the same private A record can serve both the VPC and on-premises network centrally. [Cloud DNS private zones](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones) and [DNS server policies](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview) support this configuration.

**Learn more:** [Create, modify, and delete zones | Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones) · [DNS server policies | Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview)
