You need to determine when users were granted Cloud Spanner Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles within your Google Cloud Platform (GCP) project. What should you do in the GCP Console?

options.text: Open the Cloud Spanner console to review configurations.
Open the IAM & admin console to review IAM policies for Cloud Spanner roles.
Go to the Cloud Monitoring console and review information for Cloud Spanner.
Go to the Cloud Logging console, review admin activity logs, and filter them for Cloud Spanner IAM roles.

questions.explanation:
Admin Activity audit logs automatically record calls that modify the configuration or metadata of resources, including IAM policy changes such as adding members to roles (setIamPolicy). These logs capture the identity of the caller, the timestamp of the change, and the affected resource. To find when users were added to Cloud Spanner IAM roles, you would go to Cloud Logging (formerly Stackdriver Logging), review the Admin Activity audit logs, and filter them for Cloud Spanner resource type and IAM policy change events. The IAM & admin console only shows the current state of IAM bindings, not a historical timeline of changes, so it cannot answer a "when" question. Monitoring and the Spanner console itself do not track IAM policy change history at all.

**Learn more:** [Audit Logging overview](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit) · [Cloud Spanner audit logging information](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/audit-logging)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to set up IAM access audit logging in BigQuery for external auditors, following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Add the auditors group to the 'logging.viewer' and 'bigQuery.dataViewer' predefined IAM roles.
Add the auditors group to two new custom IAM roles.
Add the auditor user accounts to the 'logging.viewer' and 'bigQuery.dataViewer' predefined IAM roles.
Add the auditor user accounts to two new custom IAM roles.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud IAM best practices recommend granting roles to Google groups rather than to individual user accounts, since this simplifies access management as auditors join or leave the engagement, and recommend using predefined IAM roles instead of creating custom roles whenever predefined roles already satisfy the requirement. The predefined role 'roles/logging.viewer' grants read-only access to Cloud Audit Logs (including Admin Activity and Data Access logs), and 'roles/bigquery.dataViewer' grants read-only access to BigQuery datasets/tables. Together these predefined roles provide external auditors exactly the access needed to review IAM activity and data without over-provisioning permissions or the added maintenance burden of custom roles, and assigning them to a group rather than individual accounts follows the recommended practice of using groups for access management.

**Learn more:** [IAM basic and predefined roles reference](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/understanding-roles) · [Best practices for using IAM](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/using-iam-securely)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is migrating its workloads to Google Cloud due to an expiring data center contract. The on-premises environment and Google Cloud are not connected. You have decided to follow a lift-and-shift approach, and you plan to modernize the workloads in a future project. Several old applications connect to each other through hard-coded internal IP addresses. You want to migrate these workloads quickly without modifying the application code. You also want to maintain all functionality. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate your DNS server first. Configure Cloud DNS with a forwarding zone to your migrated DNS server. Then migrate all other workloads with ephemeral internal IP addresses.
Create a VPC with non-overlapping CIDR ranges compared to your on-premises network. When migrating individual workloads, assign each workload a new static internal IP address.
Create a VPC with the same CIDR ranges as your on-premises network. When migrating individual workloads, assign each workload the same static internal IP address.
Migrate all workloads to a single VPC subnet. Configure Cloud NAT for the subnet and manually assign a static IP address to the Cloud NAT gateway.

questions.explanation: Because applications communicate using hard-coded internal IP addresses and cannot be modified, the migrated VPC must replicate the on-premises addressing scheme exactly: same CIDR ranges and the same static internal IP assigned to each workload, so existing hard-coded references keep resolving correctly with no code changes. Using non-overlapping CIDRs or ephemeral addresses would break the hard-coded IP dependencies that the applications rely on.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is using Google Workspace to manage employee accounts. Anticipated growth will increase the number of personnel from 100 employees to 1,000 employees within 2 years. Most employees will need access to your company’s Google Cloud account. The systems and processes will need to support 10x growth without performance degradation, unnecessary complexity, or security issues. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the users to Active Directory. Connect the Human Resources system to Active Directory. Turn on Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS) for Cloud Identity. Turn on Identity Federation from Cloud Identity to Active Directory.
Organize the users in Cloud Identity into groups. Enforce multi-factor authentication in Cloud Identity.
Turn on identity federation between Cloud Identity and Google Workspace. Enforce multi-factor authentication for domain wide delegation.
Use a third-party identity provider service through federation. Synchronize the users from Google Workplace to the third-party provider in real time.

questions.explanation: Cloud Identity and Google Workspace already share the same underlying identity store within a domain, so 'federating' one to the other is not a real capability — that phrase is a distractor. Scaling from 100 to 1,000 users without added operational complexity or security risk is achieved by organizing accounts into Cloud Identity groups, which keeps access management scalable, and by enforcing multi-factor authentication, without introducing Active Directory or a third-party identity provider that nothing in the scenario calls for.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company developed an application to deploy on Google Kubernetes Engine. Certain parts of the application are not fault-tolerant and are allowed to have downtime. Other parts of the application are critical and must always be available. You need to configure a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster while optimizing for cost. What should you do?

options.text: Create a cluster with a single node-pool by using standard VMs. Label he fault-tolerant Deployments as spot_true.
Create a cluster with a single node-pool by using Spot VMs. Label the critical Deployments as spot_false.

Create a cluster with both a Spot VM node pool and a node pool by using standard VMs. Deploy the critical deployments on the Spot VM node pool and the fault-tolerant deployments on the node pool by using standard VMs.

Create a cluster with both a Spot VM node pool and a nods pool by using standard VMs. Deploy the critical deployments on the node pool by using standard VMs and the fault-tolerant deployments on the Spot VM node pool.

questions.explanation: Spot VMs are cost-effective but subject to preemption, making them suitable for fault-tolerant workloads that tolerate interruptions. Standard VMs provide reliability needed for critical applications that must always be available. Creating separate node pools allows workload isolation and cost optimization—critical services incur standard costs while fault-tolerant services benefit from Spot VM discounts.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure optimal data storage for files stored in Cloud Storage for minimal cost. The files are used in a mission-critical analytics pipeline that is used continually. The users are in Boston, MA (United States). What should you do?

options.text: Configure regional storage for the region closest to the users. Configure a Nearline storage class.
Configure regional storage for the region closest to the users. Configure a Standard storage class.
Configure dual-regional storage for the dual region closest to the users. Configure a Nearline storage class.
Configure dual-regional storage for the dual region closest to the users. Configure a Standard storage class.

questions.explanation:
Because the pipeline accesses the files continually, Standard storage class is the cost-optimal choice — Nearline/Coldline classes add retrieval costs and latency that are only worthwhile for infrequently accessed data. With all users located in a single metro area (Boston) and no stated requirement for multi-region redundancy, a single-region bucket in the closest region minimizes both latency and cost compared to paying the premium for dual-regional storage.

**Learn more:** [Storage classes | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning to migrate your on-premises data to Google Cloud. The data includes:  
  
• 200 TB of video files in SAN storage  

• Data warehouse data stored on Amazon Redshift  

• 20 GB of PNG files stored on an S3 bucket  
  
You need to load the video files into a Cloud Storage bucket, transfer the data warehouse data into BigQuery, and load the PNG files into a second Cloud Storage bucket. You want to follow Google-recommended practices and avoid writing any code for the migration. What should you do?

options.text: Use gcloud storage for the video files, Dataflow for the data warehouse data, and Storage Transfer Service for the PNG files.
Use Transfer Appliance for the videos, BigQuery Data Transfer Service for the data warehouse data, and Storage Transfer Service for the PNG files.
Use Storage Transfer Service for the video files, BigQuery Data Transfer Service for the data warehouse data, and Storage Transfer Service for the PNG files.
Use Cloud Data Fusion for the video files, Dataflow for the data warehouse data, and Storage Transfer Service for the PNG files.

questions.explanation: For large on-premises data migration (200TB), Transfer Appliance is the appropriate tool—a physical appliance shipped to your data center. BigQuery Data Transfer Service handles cloud-to-cloud and SaaS migrations like Redshift data warehouse. Storage Transfer Service manages cloud storage and S3 migrations. This combination avoids network bandwidth constraints and minimizes migration time.

You are migrating a business critical application from your local data center into Google Cloud. As part of your high-availability strategy, you want to ensure that any data used by the application will be immediately available if a zonal failure occurs. What should you do?

options.text: Store the application data on a zonal persistent disk. Create a snapshot schedule for the disk. If an outage occurs, create a new disk from the most recent snapshot and attach it to a new VM in another zone.
Store the application data on a zonal persistent disk. If an outage occurs, create an instance in another zone with this disk attached.

Store the application data on a regional persistent disk. Create a snapshot schedule for the disk. If an outage occurs, create a new disk from the most recent snapshot and attach it to a new VM in another zone.
Store the application data on a regional persistent disk. If an outage occurs, create an instance in another zone with this disk attached.

questions.explanation: Regional persistent disks are synchronously replicated across two zones within a region, ensuring data is immediately available even during a zonal failure. If a zone fails, the disk can be force-attached to a VM in the secondary zone without data loss or recovery delays. Zonal disks with snapshots (A, C) require recovery time and manual intervention. Regional disks eliminate the need for snapshots for high-availability failover.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs numerous Google Cloud services that are consolidated in a single project. Every team also has its own separate projects for testing and development work. The DevOps team requires access to all of the production services so they can carry out their responsibilities. You want to make sure that future changes to Google Cloud products don't end up expanding the DevOps team's permissions over time, and you want to follow Google-recommended practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Grant all members of the DevOps team the role of Project Editor on the organization level.
Grant all members of the DevOps team the role of Project Editor on the production project.
Create a custom role that combines the required permissions. Grant the DevOps team the custom role on the production project.
Create a custom role that combines the required permissions. Grant the DevOps team the custom role on the organization level.

questions.explanation:
Predefined roles such as Project Editor are managed by Google and can automatically gain additional permissions whenever Google Cloud introduces new services or features, which risks unintentionally broadening access over time. A custom role, however, contains a fixed, explicitly defined set of permissions that does not change automatically when new products or features are released, giving you full control over what access is granted. Following the principle of least privilege, IAM roles should also be granted at the narrowest scope needed—in this case, the production project itself—rather than at the organization level, to limit the potential impact of the grant. Combining a custom role with project-level scoping satisfies both the requirement to prevent permission creep and Google's recommended IAM best practices.

**Learn more:** [Understanding roles | IAM Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/understanding-roles) · [Best practices for using IAM](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/using-iam-securely)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have built a containerized web application intended to serve internal colleagues only during business hours. You want to make sure that no costs are incurred during the hours when the application is not being used. You have just created a new Google Cloud project in which to deploy this application.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the container on Cloud Run for Anthos, and set the minimum number of instances to zero.
Deploy the container on Cloud Run (fully managed), and set the minimum number of instances to zero.
Deploy the container on App Engine flexible environment with autoscaling, and set the value min_instances to zero in the app.yaml.
Deploy the container on App Engine flexible environment with manual scaling, and set the value instances to zero in the app.yaml.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run (fully managed) is a serverless platform that automatically scales the number of container instances based on incoming traffic, and it supports configuring the minimum number of instances to zero. When set to zero minimum instances, Cloud Run scales the service down completely during periods of no traffic, so no compute cost is incurred outside business hours — you pay only for the CPU, memory, and requests consumed while instances are actively serving traffic. Cloud Run for Anthos requires a GKE cluster, which incurs cost for the underlying VM nodes regardless of application traffic, so it cannot achieve zero cost when idle. App Engine flexible environment runs on managed Compute Engine VMs and does not support scaling all instances down to zero — a minimum of running VM instances is always billed, whether autoscaling or manual scaling is used.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Run - Setting minimum instances](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/min-instances) · [Cloud Run pricing](https://cloud.google.com/run/pricing)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are managing a stateful application deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that can only have one replica. You recently discovered that the application becomes unstable at peak times. You have identified that the application needs more CPU than what has been configured in the manifest at these peak times. You want Kubernetes to allocate the application sufficient CPU resources during these peak times, while ensuring cost efficiency during off-peak periods. What should you do?

options.text: Enable node auto-provisioning on the GKE cluster.
Configure a Vertical Pod Autoscaler on the Deployment.
Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on the Deployment.
Enable cluster autoscaling on the GKE cluster.

questions.explanation:
Because the application is stateful and limited to a single replica, it cannot be scaled out horizontally; a Vertical Pod Autoscaler automatically adjusts the pod's CPU (and memory) requests/limits up during peak demand and back down during off-peak periods, preserving cost efficiency. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and cluster/node auto-provisioning add or resize replicas/nodes rather than resizing the single pod's own resource allocation, which does not fit a single-replica stateful workload.

**Learn more:** [Configuring Vertical Pod Autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/vertical-pod-autoscaling)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure application performance monitoring for Google Cloud projects A, B, and C so that everything can be viewed through a single pane of glass. You want to monitor CPU, memory, and disk. What should you do?

options.text: Enable API and then share charts from project A, B, and C.
Enable API and then give the metrics.reader role to projects A, B, and C.
Enable API and then use default dashboards to view all projects in sequence.
Enable API, create a workspace under project A, and then add projects B and C.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring lets you create a Workspace (metrics scope) associated with one Google Cloud project (the scoping project) and then add other projects as monitored projects. Once projects B and C are added to the Workspace created under project A, you can view and correlate CPU, memory, disk, and other metrics from all three projects together in shared dashboards and charts, achieving a true single-pane-of-glass monitoring experience. Simply sharing charts, assigning IAM roles, or toggling between separate default dashboards does not consolidate multi-project metrics into one unified view.

**Learn more:** [Configure a metrics scope | Cloud Monitoring | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/settings/multiple-projects) · [Multi-Project Cloud Monitoring made easier | Google Cloud Blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/operations/multi-project-cloud-monitoring-made-easier)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses Cloud Storage to hold application backup files for disaster recovery purposes. Following Google's recommended best practices, which storage option should you choose?

options.text: Multi-Regional Storage
Regional Storage
Nearline Storage
Coldline Storage

questions.explanation:
Google recommends Nearline Storage for data such as backups and disaster recovery files that are accessed infrequently (less than once a month) but must remain readily available when needed. Nearline Storage provides the same low-latency, high-durability characteristics as Standard storage classes at a lower storage cost, with a 30-day minimum storage duration, making it well-suited for typical backup retention cycles. Multi-Regional and Regional storage are intended for frequently accessed, latency-sensitive data, which is unnecessarily costly for periodic backups, while Coldline Storage targets data accessed roughly once a year or less, such as archival data, which does not match typical disaster-recovery backup access patterns as closely as Nearline does.

**Learn more:** [Storage classes | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is running a critical workload on a single Compute Engine VM instance. Your company's disaster recovery policies require you to back up the entire instance’s disk data every day. The backups must be retained for 7 days. You must configure a backup solution that complies with your company’s security policies and requires minimal setup and configuration. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the instance to use persistent disk asynchronous replication.
Configure daily scheduled persistent disk snapshots with a retention period of 7 days.
Configure Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function each day that creates a new machine image and deletes machine images that are older than 7 days.

Configure a bash script using gsutil to run daily through a cron job. Copy the disk’s files to a Cloud Storage bucket with archive storage class and an object lifecycle rule to delete the objects after 7 days.

questions.explanation: Persistent disk snapshots are the Google-recommended solution for backing up entire VM instance disks. Snapshots are incremental, storing only changes since the last snapshot, which minimizes storage costs while meeting the 7-day retention requirement. They provide minimal setup overhead and integrate with Compute Engine's scheduling capabilities for automated daily backups.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to run several applications, each on its own Compute Engine instance, within the same project. You want to control, at a more granular level, which service account each instance uses when it calls Google Cloud APIs. What should you do?

options.text: When creating the instances, specify a Service Account for each instance.
When creating the instances, assign the name of each Service Account as instance metadata.
After starting the instances, use gcloud compute instances update to specify a Service Account for each instance.
After starting the instances, use gcloud compute instances update to assign the name of the relevant Service Account as instance metadata.

questions.explanation:
Each Compute Engine instance can be assigned its own user-managed service account, which determines the identity and IAM permissions the instance uses when calling Google Cloud APIs. By specifying a distinct service account for each instance at creation time, you can grant each application only the specific IAM roles it needs, following the principle of least privilege. Instance metadata is not used to assign a service account—it only stores configuration data (such as startup scripts or custom key-value pairs) and has no effect on which identity the instance authenticates as when accessing Google Cloud APIs.

**Learn more:** [Create a VM that uses a user-managed service account | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/create-enable-service-accounts-for-instances) · [Service accounts | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/service-accounts)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company would like to store invoices and other financial documents in Google Cloud. You need to identify a Google-managed solution to store this information for your company. You must ensure that the documents are kept for a duration of three years. Your company’s analysts need frequent access to invoices from the past six months. After six months, invoices should be archived for audit purposes only. You want to minimize costs and follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Storage with Object Lifecycle Management to change the object storage class to Coldline after six months.
Use Cloud Storage with Object Lifecycle Management to change the object storage class to Standard after six months.
Store your documents on Filestore, and move the documents to Cloud Storage with object storage class set to Coldline after six months.
Store your documents on Filestore, and move the documents to Cloud Storage with object storage class set to Standard after six months.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage is Google's managed solution for document storage. Object Lifecycle Management automatically transitions objects from Standard (for frequent access) to Coldline (for archival) after six months, optimizing cost while meeting access patterns. This eliminates manual data movement and ensures compliance with the 3-year retention requirement.

questions.domain: Setting up a cloud solution environment
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The sales team has a project named Sales Data Digest that has the ID acme-data-digest. You need to set up similar Google Cloud resources for the marketing team but their resources must be organized independently of the sales team. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the Project Editor role to the Marketing team for acme-data-digest.
Create a Project Lien on acme-data-digest and then grant the Project Editor role to the Marketing team.
Create another project with the ID acme-marketing-data-digest for the Marketing team and deploy the resources there.
Create a new project named Marketing Data Digest and use the ID acme-data-digest. Grant the Project Editor role to the Marketing team.

questions.explanation: To ensure resources are organized independently between teams, each team should have a separate Google Cloud project. Projects are the fundamental unit of resource isolation and access control in Google Cloud. Creating a distinct project with a clear naming convention (acme-marketing-data-digest) ensures complete separation of resources, billing, and IAM policies.

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a single batch process on an on-premises server that takes about 30 hours to finish. The job runs once a month, can be executed offline, and must be restarted from the beginning if it is interrupted. The company wants to migrate this workload to the cloud while keeping costs as low as possible.  
  
What should be done?

options.text: Migrate the workload to a Compute Engine Preemptible VM.
Migrate the workload to a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster with Preemptible nodes.
Migrate the workload to a Compute Engine VM. Start and stop the instance as needed.
Create an Instance Template with Preemptible VMs On. Create a Managed Instance Group from the template and adjust Target CPU Utilization. Migrate the workload.

questions.explanation:
Preemptible VM instances always stop after running for 24 hours, and Compute Engine can reclaim them at any time before that as well. Since this batch job takes roughly 30 hours and must restart completely if interrupted, it cannot reliably run to completion on preemptible capacity (whether standalone, in GKE, or in a preemptible-backed Managed Instance Group with autoscaling). Running the job on a standard Compute Engine VM and starting the instance only when the monthly job needs to execute, then stopping it once finished, ensures the job completes without forced termination while minimizing cost, since billing only applies during the roughly 30 hours per month the VM is actually running.

**Learn more:** [Preemptible VM instances | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/preemptible) · [Create and use preemptible VMs | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/create-use-preemptible)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to select and configure compute resources for a set of batch processing jobs. These jobs:  
  
- Take approximately 2 hours to complete  
- Run nightly  
  
You want to minimize service costs. What should you do?

options.text: Select Google Kubernetes Engine. Use a single-node cluster with a small instance type.
Select Google Kubernetes Engine. Use a three-node cluster with micro instance types.
Select Compute Engine. Use preemptible VM instances of the appropriate standard machine type.
Select Compute Engine. Use VM instance types that support micro bursting.

questions.explanation:
Preemptible VM instances (now known as Spot VMs) on Compute Engine are designed for workloads that are fault-tolerant and can withstand possible instance termination, such as batch processing jobs. They offer substantial cost savings—up to 60-91% off the price of standard on-demand instances—because Google can reclaim the capacity when needed elsewhere. Since these batch jobs run nightly for a finite duration (2 hours) and are not required to run continuously, they are well-suited to preemptible instances, which have a maximum runtime limit and may be interrupted, but this trade-off is acceptable for scheduled, short-duration, restartable batch workloads. Using preemptible VMs with an appropriately sized standard machine type ensures the compute resources match the workload needs while minimizing costs, which is more cost-effective than running a persistent GKE cluster (options A and B) or using undersized/inappropriate micro instance types for batch processing.

**Learn more:** [Spot VMs | Compute Engine Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: You have an instance group that you want to load balance. You want the load balancer to terminate the client SSL session. The instance group is used to serve a public web application over HTTPS. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Configure an HTTP(S) load balancer.
Configure an internal TCP load balancer.
Configure an external SSL proxy load balancer.
Configure an external TCP proxy load balancer.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud recommends HTTP(S) Load Balancing for terminating SSL sessions on public web applications over HTTPS. The HTTP(S) LB terminates the client SSL session at the load balancer and re-encrypts traffic to backends if needed. SSL Proxy Load Balancers are explicitly designed for non-HTTP(S) traffic, not web applications; internal load balancers are for private traffic, and TCP proxies do not terminate SSL.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: You have an instance group that you want to load balance. You want the load balancer to terminate the client SSL session. The instance group is used to serve a public web application over HTTPS. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use service account credentials in your on-premises application.
Use gcloud to create a key file for the service account that has appropriate permissions.
Set up direct interconnect between your data center and Google Cloud Platform to enable authentication for your on-premises applications.
Go to the IAM & admin console, grant a user account permissions similar to the service account permissions, and use this user account for authentication from your data center.

questions.explanation:
When an application runs outside of Google Cloud (such as in an on-premises data center), it cannot rely on the metadata server to automatically supply Application Default Credentials for a service account. Instead, you must generate a service account key file using the `gcloud iam service-accounts keys create` command (or the equivalent Console/API action), download the JSON key, and make it available to the application (typically by setting the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable). This lets the on-premises application authenticate as the service account that already has the correct AutoML permissions, without needing network-level connectivity solutions like Cloud Interconnect or substituting a user account for the service account.

**Learn more:** [Creating and managing service account keys](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/keys-create-delete) · [Authenticating as a service account](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/production)

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: Your company uses BigQuery to store and analyze data. Upon submitting your query in BigQuery, the query fails with a quotaExceeded error. You need to diagnose the issue causing the error. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use BigQuery BI Engine to analyze the issue.
Use the INFORMATION_SCHEMA views to analyze the underlying issue.
Configure Cloud Trace to analyze the issue.
Search errors in Cloud Audit Logs to analyze the issue.
View errors in Cloud Monitoring to analyze the issue.

questions.explanation: INFORMATION_SCHEMA views provide detailed metadata about query jobs and resource consumption, helping identify which queries exceed quotas. Cloud Audit Logs record API calls and administrative actions with full error context, making it easy to correlate quotaExceeded errors with specific requests. Both methods are essential for comprehensive quota diagnostics.

questions.domain: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
questions.question: You have deployed an application on a single Compute Engine instance. The application writes logs to disk. Users start reporting errors with the application. You want to diagnose the problem. What should you do?

options.text: Navigate to Cloud Logging and view the application logs.
Configure a health check on the instance and set a “consecutive successes” Healthy threshold value of 1.
Connect to the instance’s serial console and read the application logs.
Install and configure the Ops agent and view the logs from Cloud Logging.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine instances do not have a logging agent pre-installed by default. The Ops Agent must be installed to collect application logs from disk and forward them to Cloud Logging, where they can be queried and analyzed. Direct Cloud Logging navigation without an agent yields no data.

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: You have deployed an application on a single Compute Engine instance. The application writes logs to disk. Users start reporting errors with the application. You want to diagnose the problem. What should you do?

options.text: Create a separate Cloud Billing account for all sandbox projects. Link a credit card with a limit of $1,000 to this billing account. Ensure all sandbox projects are linked to this new Cloud Billing account.

Create a Google Cloud Folder and ensure that all sandbox projects are located under that Folder. Create a Budget Alert for $1,000 and scope it to the Folder. Configure an email alert to billing administrators and users once the budget is 90% reached.

Create an email template reminding people to regularly check their Google Cloud spend. Create a Cloud Function that sends the email to all the project owners. Create a daily job in Cloud Scheduler that triggers the Cloud Function. Deploy this solution for each sandbox.
Configure a billing data export to a BigQuery dataset on the Cloud Billing account. Create a dashboard for all costs related to the sandbox experiments. Share the dashboard with all engineers.

questions.explanation:
Grouping all sandbox projects under a Folder lets a single Budget Alert be scoped at the Folder level rather than per-project, and configuring an email alert at 90% of the $1,000 threshold notifies both billing administrators and users automatically with no custom code to build or maintain. A per-card spending limit or a custom Cloud Function/Scheduler solution requires more manual setup and does not scale cleanly as sandbox projects are added.

**Learn more:** [Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets)

Using the gcloud command line in Cloud Shell, you need to generate a list of the APIs that are currently enabled for a Google Cloud Platform project named my-project. What should you do?

options.text: Run gcloud projects list to get the project ID, and then run gcloud services list --project <project ID>.
Run gcloud init to set the current project to my-project, and then run gcloud services list --available.
Run gcloud info to view the account value, and then run gcloud services list --account <Account>.
Run gcloud projects describe <project ID> to verify the project value, and then run gcloud services list --available.

questions.explanation:
The gcloud services list command defaults to the --enabled behavior, returning only the services (APIs) that are currently enabled for a given project. The --available flag, by contrast, returns all services available to the project, including ones that are not yet enabled, which does not meet the requirement of listing only enabled APIs. Because gcloud services list operates on a project ID, you first retrieve the project ID with gcloud projects list, and then run gcloud services list --project <project ID> to get the enabled APIs for that specific project.

**Learn more:** [gcloud services list | Google Cloud SDK | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/services/list) · [List services | Service Usage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-usage/docs/list-services)

Your company is transitioning from an on-premises environment to Google Cloud. Several development teams currently rely on Cassandra environments as backend databases. Each team requires a development environment that is isolated from the other Cassandra instances used by other teams. You want to complete this move to Google Cloud quickly and with minimal ongoing support effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. Build an instruction guide to install Cassandra on Google Cloud. 2. Make the instruction guide accessible to your developers.
1. Advise your developers to go to Cloud Marketplace. 2. Ask the developers to launch a Cassandra image for their development work.
1. Build a Cassandra Compute Engine instance and take a snapshot of it. 2. Use the snapshot to create instances for your developers.

1. Build a Cassandra Compute Engine instance and take a snapshot of it. 2. Upload the snapshot to Cloud Storage and make it accessible to your developers. 3. Build instructions to create a Compute Engine instance from the snapshot so that developers can do it themselves.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Marketplace provides ready-to-deploy, pre-configured solution images (such as Bitnami's Cassandra offering) that developers can launch directly as isolated Compute Engine instances with just a few clicks. This approach lets each development team self-serve their own isolated Cassandra environment quickly, without the central team needing to author custom installation guides, manage golden image snapshots, or handle ongoing instance provisioning — satisfying both the speed and minimal-support-effort requirements.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Marketplace documentation](https://cloud.google.com/marketplace/docs)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You used the gcloud container clusters command to create two Google Cloud Kubernetes (GKE) clusters: prod-cluster and dev-cluster.  
  
• prod-cluster is a standard cluster.  

• dev-cluster is an auto-pilot cluster.  
  
When you run the kubectl get nodes command, you only see the nodes from prod-cluster. Which commands should you run to check the node status for dev-cluster?

options.text: gcloud container clusters get-credentials dev-clusterkubectl get nodes
gcloud container clusters update -generate-password dev-cluster kubectl get nodes
kubectl config set-context dev-clusterkubectl cluster-info
kubectl config set-credentials dev-clusterkubectl cluster-info

questions.explanation: The gcloud container clusters get-credentials command configures kubectl to point to the dev-cluster by updating the kubeconfig file and setting the context. After this command, kubectl get nodes will return nodes from dev-cluster. This is the standard way to switch between clusters when both are managed by GKE.

questions.question: Your company plans to migrate data from an on-premises relational database to Google Cloud. The existing database can no longer scale with the growth in users, and the user population is expected to increase rapidly. You need to select a relational database that can scale globally while minimizing management and administrative effort. You also want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL.
Use Spanner.
Use Firestore.
Use BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Spanner is a fully managed, globally distributed relational database service that provides transactional consistency at global scale and horizontal scalability, making it suitable for rapidly growing global operational workloads with minimal infrastructure administration.\
\
**Learn more:** [Spanner documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs) · [Spanner product overview](https://cloud.google.com/spanner)

questions.question: Your company plans to migrate data from an on-premises relational database to Google Cloud. The existing database can no longer scale with the growth in users, and the user population is expected to increase rapidly. You need to select a relational database that can scale globally while minimizing management and administrative effort. You also want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Enable OS Login for all VMs. Use IAM roles to grant user permissions.
Require your developers to create public SSH keys. Write custom startup scripts to update user permissions.
Require your developers to create public SSH keys. Make the owner of the public key the root user.
Enable OS Login for all VMs. Write custom startup scripts to update user permissions.

questions.explanation:
OS Login centralizes Linux account lifecycle management by tying SSH access directly to Google identities, so granting or revoking IAM roles (such as roles/compute.osLogin) automatically provisions or removes POSIX accounts on every VM without custom scripts. Manually distributing SSH keys or writing startup scripts to manage permissions is exactly the operational overhead OS Login is designed to eliminate.

**Learn more:** [Manage OS Login in an organization](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/oslogin)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are reviewing Google Cloud Platform service costs across three separate projects. You need to use this cost data to build service cost estimates by service type, broken down daily and monthly, projected for the next six months, using standard query syntax. What should you do?

options.text: Export your bill to a Cloud Storage bucket, and then import into Cloud Bigtable for analysis.
Export your bill to a Cloud Storage bucket, and then import into Google Sheets for analysis.
Export your transactions to a local file, and perform analysis with a desktop tool.
Export your bill to a BigQuery dataset, and then write time window-based SQL queries for analysis.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Billing allows you to export detailed billing data (including usage, cost, and service-level breakdowns) directly into a BigQuery dataset. Once in BigQuery, you can use standard SQL to write time window-based queries that aggregate costs by service, by day, by month, and project future estimates across multiple projects. This is the officially recommended approach for detailed, query-based billing analysis, as documented in Google's 'Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery' guide. Cloud Bigtable and Google Sheets do not support standard SQL query syntax at the scale needed, and exporting to a local file for desktop analysis is not scalable or efficient for ongoing multi-project cost estimation.

**Learn more:** [Set up Cloud Billing data export to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to run a single caching HTTP reverse proxy on Google Cloud for a latency-sensitive website. This particular reverse proxy consumes almost no CPU. You want to provide it with:  
  
- A 30-GB in-memory cache  
- An additional 2 GB of memory for the rest of the processes  
  
You want to minimize cost. How should you run this reverse proxy?

options.text: Create a Cloud Memorystore for Redis instance with 32-GB capacity.
Run it on Compute Engine, and choose a custom instance type with 6 vCPUs and 32 GB of memory.
Package it in a container image, and run it on Kubernetes Engine, using n1-standard-32 instances as nodes.
Run it on Compute Engine, choose the instance type n1-standard-1, and add an SSD persistent disk of 32 GB.

questions.explanation:
Because the proxy barely uses CPU but needs roughly 32 GB of memory (30 GB cache + 2 GB overhead), the most cost-effective approach on Compute Engine is a custom machine type that lets you specify vCPU and memory independently instead of being forced into a fixed ratio like the standard machine families. For N1 custom machine types, Google Cloud enforces a memory-per-vCPU ratio (approximately 0.9 GB to 6.5 GB per vCPU) and requires an even vCPU count (except for 1 vCPU), so to reach 32 GB of memory the minimum valid configuration is 6 vCPUs, giving you the memory you need at the lowest possible vCPU (and cost) rather than over-provisioning CPU as would happen with an n1-standard-32 GKE node pool. A managed Redis instance (Memorystore) is unnecessary and adds network overhead for what is essentially a local, single-instance in-process cache, and adding an SSD persistent disk does not provide in-memory caching capacity at all.

**Learn more:** [Custom machine types | Compute Engine Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/general-purpose-machines#custom_machine_types)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You developed a web application that will serve traffic for a local event and expect the traffic volume to be unpredictable. You have containerized the application and now want to deploy it on Google Cloud while minimizing costs. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the web application as a Cloud Run job.
Deploy the web application on Google Kubernetes Engine in Standard mode.
Deploy the web application as a Cloud Run service.
Deploy the web application on Google Kubernetes Engine in Autopilot mode.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run services provide an HTTPS endpoint for containerized web applications, automatically scale with request demand, and can scale to zero when no requests are arriving. This accommodates unpredictable traffic while avoiding charges for continuously running idle application instances.

**Learn more:** [What is Cloud Run?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) · [About instance autoscaling in Cloud Run services](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-instance-autoscaling)

You are developing a new version of an application that runs in the App Engine environment. Before fully cutting over to the new version, you want to test it with only 1% of your users. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a new version of your application in Google Kubernetes Engine instead of App Engine and then use GCP Console to split traffic.
Deploy a new version of your application in a Compute Engine instance instead of App Engine and then use GCP Console to split traffic.
Deploy a new version as a separate app in App Engine. Then configure App Engine using GCP Console to split traffic between the two apps.
Deploy a new version of your application in App Engine. Then go to App Engine settings in GCP Console and split traffic between the current version and newly deployed versions accordingly.

questions.explanation:
App Engine supports traffic splitting natively at the version level within a service. You deploy the new version without promoting it as the default, then use the App Engine traffic splitting feature in the Google Cloud Console (or gcloud) to allocate a percentage of incoming requests—such as 1%—to the new version while the remainder continues to be served by the existing version. This enables canary-style testing without needing to migrate the application to a different compute platform such as GKE or Compute Engine, and without creating a separate application, since traffic splitting operates across versions of the same App Engine service.

**Learn more:** [Splitting Traffic | App Engine flexible environment docs](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/flexible/splitting-traffic) · [Migrating and Splitting Traffic | App Engine standard environment docs](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/splitting-traffic)

questions.question: Your web application is hosted on Cloud Run and needs to query a Cloud SQL database. Every morning during a traffic spike, you notice API quota errors in Cloud SQL logs. The project has already reached the maximum API quota. You want to make a configuration change to mitigate the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the minimum number of Cloud Run instances.
Use traffic splitting.
Modify the maximum number of Cloud Run instances.
Set a minimum concurrent requests environment variable for the application.

questions.explanation: Setting a minimum number of Cloud Run instances prevents cold starts during traffic spikes. Cloud Run scales to zero by default, and rapid scale-up during morning spikes causes multiple simultaneous database connection requests, exceeding the quota. Maintaining minimum instances keeps connections warm and reduces the concurrent spike in API calls to the database.

questions.question: Your web application is hosted on Cloud Run and needs to query a Cloud SQL database. Every morning during a traffic spike, you notice API quota errors in Cloud SQL logs. The project has already reached the maximum API quota. You want to make a configuration change to mitigate the issue. What should you do?

questions.explanation:
To protect against the loss of an entire zone while avoiding downtime and keeping costs low, you should provision the application's Compute Engine resources in a second zone within the same region — us-central1-b — and distribute (load-balance) traffic across both us-central1-a and us-central1-b. Because both zones actively serve traffic, if one zone fails the other continues handling requests seamlessly, resulting in no downtime. Staying within a single region (rather than deploying across multiple regions) keeps network costs and complexity minimal while still meeting the zonal-redundancy requirement, consistent with Google Cloud's guidance on designing robust, highly available systems across multiple zones in a region.

**Learn more:** [Designing resilient systems | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/tutorials/robustsystems) · [Regions and zones | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/regions-zones)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application already running in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that consists of multiple pods running on four GKE n1-standard-2 nodes. You need to deploy additional pods that require n2-highmem-16 nodes, and this must be done without any downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Use gcloud container clusters upgrade. Deploy the new services.
Create a new Node Pool and specify machine type n2ג€
Create a new cluster with n2ג€
Create a new cluster with both n1ג€

questions.explanation:
GKE clusters support multiple node pools, and each node pool can use a different machine type. Creating a new node pool with machine type n2-highmem-16 lets you add nodes with the required resources alongside the existing n1-standard-2 node pool, without disrupting the currently running pods or requiring cluster recreation. You can then deploy the new pods so they are scheduled onto the new node pool (for example using node selectors or taints/tolerations), achieving the required capacity with zero downtime for existing workloads. Recreating a cluster (as in options C and D) would require redeploying all pods and could cause downtime, and running `gcloud container clusters upgrade` (option A) only upgrades the Kubernetes version and does not add nodes of a different machine type.

**Learn more:** [Add and manage node pools | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/node-pools) · [Migrate nodes to a different machine type | GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/migrate-nodes)

questions.domain: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a VPC network in Google Cloud whose subnet is quickly nearing its private IP address capacity. You anticipate that the number of Compute Engine VM instances in the same region will double within a week. You must implement a Google-recommended solution that minimizes operational costs and requires no downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Create a second VPC with the same subnet IP range, and connect this VPC to the existing VPC by using VPC Network Peering.
Delete the existing subnet, and create a new subnet with double the IP range available.
Permit additional traffic from the expected range of private IP addresses to reach your VMs by configuring firewall rules.
Use the Google Cloud CLI tool to expand the primary IP range of your subnet.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud supports expanding an existing subnet’s primary IPv4 range in place by using `gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range`. The expansion increases address capacity without interrupting traffic within the subnet, avoiding the operational overhead of a second peered VPC or the disruption of deleting and recreating the subnet.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage VPC networks — Expand a primary IPv4 range](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/create-modify-vpc-networks#expand-ip-range) · [gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/networks/subnets/expand-ip-range)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You created an instance of SQL Server 2017 on Compute Engine to test features in the new version. You want to connect to this instance using the fewest number of steps. What should you do?

options.text: Install a RDP client on your desktop. Verify that a firewall rule for port 3389 exists.
Install a RDP client in your desktop. Set a Windows username and password in the GCP Console. Use the credentials to log in to the instance.
Set a Windows password in the GCP Console. Verify that a firewall rule for port 22 exists. Click the RDP button in the GCP Console and supply the credentials to log in.
Set a Windows username and password in the GCP Console. Verify that a firewall rule for port 3389 exists. Click the RDP button in the GCP Console, and supply the credentials to log in.

questions.explanation:
Windows Server instances on Compute Engine (such as the SQL Server 2017 image) are accessed via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), which requires TCP port 3389 to be open, not port 22 (which is used for SSH on Linux instances). The correct workflow is to set a Windows username and password through the Google Cloud Console (which generates the necessary credentials), confirm that a firewall rule permitting port 3389 exists, and then use the console's built-in RDP button along with those credentials to connect directly — this is the most streamlined, fewest-step method since it avoids manually installing and configuring a separate RDP client from scratch.

**Learn more:** [Connecting to Windows instances](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/connecting-to-windows)

questions.domain: Configuring access and security
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application produces daily reports on a Compute Engine virtual machine (VM) that resides in the project corp-iot-insights. Your team, which works exclusively in the project corp-aggregate-reports, needs a copy of these daily exports placed in the bucket corp-aggregate-reports-storage.  
  
You want to configure access so that:  
  
- The daily reports generated by the VM become available in the bucket corp-aggregate-reports-storage.  
- The configuration uses as few steps as possible.  
- The approach follows Google-recommended practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Move both projects under the same folder.
Grant the VM Service Account the role Storage Object Creator on corp-aggregate-reports-storage.
Create a Shared VPC network between both projects. Grant the VM Service Account the role Storage Object Creator on corp-iot-insights.
Make corp-aggregate-reports-storage public and create a folder with a pseudo-randomized suffix name. Share the folder with the IoT team.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage bucket-level IAM bindings can be assigned to any principal, including a service account belonging to a different project, since Cloud Storage is a global resource independent of any VPC or project folder hierarchy. Granting the VM's service account the Storage Object Creator role directly on corp-aggregate-reports-storage lets the VM write its daily report objects into that bucket with minimal permissions and configuration steps, following the principle of least privilege and Google's recommended cross-project IAM approach for Cloud Storage access, without requiring networking changes (Shared VPC), organizational restructuring, or making the bucket public.

**Learn more:** [Using Cloud IAM permissions - Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam) · [IAM roles for Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles)

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has an internal application for managing transactional orders. The application is used exclusively by employees in a single physical location. The application requires strong consistency, fast queries, and ACID guarantees for multi-table transactional updates. The first version of the application is implemented in PostgreSQL, and you want to deploy it to the cloud with minimal code changes. Which database is most appropriate for this application?

options.text: BigQuery
Cloud SQL
Cloud Spanner
Cloud Datastore

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL with PostgreSQL is the optimal choice for this use case. The application requires minimal code changes since it is already built on PostgreSQL, and Cloud SQL PostgreSQL provides the strong consistency, fast queries, and ACID guarantees needed. Since the application serves a single physical location only, the global distribution and complexity of Cloud Spanner is unnecessary and would require significant code rewrites.

questions.domain: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a new web application that will be deployed on Google Cloud Platform. As part of your release cycle, you want to test updates to your application on a small portion of real user traffic. The majority of the users should still be directed towards a stable version of your application. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the application on App Engine. For each update, create a new version of the same service. Configure traffic splitting to send a small percentage of traffic to the new version.
Deploy the application on App Engine. For each update, create a new service. Configure traffic splitting to send a small percentage of traffic to the new service.
Deploy the application on Kubernetes Engine. For a new release, update the deployment to use the new version.
Deploy the application on Kubernetes Engine. For a new release, create a new deployment for the new version. Update the service to use the new deployment.

questions.explanation: App Engine's traffic splitting feature allows you to deploy a new version and gradually send a percentage of traffic to it while keeping the majority on the stable version. This is the standard approach for canary deployments and A/B testing. Services are organizational units, not versions; traffic splitting applies within a service across its versions.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company's core business involves renting out construction equipment at large scale. All rented equipment is fitted with multiple sensors that transmit event information every few seconds. These signals can vary and include:  
  
- Engine status  
- Distance traveled  
- Fuel level  
- And more  
  
Customers are billed according to the consumption data captured by these sensors. You anticipate high throughput — up to thousands of events per hour per device — and need to retrieve consistent data based on the time of the event. Storing and retrieving individual signals must be atomic.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a file in Cloud Storage per device and append new data to that file.
Create a file in Cloud Filestore per device and append new data to that file.
Ingest the data into Datastore. Store data in an entity group based on the device.
Ingest the data into Cloud Bigtable. Create a row key based on the event timestamp.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Bigtable is purpose-built for high-throughput, low-latency ingestion of time-series data such as sensor telemetry, and each row write/read in Bigtable is atomic. By designing a row key that incorporates the event timestamp (typically combined with the device identifier), you can efficiently query and retrieve consistent data ordered and filtered by time. In contrast, Cloud Datastore entity groups are constrained to roughly one write per second, which cannot sustain thousands of events per hour per device without contention; Cloud Storage and Cloud Filestore file-append patterns are not designed for atomic, high-frequency structured event writes or efficient time-based range queries. This makes Bigtable the appropriate storage system for this workload.

**Learn more:** [Schema design for time series data | Bigtable | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/schema-design-time-series)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to manage several Google Cloud projects using as few steps as possible. You want to set up the Google Cloud SDK command-line interface (CLI) so that switching between multiple projects is easy. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a configuration for each project you need to manage. 2. Activate the appropriate configuration when you work with each of your assigned Google Cloud projects.
1. Create a configuration for each project you need to manage. 2. Use gcloud init to update the configuration values when you need to work with a non-default project
1. Use the default configuration for one project you need to manage. 2. Activate the appropriate configuration when you work with each of your assigned Google Cloud projects.
1. Use the default configuration for one project you need to manage. 2. Use gcloud init to update the configuration values when you need to work with a non-default project.

questions.explanation:
The Google Cloud SDK supports named configurations, each of which stores a distinct set of CLI properties (such as project ID, account, default region/zone). The recommended and most efficient workflow for managing multiple projects is to create a dedicated configuration for each project with `gcloud config configurations create [NAME]`, then simply switch context by running `gcloud config configurations activate [NAME]` when you need to work with a different project. This avoids re-running the more heavyweight `gcloud init` process (which walks through account selection, project selection, and default settings) every time you need to change projects, making configuration activation the fastest and fewest-step approach.

**Learn more:** [Managing gcloud CLI configurations](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/configurations)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a web application that must read objects from a shared Cloud Storage bucket. Grant a Cloud Run service access to objects in the existing bucket whose names use the `site1-data/` prefix, while ensuring it can access newly uploaded objects. The solution should take minimal effort to implement and maintain. What should you do?

options.text: Enable fine-grained access control, and configure the uploader to set a per object access control list for the Cloud Run service identity to have the READER role when objects with the site1-data/ prefix are uploaded.
Create a new bucket to store only objects with the site1-data/ prefix. Grant the Cloud Run service identity the roles/storage.objectViewer IAM role on the project.
Create a new bucket to store only objects with the site1-data/ prefix. Grant the Cloud Run service identity the roles/storage.objectViewer IAM role on the bucket.

Enable uniform bucket-level access, and configure an IAM binding on the existing bucket. Grant the Cloud Run service identity the roles/storage.objectViewer IAM role on the bucket with an IAM condition for objects with the site1-data/ prefix.

questions.explanation:
Uniform bucket-level access permits IAM Conditions directly on a Cloud Storage bucket. A conditional bucket IAM binding for `roles/storage.objectViewer`, limited to object names with the `site1-data/` prefix, grants read access to both existing and future matching objects without maintaining individual object ACLs or creating and managing another bucket.

**Learn more:** [Set and manage IAM policies on buckets](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/using-iam-permissions) · [Uniform bucket-level access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/uniform-bucket-level-access)

questions.question: You plan to manage all your Google Cloud resources using Terraform. You have multiple applications that you want to manage independently. You need to organize your Terraform code repository to support this separation. What should you do?

options.text: Create a single module for each resource type, and place all modules in the same directory.
Put the Terraform configuration resources for each application in its own root directory.
Create a single module for each application, and place all modules in the same directory.
Put resources of the same type in their own root directory.

questions.explanation:
Terraform resources for each application should be placed in that application's own root directory. This creates independent root configurations and state boundaries, allowing each application to be planned and managed separately.\
\

questions.question: You plan to manage all your Google Cloud resources using Terraform. You have multiple applications that you want to manage independently. You need to organize your Terraform code repository to support this separation. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a VPC Network Peering connection between your VPC network and a VPC network with internet access.
Create a bastion host with an external IP address, and use it to connect to the VM using SSH.
Assign an internal static IP address to the VM.
Configure Cloud NAT for the subnet that the VM is in.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access for Compute Engine VMs that do not have external IP addresses. When it is configured to serve the VM’s subnet, the VM can use its internal IP address for outbound connections and receive only the corresponding response traffic, satisfying the restriction against assigning an external IP address to the VM.

**Learn more:** [Cloud NAT overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use the `gcloud container clusters create app-cluster` command to deploy a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster in a new Google Cloud project. The command fails with the following error:  
  
```text  
ERROR: (gcloud.container.clusters.create) ResponseError: code=403, message=Kubernetes Engine API has not been used in the project before or it is disabled.  
```  
  
You need to fix the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Rerun the command with the --enable-autoprovisioning flag.
Disable the “Require enabling Workload Identity Federation for GKE” organization policy, and then run the cluster creation command again.
Add the Kubernetes Engine Admin IAM role to your user account, and then run the cluster creation command again.
Run the gcloud services enable container.googleapis.com command, and then run the cluster creation command again.

questions.explanation:
GKE requires the Kubernetes Engine API to be enabled in the project before a cluster can be created. The GKE API service name is `container.googleapis.com`; enabling it with `gcloud services enable container.googleapis.com` satisfies this prerequisite.

**Learn more:** [Quickstart: Create a GKE cluster using Terraform](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/quickstarts/create-cluster-using-terraform) · [Kubernetes Engine API reference](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/reference/rest)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has created hundreds of service accounts for various applications hosted on-premises and in other clouds that use Google Cloud APIs. You must audit the service account keys that were created and identify keys older than 90 days. What should you do?

options.text: Execute the gcloud kms keys list--filter=“createTime < [DATE_90_DAYS_AGO]” command.
Execute the gcloud iam service-accounts list--filter=“createTime < [DATE_90_DAYS_AGO]” command.

Execute the gcloud asset search-all-resources--scope=“organizations/[ORG_ID]”--query=“createTime < [DATE_90_DAYS_AGO]”--asset-types=“iam.googleapis.com/ServiceAccountKey”--order-by=“createTime” command.
Execute the gcloud asset search-all-resources--scope=“organizations/[ORG_ID]”--query=“createTime < [DATE_90_DAYS_AGO]”--asset-types=“apikeys.googleapis.com/Key”--order-by=“createTime” command.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Asset Inventory supports organization-scoped resource searches, filtering on `createTime`, and the `iam.googleapis.com/ServiceAccountKey` asset type. Restricting the search to that asset type and querying for creation times older than the 90-day cutoff returns the relevant service account keys across the organization.

**Learn more:** [Search for resources | Cloud Asset Inventory](https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/search-resources) · [Asset names | Cloud Asset Inventory](https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/asset-names)

You administer your company’s Google Cloud environment. Your company has a budget and wants to centralize cost management by consolidating every project under one Cloud Billing account. The finance team needs a daily export of all billing data to a central BigQuery dataset for analysis, including resource-level cost data. You must implement the most cost-effective solution with minimal administrative overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Link each project to the Cloud Billing account. Create a new Cloud Billing budget alert with Pub/Sub as the destination, and use a Cloud Run function to write the alerts to BigQuery.
Link each project to the Cloud Billing account. Enable the standard and detailed usage cost exports on the billing account, specifying a BigQuery dataset as the destination.
Link each project to the Cloud Billing account. Enable the standard usage cost export on the billing account, specifying a BigQuery dataset as the destination.

Link each project to the Cloud Billing account. Use the gcloud billing budgets create command to set a budget for each project, and then use the cost breakdown report in the Google Cloud console to manually export the daily costs.

questions.explanation:
Standard and detailed usage-cost exports are configured once on a Cloud Billing account and include usage and cost data for every Google Cloud project paid by that account. The detailed export adds granular resource-level costs, while the standard export provides the standard cost dataset. Cloud Billing automatically exports the data to the selected BigQuery dataset, avoiding custom processing and manual daily exports.

**Learn more:** [Set up Cloud Billing data export to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery-setup) · [Structure of detailed usage cost data export](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery-tables/detailed-usage)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage your company's archival records in a Cloud Storage bucket that uses the Multi-Regional storage class. These objects are seldom accessed after 90 days but must be kept indefinitely for regulatory compliance.  
  
You need a cost-effective process that automatically moves these objects to the lowest-cost storage class appropriate for long-term retention immediately after the 90-day period. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Object Versioning on the bucket, and create an Object Lifecycle Management rule that sets the daysSinceNoncurrentTime condition to 90 days, transitioning noncurrent versions to Archive storage.
Create an Object Lifecycle Management rule on the bucket that specifies an age condition of 90 days and uses the SetStorageClass action to transition the objects to Archive storage.
Create a nightly scheduled Cloud Run function that uses the Cloud Storage API to change the storage class of all objects older than 90 days to Archive storage.
Create an Object Lifecycle Management rule on the bucket that specifies the createdBefore condition set to 90 days ago and uses the Delete action to remove the objects.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management can automatically apply `SetStorageClass` when an object reaches a specified `age`. Setting `age` to 90 days and the target class to Archive transitions the retained objects to Archive storage, which is intended for long-term, rarely accessed data. This preserves the objects rather than deleting them and does not depend on object versions becoming noncurrent.

**Learn more:** [Object Lifecycle Management | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle) · [Configuration examples for Object Lifecycle Management | Cloud Storage | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle-configurations)
